title: Mercedes Power Converter decouples high-voltage supply from battery state - electrive.com
content:
Automobile
Mercedes is developing new technology to constantly provide a voltage of 800 volts in electric vehicles. With current technology, the system voltage is directly dependent on the state of the battery cells. In the future, Mercedes wants to use a so-called Power Converter that bypasses this dependency through individual micro-converters per cell unit.
Image: Mercedes-Benz
Mercedes has announced a new architecture for electric vehicles that uses advanced power electronics to decouple the high-voltage supply from the battery’s state of charge.
In conventional electric vehicles, the system voltage is determined by the number of battery cells connected in series. As the state of charge decreases, this voltage drops during operation. Ageing or weakened cells also impair the performance of the entire battery pack.
Decentralised microconverters replace conventional cell series connection
Mercedes’ Power Converters function as individual decentralised microconverters, controlling individual battery cells or cell clusters. Multiple parallel-connected Power Converters coordinate energy flows and prevent voltage fluctuations by maintaining a stable DC high-voltage supply.
The control system selectively relieves weaker cells, increasing overall efficiency. Functions such as AC and DC charging, as well as bidirectional charging, can be integrated into the electronic devices. The converter has a power output of up to three kilowatts.
Omitting the on-board charger saves weight and space
The main advantage of this design lies in the consolidation of previously separate components. Since the new microconverters can handle the conversion of AC and DC voltage directly, the conventional, separate on-board charger (OBC) can be omitted from the vehicle. This saves weight, space and production costs.
At the same time, the traction inverter always receives a constant input of 800 volts and no longer needs to be designed for fluctuating input voltages. This improves its efficiency and makes it easier to use identical powertrain components across different drivetrain concepts.
Potential for OTA features and digital business models
It remains to be seen if there is a greater repair effort required for the more complex technology directly at the battery. At the same time, the microconverters already provide physical prerequisites ex-works that mean functions like bidirectional charging and maximum charging power can be controlled purely via software. This is likely to open up new opportunities for the manufacturer to offer paid over-the-air unlocks.

title: Hadfield takes over as CEO of Nyrstar – Batteries International
content: Trafigura-owned Nyrstar said on November 3 it had appointed Matt Hadfield as group CEO with immediate effect. He succeeds Guido Janssen, who has stepped down after leading Nyrstar for the past four years and now becomes CTO — focusing on what Nyrstar said were technology priorities key to the group’s transformation. Hadfield was previously chief transformation officer for Netherlands-headquartered Nyrstar and head of metals and minerals assets in Trafigura’s operating assets division. Nyrstar’s said its European leadership team and Wendy McMillan — who was appointed CEO of Nyrstar’s Australian business in July 2026 — will report to Hadfield. Jiri Zrust, Trafigura’s global head of operating assets, said Hadfield had extensive experience of the metals industry, deep knowledge of Nyrstar’s operations and expertise in leading complex change. “The metals Nyrstar produces are essential to economic, military and national security, and the transformation of its operations is a strategic priority for Trafigura as its owner. Matt is well placed to drive this transformation, with the aim of recovering additional critical raw materials, driving technological improvements and securing the long-term competitiveness of the business.” Batteries International reported last October that the future of Nyrstar’s Budel zinc smelter in the Netherlands was uncertain after the group launched a review against a backdrop of soaring energy costs and geopolitical instability. The review will consider future options for the site which produces zinc and zinc alloys, sulfuric acid and ‘Budel Leach Product’ — containing lead and precious metals used as a raw material by secondary smelters. title: TAA Compliance Shapes Battery Strategy in America’s Drone Market
content:
Industry Outlook
Battery Applications
Battery News
Industry Trends
Enovix and Rincell show how TAA compliance and battery supply chains are shaping federal opportunities in the US drone market.
November 3, 2026
4 Min Read
A soldier participates in a drone drop resupply demonstration in coordination with the Army Applications Laboratory at Fort Hood, Texas.
Army Capt. Jasmine Mathews
According to Research and Markets, the U.S. drone
market was valued
at $14.70B in 2025, and it is projected to grow to $44.19B by 2036, representing a CAGR of 9.8% during the 2026-2036 forecast period. That growth reflects expanding demand across defense, public safety, infrastructure inspection, logistics, and industrial operations. As the market matures, more drone manufacturers and component suppliers are looking beyond commercial sales and toward federal procurement opportunities. In that environment, compliance becomes strategic, and one of the most important frameworks to understand is the Trade Agreements Act, or TAA.
Why TAA matters for batteries in government procurement
At the Battery Show North America, during the Chairman's Welcome Address,
John Warner said
that one of the forces currently shaping the battery sector is defense, which is becoming a new center of gravity for the battery industry. For battery manufacturers and drone companies looking to sell to the US government market, the Trade Agreements Act, or TAA, is a key part of the compliance landscape. At a basic level, TAA governs the country of origin of products sold under certain US government contracts. To qualify, an item generally must be manufactured in the United States or in a designated country, or it must be substantially transformed there into a new and different product.
Related:
Batteries & the Ballot: Grading Washington's Mixed Record on EVs in 2026
But batteries complicate the issue. A battery includes cells, cathode and anode materials, battery management systems, enclosures, and other electronics, often sourced from multiple countries. That complexity has become even more significant as US drone makers try to reduce exposure to Chinese inputs. As Bloomberg
, “US drone makers have sought new sources domestically and among American allies while trying to ensure that subcomponents aren’t sourced in China, but securing supplies while maintaining quality and keeping prices down is difficult.” That quote captures the sector's commercial reality. Compliance goals may be clear, but execution is harder when companies must also protect performance, scale production, and remain cost competitive.
Air Force Senior Airman Kaleb Heard operates a drone during counter-small unmanned aerial systems training. Courtesy of Airman 1st Class Stassney Davis.
A battery can directly affect whether a drone is suitable for surveillance, inspection, logistics, or defense applications. If the drone manufacturer is selling to the Department of Defense, a civilian federal agency, or an integrator serving those customers, battery sourcing may receive close scrutiny. A drone assembled in the US could still face procurement challenges if one of its key components fails origin requirements under a contract that includes TAA obligations.
Related:
John Warner Maps Four Trends Transforming Today’s Battery Industry
US companies positioning around TAA compliance
Enovix: This US battery manufacturer shows how companies are using TAA compliance to expand government-facing drone opportunities. The company said its drone and defense battery portfolio, manufactured in South Korea, is TAA-compliant, helping broaden its ability to serve US government defense programs. The company framed the issue not simply as a regulatory achievement, but as a way to strengthen access to defense programs and to support customers through a more trusted supply chain. As Ryan Benton, Interim Chief Executive Officer of Enovix, put it, “Achieving TAA compliance, combined with our planned capacity expansion in South Korea, strengthens our ability to support that mission with high-performance batteries produced at scale through a trusted supply chain.”
Rincell RC50T Drone 6S3P and 6S4P Battery Packs. Courtesy of Rincell.
Rincell: This American company is another example. Rincell operates a pilot production line at its headquarters in Fremont, California. The company has partnered with Re:Build Manufacturing to build a full-scale domestic battery cell manufacturing facility, with U.S. commercial production slated to come online in late 2027. Once operational, these US manufactured cells will be fully TAA-compliant.
Related:
Peak Energy’s Dr. Lucy Li on Sodium-Ion Battery Innovations
Through its partnership with First Breach,
is supporting US drone manufacturing with its battery systems. According to the company, Rincell's RC41 (4.1Ah 18650) and RC58 (5.8Ah 21700) cell characteristics enable longer flight times, faster turnaround, and superior cold‑weather performance—all critical for the
Drone Dominance Gauntlet
evaluations and future battlefield use.
As federal demand for drones accelerates, battery sourcing is becoming a strategic factor in market access. Enovix and Rincell show two different but aligned approaches: building trusted supply chains, expanding production in compliant locations, and positioning advanced battery technology for defense and government applications. In a drone market defined by performance, resilience, and origin scrutiny, the companies that can deliver all three will be best placed to win the next wave of federal opportunities.

Guerra's career spans power systems engineering, oil & gas consulting, and technical writing and editing. She worked for several years at Kellogg, Brown & Root Ltd. title: EV Motors Move Beyond Rare Earth Magnets
content:
Automotive & Mobility
Design & Manufacturing
Carmakers and suppliers explore magnet-free motor designs to cut reliance on Chinese rare earth supply chains.
November 3, 2026
10 Min Read
The 2027 BMW iX3 M60 xDrive EV uses no rare earth elements in its magnet-free traction motors.
At a Glance
Bosch is building supply bases outside China to manage disruption risk
Niron targets 2029 to 2032 for rare-earth-free automotive magnets
BMW and Mercedes already sell EVs using magnet-free motor designs
Rare earth materials such as neodymium and dysprosium are crucial to the power and efficiency of the permanent magnets used in most EV motors. The total amount of these materials used in each EV motor isn’t great, 200 grams for neodymium and 30g for dysprosium,
according to the US Geological Survey
But in aggregate, the volume of these materials is great, and it's growing. IDTechEx estimates that the
market will balloon to $9.19B
What’s rare about rare earths?
The name “rare earth elements” is something of a misnomer, because they aren’t really that rare,
reports the International Energy Agency
. “Though relatively plentiful in the Earth’s crust, this set of 17 elements has garnered the label ‘rare’ because economically viable concentrations are uncommon and they are seldom found in pure form,” the report stated. “Their chemical similarities make them hard to separate during the extraction process.”
The IDTechEx report describes the refining process that follows extraction from the ground:
“Ores are crushed and milled to liberate minerals, which are then concentrated. Separation – the technical core of processing – converts mixed rare earth feeds into individual oxides. Refined oxides are then transformed into metals, and then into alloy powders, the primary inputs for magnet production.”
The extraction and processing challenges are the factors that create environmental challenges and supply chain risks, despite their relatively broad distribution in the Earth’s crust. This causes them to be considered critical minerals, just like harder-to-find elements like
cobalt and nickel used in EV batteries
“Rare earth elements used in magnets are critical materials, with highly consolidated supply from China and increasing economic importance,” stated the report, “
Rare Earth Magnets 2026-236: Technologies, Supply, Markets, Forecasts
,” by IDTechEx. “China represents 69% of global rare earth element mining in 2025, with this share increasing towards 90% moving downstream through rare earth separation, metallization, and magnet production stages.”
China’s dominance and supply chain risk
Potential supply chain risks concern some carmakers more than others, reports Jason Schwanke, director of traction machine and e-axle engineering for Bosch Mobility USA, which supplies EV motors to carmakers.
“The material side of things is complicated, both the raw materials and also the processing of those materials,” he said. “At Bosch, we're really, from a robustness standpoint, developing supply bases outside of China to be able to manage that should some disruption occur. Some customers are very concerned, some are not. Some are perfectly comfortable with the way that things are, and we continue to make machines in that space.”
Bosch's Global e-Axle uses less rare earth material than conventional electric motors. BOSCH
Companies with a clearer recall of the dire supply chain failures during the pandemic might be less interested in finding out the hard way a second time, and weaning their products away from the use of largely Chinese-sourced rare earths would provide a beneficial insurance policy against unwelcome shocks in the future.
The reason permanent magnet electric motors need rare earth elements is that they provide resilience for the magnet. “We call them permanent magnets, but they can be demagnetized, especially at temperature,” explained Schwanke. “That's what those materials are doing. They're diffused inside the magnets, and you add more and more of them, as you need to have higher and higher temperature resilience.”
Bosch has recently introduced permanent magnet
EV motors that have reduced rare earth content
. They achieved this by improving the motors’ cooling, which reduces the need for the magnets to be heat-tolerant. The let Bosch entirely eliminate so-called heavy rare earths, such as dysprosium and terbium, Schwanke said.
With this in mind, shouldn’t the auto industry be looking to move away from the need for rare earth elements in its EV motors? “It's a valid question, and it's one that everybody should be asking,” said Paul Waatti, Director, Industry Analysis for Autopacific. “The short answer is 'Yeah, there are ways they can shift away.' They have alternatives. I know that some of these manufacturers, in the last 12 months, have put out publicly that they're endeavoring to find alternative ways to run their vehicles, not having to rely on these rare earths and these magnets.”
Reducing or eliminating rare earths in magnets
To eliminate rare earths entirely, there are two paths: EV motors whose magnets have no rare earth elements in them, or EV motors that have no magnets in them. Start-up magnet technology company Niron Magnetics is pursuing this first path, with investments from carmakers General Motors, Honda, and Stellantis and industry supplier Magna.
“If you've got two kilograms of permanent magnets that can stop you from selling $100,000 electric car, you're going to take that really seriously,” said Karl Sprentall, vice president, commercial for Niron. The company is developing iron nitride permanent magnets for EV applications to replace today’s rare-earth-containing magnets.
The rotor in a Niron iron nitride electric motor. NIRON
“Our magnets are made just with essentially waste products from the steel-making industry,” he said. “So it's a much cleaner proposition. But you know, if I were to rank it today, I would say for the majority of customers, the supply chain is the predominant factor to look at alternatives.”
Niron is making good progress toward mass-producing magnets for automotive applications, with a window between 2029 and 2032 as the most likely time when cars using the company’s magnets would hit the road, Sprentall said.
Bosch is watching this space, according to Schwanke. “Bosch is actively researching alternative permanent magnets,” he said. “We're quite familiar in that space because we make a lot of motors with ferrites and other type of cores. There is always a possibility to do this.”
But Schwanke voiced some concerns. “There are trade-offs. When you look at the requirements for passenger car applications being quite demanding, and that we have a lot of cases that we have to consider that are kind of corner cases, what we call them, to protect the machine over its lifetime against any damage or degradation, you do have some fundamental challenges there.” So-called “boost axles” that assist a hybrid-electric drivetrain might be a more immediate application than battery EVs, he suggested.
But magnet-free induction motors are already in some EVs, and that could be the easiest path to avoiding rare earth elements. “I think the inductive motors, I think that they've already been put out and some of these vehicles are already operating out in the real world right now,” said Luke Wray, Senior Vice President of Critical Materials & Defense at Paladin Envirotech. “I think that's the lowest barrier to entry, and they can probably stand something up relatively quickly.”
The challenge is convincing the industry to consider switching to inductive EV motors. “When it comes to permanent magnet machines, they're generally very hard to beat when it comes to power and torque density, especially with the efficiencies that you get,” Schwanke noted. “When you talk about induction motors, induction motors are very attractive at light loads. They tend to have a lot of issues at low speeds and at very high loads,” such as launching a heavy EV from a stop.
“If you're trying to make the most efficient EV motor possible, magnets are always going to have a strong role to play in that,” echoed Niron’s Sprentall. “So, like anything, it's ‘What trade-offs are the OEMs willing to make?’”
Magnet-free motor alternatives
There are a few options for companies considering a move to magnet-free EV motors. BMW applies two of these technologies to its EVs today: electrically excited synchronous motor (EESM) and asynchronous motor (ASM) technology. EESM motors are also known as wound-rotor synchronous motors (WRSM).
BMW's EESM rear motor. BMW
In the company’s latest EV models, the rear axle is driven by an EESM motor, which BMW says has “excellent levels of efficiency in customer-relevant operating points and consistent power output at high rotational speeds.” Its efficiency is critical for achieving the long driving distance between recharges that customers demand.
The ASM motors are used to drive the front axle in BMW’s new cars. These boast a more compact design, lower cost, and lighter weight as their advantages. The increased efficiency of the drivetrain contributes an extra 53 miles of driving range for BMW’s 6
-generation EV models compared to their predecessors, according to the company. Total driving range for the BMW iX3 is 500 miles on Europe’s lenient WLTP test cycle.
BMW's more compact ASM front motor. BMW
Lenient or not, anything close to 500 miles of range should satisfy customers and leave BMW pondering whether the car’s battery is bigger, heavier, and more expensive than it really needs to be in this car. Additionally, the iX3 is rated at a combined 603 horsepower and 645 lb.-ft. of torque for the two motors, good enough to vault the car to 62 mph (100 kph) in just 3.9 seconds.
These are the motors that magnet advocates say aren’t sufficiently efficient or muscular to satisfy customers, but BMW is delivering them today.
Axial-flux motors and cost vs. performance
For still more power, there’s yet another magnet-free electric motor technology:
axial-flux motors
. This design reorients the way the magnetic field is applied inside the motor. They have the advantage of being both smaller and more powerful than conventional radial-flux motors, thanks to the larger diameter letting the magnetic field apply greater leverage to the output shaft.
The teardown and analysis gurus at
Munro Live disassembled a commercially available Chinese axial-flux motor
to get a look at what makes them tick. Looking at the pieces helps clarify the difference between these and radial-flux motors, and Munro Live lead engineer Paul Turnbull marveled at the motor’s design and construction.
YASA claims
that its motor produces 480 hp and 590 lb.-ft. of torque from a device that weighs only 53 lbs. and occupies 610 cubic inches (5 liters) of volume. A comparable radial-flux motor produces only 250 hp and 285 lb.-ft. of torque, while weighing more than twice as much and occupying double the volume.
Axial-flux motors have existed for many years in industrial applications, but manufacturing them in volume for automotive requirements was daunting. British start-up YASA overcame the obstacles so successfully that Mercedes-Benz, a company with a history of technical pride, acquired YASA and now builds motors using its technology for the new
Mercedes-AMG AMG GT Coupe
SUV models
. The Coupe boasts 1,153 horsepower and a 435-mile driving range, all without magnets in its motors.
Axial-flux versus radial-flux EV motor construction. TURNTIDE TECHNOLOGIES
The challenge here is currently the cost of building axial-flux motors and the value of their impressive performance. Stefan Weckbach, Chairman of the Board of Management of Mercedes-AMG, explained that his brand’s high-performance models have unique requirements that demand technical solutions such as axial-flux motors and liquid-cooled battery packs that aren’t necessary for mainstream Mercedes-Benz models, dashing hopes that Mercedes could see these magnet-free motors trickle down through the product line.
An exploded view of a YASA axial-flux electric motor used in the AMG GT Coupe and SUV. DAN CARNEY
“Talking AMG only, we need to invest, and we will invest in this technology, and we will be ready, willing, and able to spend a little bit more money on that technology because it is important for the positioning of our cars, for our price point as well,” said Weckbach during a media roundtable discussion in Stuttgart. “Maybe that is not true for all Mercedes models, or not required for all Mercedes models, because they are simply positioned in a different segment of the market.”
Nevertheless, BMW is showing the way for companies to simultaneously reduce their bill of materials and their exposure to supply chain interruptions while reducing the demand for environmentally disruptive mining operations.

title: Gartner Explores the Impact of AI on Supply Chain Headcounts
content:
Gartner Explores the Impact of AI on Supply Chain Headcounts
Prioritise Us
on Google
The number of entry-level job roles is decreasing. Credit: Gartner
Tess Frenzel, Director Analyst in Gartner’s Supply Chain practice, explores how the integration of AI has reduced entry level roles and company headcount
Supply chains as we know them are changing. As pressure to do more has increased, as too have ambitions for cost savings.
With the integration of AI becoming a more focused strategy, there is less hiring for entry level jobs.
As a result, the workforce is thinning, and supply chain roles are being redefined.
AI in the workplace
According to Gartner, supply chains around the world are reducing headcounts, falling in direct
consequence of the influence of AI
. Gartner surveyed 303 leaders from across North America, Western Europe, Asia-Pacific and Latin America.
Respondents represented organisations which had integrated AI into their operations and each had visibility into or influence over the AI strategy.
The findings revealed that nearly half of supply chains have reduced headcount by an average of 10.5% over the past two years. Looking at these figures closer, 66% of supply chain leaders state this is concentrated at the entry level.
“AI is thinning the entry-level supply chain workforce faster than most chief supply chain officers (CSCOs) are redesigning the talent pipeline, creating a future capability gap that will actually weaken their organisations’ AI performance,” explains Tess Frenzel, Director Analyst in Gartner’s Supply Chain practice.
Tess Frenzel, Director Analyst in Gartner’s Supply Chain practice
“While impacts to entry-level positions from AI continue to grab the most attention, our research also shows a notable change in expectations for the skills required for middle-management positions, compared with just two years ago.
“Producing fewer candidates for traditionally defined leadership roles is a miscalculation, as supply chains will require new competencies both for entry-level and leadership positions as a result of working alongside AI.”
At a glance
47% of supply chains have reduced headcount by an average of 10.5% in the last two years
66% of leaders report it being concentrated at the entry level
Headcount at the executive level has stayed the same, according to 64% of leaders
Gartner recommends entry level employees should be paired with mid- and senior-level employees
Headcount has increased by 9% for mid/senior level employees
Headcount reduction is not evenly spread. Credit: Gartner
Supply chain leadership
The integration of AI in conjunction with the reduction of entry-level roles demonstrates where AI is being used. It coincides with repetitive tasks that entry-level roles typically take on, with more admin and research responsibilities.
While these are often seen as easily-automated positions, they are a critical part of the talent pipeline. Gartner warns that reducing hiring in entry-level positions without making changes to role responsibilities creates
fragility in the workplace ecosystem
Without a strong field of entry level employees, there is a much smaller talent pool to hire into the more senior positions. In traditional supply chain organisations, there is significant upskilling and internal hiring – the entry level workforces produce qualified candidates for senior positions along the line.
Gartner also found that companies who have strong AI integration, AI-enabled automation and defined business outcomes are redefining entry level roles.
“Compared with two years ago, these organisations require more domain-specific and analytics skills and greater supply chain experience, while involving entry-level employees in less repetitive work and more consequential decisions,” Tess adds.
“This approach can attract and engage higher-skilled talent while better preparing employees to advance into the senior positions which will also evolve as AI is embedded within the organisation.”
As businesses are cutting entry-level headcounts, they need to be more nurturing with staff to increase management potential. Credit: Getty Images
Growing talent pipelines
In order to capitalise on the implementation of AI in the supply chain, Gartner recommends CSCOs need to elevate entry-level roles. This way, they will encourage stronger talent pipelines and more effective AI outcomes.
Gartner recommends that technically skilled entry-level employees should be paired with mid- and senior-level employees in order to develop stronger business results. In doing this, there will be a nurturing of emerging talent, better workplace relationships and more capabilities in supporting AI deployment and oversight.
Alongside this, there should be more visibility into AI use, with regular tests on the assumptions and data that are forming the AI models. Following this, there should be clear accountability assigned for outcomes.
Leaders also need to adopt cross-pollinated supply chain team structures. This will result in more aligned KPIs and a more diverse knowledge base across high-value AI deployments.
As headcount in supply chain roles decreases, it is the responsibility of leadership to ensure the talent the teams adopt is being nurtured. Without changes to the definition of the entry-level role, there will be limited growth opportunities and a lack of skill to take on management positions.
Gartner recommends that leaders need to invest time and
training into nurturing the skills
of those hired in the minimising entry-level positions.
Supply chains will require new competencies both for entry-level and leadership positions as a result of working alongside AI.
Tess Frenzel, Director Analyst in Gartner’s Supply Chain practice
Key companies
Gartner is a global research and advisory firm providing insights to executives and their teams across enterprise functions. With expertise spanning technology, supply chain, finance, and HR, Gartner delivers actionable research through syndicated reports, consulting engagements, and conferences. Their supply chain practice helps CSCOs navigate digital transformation, AI integration, talent strategies, and operational resilience, serving thousands of organisations worldwide with data-driven recommendations for strategic decision-making.

title: IFS Softeon launches Warehouse AI for supply chain logistics
content:
IFS Softeon launches Warehouse AI for supply chain logistics
Prioritise Us
on Google
IFS Softeon has introduced a new agentic AI tool to bring context-aware intelligence into warehouse fulfilment operations. Credit: IFS
Mark Fralick, CTO at IFS Softeon, on how Industrial AI and digital workers optimise inventory management across global supply chain logistics
The increasing sophistication of warehouse management systems (WMS) offers multiple opportunities for agentic AI to improve decision-making across planning, sourcing, manufacturing and delivery steps.
However, operational data from modern fulfilment centres can be siloed between inbound orders, labour deployment and inventories. Without integration, interpreting this information has tended to result in isolated optimisation, such as improving wave planning at the expense of replenishment, for instance.
To meet this demand and optimise critical logistics networks, IFS Softeon has launched Fulfillment Flow, a context-aware Industrial AI capability designed to streamline material handling, labor management, and inventory replenishment for enterprise fulfilment centres.
IFS Softeon's Fulfillment Flow is built from the WMS model up, so the context is native rather than bolted on
Context-Aware Intelligence in Logistics
Fulfillment Flow fundamentally addresses this challenge by bringing contextual intelligence into the actual flow of warehouse operations. Rather than forcing supervisors to toggle between multiple screens and static reports, the system evaluates how a single decision impacts the entire facility, including adjacencies like receiving yards and manufacturing line feeds, ensuring adaptive, continuously optimised material handling.
"Fulfillment Flow brings AI directly into the flow of warehouse operations, where decisions are being made every day," says Mark Fralick, CTO at IFS Softeon.
Mark Fralick, IFS Softeon CTO
Digital Workers and Inventory Management
At the core of the Fulfillment Flow platform are "digital workers" - specialised AI agents dedicated to discrete operational zones such as inbound logistics, wave management, labour allocation, and outbound shipping. The AI agents monitor live operations and escalate optimisation opportunities to a central operational agent.
"A generic AI system may be able to tell you that orders are behind schedule, but the real value comes from understanding what is driving that situation, what other operational factors are involved, and what can be done about it. The warehouse manager stays in control. That’s what builds the trust AI needs to actually work on the floor," Mark adds.
Driven by a human-in-the-loop architecture, Fulfillment Flow empowers supply chain managers to query the system using natural language. The AI provides next-best-action recommendations based on current facility conditions, allowing warehouse teams to rapidly identify bottlenecks in order delivery while human supervisors execute the final decisions.
Key facts
Fulfillment Flow utilises six core intelligence pillars to monitor live facility operations, site goals, and equipment dependencies
The platform deploys specialised AI agents to actively manage wave planning, slotting, and inbound/outbound logistics
Industrial AI integration eliminates data silos, generating real-time, next-best-action recommendations for warehouse managers
The human-in-the-loop architecture ensures human logistics supervisors retain final decision-making authority over all automated suggestions
IFS operates globally, and employs a workforce of over 7,000 personnel spanning 80 countries
Key Supply Chain and Technology Partners
Microsoft -
Microsoft provides the foundational cloud computing architecture that enables IFS Softeon’s advanced Industrial AI applications. By leveraging scalable Azure environments, IFS can deploy digital workers and process massive supply chain datasets in real-time. This ensures high-performance connectivity and data security for 3PLs managing complex fulfilment centres and global distribution networks to meet strict consumer demands.
Accenture
Accenture serves as a premier systems integration and consulting partner for IFS deployments within the global supply chain sector. The consultancy assists enterprise logistics organizations in redesigning their warehouse management workflows to maximize the benefits of Fulfillment Flow. Accenture’s deep industry expertise ensures smooth digital transformations, aligning AI-driven automation with broader operational efficiency goals and inventory accuracy.
GXO Logistics -
Global 3PLs like GXO Logistics represent the ideal end-users for context-aware Industrial AI. Operating large-scale fulfilment centres for blue-chip retail brands, these logistics providers require highly efficient warehouse operations to distribute goods accurately and rapidly. Utilising advanced software like IFS Softeon enables complex logistics networks to optimise inventory visibility and meet strict consumer delivery SLAs.

title: Cyber Attack on Supermarket Freezers Targets Control Systems
content:
Cyber Attack on Supermarket Freezers Targets Control Systems
Prioritise Us
on Google
ICA's central systems have not been affected by the cyber attack, which appeared to target stores outside ICA's centrally managed store network, ICA's Press Manager confirmed. (Credit: ICA)
ICA, Coop and Delhaize suffer cyber attack as hackers appear to target 3rd party refrigeration and freezer control systems, forcing units into defrost mode
A widespread cyberattack has disrupted food retailers and supply chains across Europe, impacting retailers across multiple jurisdictions, including Delhaize locations in Belgium and Luxembourg, ICA and Coop outlets and an Ikea store in Sweden, SuperValu in Ireland, Selver in Estonia, several Finnish K-stores, and 17 businesses across the Netherlands.
"The refrigeration and freezer systems at 23 ICA stores have been affected. Eight of the stores have had to dispose of refrigerated and frozen products, while the impact on the remaining stores has been more limited," Mattias Elander Forsgren, ICA press manager, confirms to Supply Chain Digital.
In ICA's case, the cyberattack appears to have targeted refrigeration and freezer control systems supplied by an external provider. "ICA’s central systems have not been affected by the incident. All affected stores had their equipment connected outside ICA’s centrally managed store network," Mattias confirms. "ICA is supporting the affected stores in areas including IT security, food safety and logistics."
The affected retailers have been forced to dispose of tons of spoiled stock after threat actors switched evaporator units into defrost mode.
Piles of spoiled food had to be thrown out post-incident, where freezer temperatures rose in a cyberattack affecting seven countries in Europe
The disruption has also spread to the UK supply chain, where a small number of freezers belonging to members of the British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers saw temperatures spike to 100°C.
The incidents mirror an attack vector observed weeks earlier in France, where hundreds of supermarket units were compromised by threat actors exploiting
vulnerabilities
in exposed remote-management interfaces.
NCSC warning: AI velocity meets legacy infrastructure
The wave of attacks landed alongside the release of the NCSC’s State of the Cyber Nation report, which cautions that AI adoption among hostile actors will “highly likely” amplify the velocity, scale, and efficiency of vulnerability exploitation, ransomware, and social engineering campaigns over the next two years.
A former executive at the NCSC, Alex Harland, co-founder and CEO of London-based AI governance and risk management platform AI Score, warns that the widespread adoption of AI is
"creat[ing] a new layer of enterprise risk that rivals the traditional cyber landscape in its complexity. Yet many organisations are still trying to manage it using tools and processes that weren’t built for AI’s speed, scale or autonomy. You can’t simply bolt AI governance onto existing cybersecurity controls and expect them to work."
ICA was one of several stores impacted by the cyberattack, in which hackers appear to have targeted refrigeration and freezer control systems supplied by an external provider. Credit: ICA
AI is making traditional cyber
more acute, but it is also introducing an entirely new set of risks as organisations embed AI into their workflows, products, processes and systems, often without the visibility needed to understand what’s actually happening
Alex Harland, CEO of AI Score
Quick facts
Hackers compromised commercial refrigeration and evaporator units, triggering unauthorised defrost cycles.
Outages impacted retailers across Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, Ireland, Finland, Estonia and the Netherlands.
UK meat suppliers under AIMS saw specialised storage temperatures spike up to 100°C.
Threat actors exploited unpatched vulnerabilities in internet-exposed remote management interfaces.
NCSC declared attribution unconfirmed while executing overnight mitigation alerts to exposed facilities.
Industrial cyber defence
Industry practitioners emphasise that OT
vulnerabilities
and legacy architectural debt have made such attacks an immediate reality rather than a distant projection.
“Perhaps the worst element of this report is the timing,” says Marie Wilcox, Vice President of Market Strategy at automated cyber investigation platform Binalyze. “In the weeks since the NCSC’s reporting closed, PHP2Shell showed how a combination of AI and loose lips can turn flaws that have sat undisturbed in widely used software for years into a grenade.
“The NCSC’s right that we face a decade of AI-driven change. But the timeline is measured in weeks, not years. Patching ageing systems and layering new tools over environments that were never built for today’s threats has run its course. Operators will be forced to rip out and replace legacy technology, with security and continuous visibility built in from the start.
“Someone has to pay for that. The UK has committed to spending 5% of GDP on defence and resilience by 2035, and protecting the systems that keep the lights on and the water running should be near the top of the list. But replacement will take years, and attackers won’t wait. In the here and now organisations need to urgently know if they’ve been breached, what’s been affected and if the attackers are still there. It’s a two-stage process, and the short terms is just as important as the long term goal.”
Cited companies
: ICA is a leading Swedish grocery retailer managing an extended supply chain across the Nordic region. The company operates a decentralised model supported by robust central logistics and cold storage infrastructure. As a major distributor, securing ICA's temperature-controlled operational technology and warehouse networks is a key supply chain focus.
: Operating as a cooperative retail chain in Sweden, Coop manages an extensive food distribution and logistics network. The organization relies heavily on automated cold chain infrastructure to transport and store perishable goods.
Delhaize
: Delhaize is a prominent Belgian supermarket chain and part of the global Ahold Delhaize retail group. The company oversees a sophisticated, high-volume grocery logistics network.

title: Kia EV7 revealed as an upcoming midsize electric SUV
content:
Peter Johnson
| Nov 4 2026 - 7:15 am PT
Kia is crushing it with a full lineup of electric vehicles ranging from entry-level SUVs to the three-row EV9 and PV5 van. A leaked document revealed that
plans to add the EV7, a new midsize electric SUV, to fill the gap between the EV6 and the three-row EV9.
Kia EV7 is coming as a new midsize electric SUV
With 291,219 vehicles
sold last month
, up 10.3% from October 2025, Kia posted its eighth consecutive month of year-over-year sales growth.
Kia said it plans to build on the momentum by focusing on electrified vehicles in key markets, including hybrids in the US and fully electric vehicles in Europe.
After launching the EV2 earlier this year, Kia now offers one of the most complete EV lineups, including the EV2, EV3, EV4, EV5, EV6, EV9, and PV5 van.
According to a recently leaked document, a new midsize electric SUV will join the lineup.
KoreanCarBlog
uncovered an internal document from Kia’s Employment Stability Committee that reveals the company’s upcoming production plans.
The report claims “production of mid-range electric SUV ‘EV7’ to proceed” at Kia’s Gwangju factory in South Korea.
Although no other details were revealed, the EV7 will be a midsize electric SUV, slotted between the EV6 and three-row EV9.
During its
2026 CEO Investor Day
in April, Kia announced plans to expand its EV lineup to 14 models by 2030.
In Europe, Kia plans for EVs to account for 66% of sales by 2030, with a full lineup that includes the EV2, EV3, EV4, EV5, EV6, EV9, three PBVs, a new C-segment electric SUV, and its first “SDV B-segment hatchback.”
Kia reveals plans to launch its first software-defined electric vehicle (Source: Kia)
So what can we expect from the upcoming EV7? Kia said earlier this year that it’s developing a new EV platform “to significantly enhance both product performance and cost competitiveness.”
Although it didn’t offer specifics, Kia claimed the new EV platform delivers up to a 40% increase in battery capacity and a 9% improvement in motor output.
It will use Kia’s fifth-generation batteries, providing up to 15% higher energy density than its current tech.
Kia’s upcoming software-defined vehicles (SDVs) are expected to integrate Hyundai’s SDV architecture (CODA), Pleos Connect infotainment system, and Gleo AI, an in-vehicle Agenic AI.They will also have Level 2++ autonomous driving capabilities on highways.
, Kia’s current midsize electric SUV, is 4,615 mm long, 1,875 mm wide, and 1,675 mm tall, with a 2,750 mm wheelbase, which is about the size of the Sportage, so you can expect the EV7 to be slightly bigger. It will likely be closer in size to the Sorento.
Powered by an 81.4 kWh battery, the Kia’s current EV5 offers a WLTP range of up to 329 miles (530 km).
Kia EV5 (Source: Kia)
However, unlike the EV6 and EV9, the EV5 uses a 400V electrical architecture rather than an 800V. As a result, charging the battery from 10% to 80% takes about 30 minutes, rather than 18 to 25 minutes. The upcoming EV7 will likely use the 800V system for faster charging.
The document also revealed Kia will begin production of “completely redesigned models” at its Gwangmyeong Factory, including the 2028 Carnival Hybrid and a hydrogen-powered Carnival by 2029.
At its Gyeonggi Hwaseong Factory, Kia will reportedly also produce redesigned models, including the Sorento Hybrid in 2028.

title: Tesla accused of selling FSD to Korean owners who can't legally use it
content:
Tesla Autopilot
Fred Lambert
| Nov 4 2026 - 6:27 am PT
A South Korean consumer group is asking regulators to stop Tesla from marketing “Full Self-Driving” to customers whose cars can’t legally run it. By Tesla’s own numbers, that covers 99% of the Teslas it sold in Korea last year.
Citizens United for Consumer Sovereignty plans to file the complaint with the Korea Fair Trade Commission (KFTC) on Thursday, according to Reuters, which reviewed it. It comes just a week after a Seoul court threw out a refund lawsuit from Korean owners who paid for FSD.
Most Teslas in Korea can’t run FSD
It all comes down to where the car was built. The Model S, Model X, and Cybertruck come from US factories and enter Korea under the KORUS free trade agreement, which recognizes US safety standards. Those are the only Teslas that got “FSD (Supervised)” when Tesla switched it on in Korea late last year.
The problem is that those don’t represent the vast majority of Tesla vehicles sold in Korea.
The Model 3 and Model Y sold in Korea come from Giga Shanghai. There’s no equivalent deal with China, so those cars need Korean approval that FSD doesn’t have.
And that’s most of the fleet. Tesla Korea country manager Seo Young-deuk told lawmakers last month that FSD works on about 20% of Teslas registered in the country. Tesla has sold more than 170,000 Shanghai-built vehicles in Korea since 2023, per data it handed to the National Assembly, and sales of those China-made cars grew more than fivefold between 2023 and 2025.
Seo’s figure also clears up the conflicting eligibility numbers we flagged when
Korean police booked 80 Tesla drivers for using illegal FSD unlock devices
last month. A lawmaker’s data from May put it at 2.4%, while a data firm counted 20.7% in August. Tesla’s own testimony matches the higher one.
What the complaint alleges
For years, Tesla charged Korean buyers a one-time 9.043 million won (about $6,726) for FSD. It moved to a 150,000 won ($112) monthly subscription in August.
The complaint points to Tesla’s “coming soon” promotion last year and a demo video shot on Korean roads. Neither made it clear that FSD would only work on a small slice of the cars Tesla was selling. The group says Tesla knew that and kept pitching the package to every buyer anyway.
“Tesla generated substantial revenue by selling an expensive driver-assistance system to mass-market buyers who cannot use it for even a single day,” said Choi Young-suk, who heads automotive issues at the group.
It wants the KFTC to temporarily order Tesla to stop marketing FSD for ineligible cars. It’s also asking for fines and for the case to be sent to state investigators.
The KFTC is already looking at this. An official told Reuters the agency opened a probe into Tesla’s FSD advertising earlier this year and has received written responses from the company. Tesla didn’t respond to Reuters’ requests for comment.
Tesla only applied for approval last month
Tesla has collected FSD money from buyers of China-made cars in Korea for more than three years. But at an October 8 parliamentary hearing, Seo testified that Tesla had never formally asked the transport ministry to test FSD. Tesla filed for certification about two weeks later.
Approval won’t be a rubber stamp either. The ministry told a lawmaker that FSD doesn’t comply with local safety rules, including the requirement that drivers keep their hands on the wheel. Current FSD versions let drivers go hands-free as long as the cabin camera sees them watching the road.
None of this slowed sales. Tesla passed BMW this year to become Korea’s top imported car brand.
So far, owners haven’t had much luck in court. Last month, a Seoul court dismissed a lawsuit from Tesla owners seeking FSD refunds, with the judge pointing to Korean regulations, not Tesla, as the reason more features never launched.

title: What does a blue Texas sweep mean for Elon Musk, Tesla & SpaceX?
content:
Elon Musk
Jameson Dow
| Nov 4 2026 - 6:00 am PT
historic election defeat
in one of the most expensive elections in US election history, the state of Texas has turned blue. Along with this come potential implications for Elon Musk and his companies.
The US midterm election was yesterday, and ended up in a stunning result, with Democrats taking control of both houses of Congress by wide margins, and flipping seats that had been considered safe around the nation.
Perhaps most notably, many of these seats were in Texas – a republican stronghold which saw a clean sweep, with the Democrats winning
statewide contest. Republicans maintained some state legislative power and won the State Senate, but as of this writing Democrats are currently ahead in the count for the State House.
Despite huge spending, Democrats won almost everything
The highest profile contest was for Texas Senate, where James Talarico won by a 55-43 margin. This race set the record for the most expensive Senate race in the nation’s history, with
over half a billion dollars spent
on this one seat alone.
About half of the total money spent on the race came courtesy of republican PACs, a method by which companies and the ultra-wealthy can launder money into bribes to buy elections. And most of the PAC money in the race came from one man, Elon Musk, who
spent $212 million
to support the enormously unpopular and
scandal-ridden
outgoing Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton
That’s nearly half of the $474 million dollars that Musk put into this election cycle, suggesting that he saw this race of particular importance. And yet, his candidate lost miserably.
But the rout did not stop with Paxton. Paxton’s old job as AG is now going to be filled by Democrat Nathan Johnson. And Greg Abbott, the outgoing Governor, was defeated by Gina Hinojosa. Even the less high-profile races for court seats were swept by Democrats – three seats on the 15th Court of Appeals and four seats on the Texas Supreme Court.
And those results, even beyond the big-spending Senate race, could all matter quite a lot to Elon Musk.
Republicans rolled out the red carpet for Musk in Texas
In 2021, Musk announced that Tesla would
move its headquarters to Texas
, after Musk got in a spat with California government because he didn’t want to follow COVID restrictions for worker safety.
But the move wasn’t only about COVID restrictions – it was also about Musk’s vision of having more control over the business environment. And, by making allies with Ken Paxton and Greg Abbott, he has had quite a bit of control in Texas.
The two have rolled out the red carpet for Musk, giving him carte blanche in his adopted state.
Autonomous vehicle regulations have been changed, allowing
driverless Robotaxis to operate
where other states with more advanced regulations and transparency requirements would not. And
many other laws
benefitting Tesla and SpaceX have been passed. Paxton even
sued Sam Altman
, Musk’s chief AI rival, just weeks ago.
Perhaps more notably for Musk personally, Texas has promised to allow Musk to get away with more
financial shenanigans
than states with more established business regulations might.
With Tesla both headquartered and
incorporated
in Texas, it can now use special “
business courts
” instituted by Abbott at Musk’s own urging. If cases from these courts are appealed, they go to the 15th Court of Appeals, a court created by Abbott and filled with 3 hand-picked judges, intended to reduce the chance that a Democratic district court (say, one in Austin, whereTesla is headquartered) gets final say on any issue.
Several specific seats overseeing Musk went blue
But, the 15th Court of Appeals just had elections last night – and its three seats were flipped to Democratic control.
The 15th Court of Appeals also, just
last week
stopped an inquiry
into thousands of pages of emails between Abbott and Musk. The emails had been
released
, but are heavily redacted, with Abbott referring to the redacted portions as having “
intimate
” information in them.
And who made that request for inquiry into the emails? Gina Hinojosa, a name you might recognize, as she is the next Governor of Texas, as of last night.
As of yet, those emails have not all been released, so we don’t actually know exactly how much influence Musk was able to exercise over the state’s outgoing Governor. But given the changes we know about, the money Musk spent in Texas, and the thousands of pages of emails that have been redacted, it seems likely that there is something more to be found in them.
What does this mean for Musk’s companies?
So what does this all mean for Tesla, our main area of coverage here at
Electrek
On a Texas state level, probably not all that much. There’s no reason that Democrats in the state would interfere with Tesla’s production of electric vehicles – in fact, they’d probably encourage it more than republicans do. Talarico has stated that he supports Tesla – it is a large employer in the state, after all.
And certainly, the national wins by Democrats could be a boon for EVs, and for
climate action
, given how hostile republicans have been to them (and Musk has been the
single largest supporter
of that hostility towards EVs, which has
cost Tesla billions
The same likely goes for SpaceX – perhaps a blue Texas will be more restrictive of the company’s improper usage of
protected habitats
building of data centers
whatever the hell is going on on twitter
. But the core businesses of space launches and Starlink don’t seem likely to go anywhere.
What does it mean for Musk himself?
For Elon Musk, though, things could be different. Given his “intimate” relationship with Abbott, the extreme amounts of money he spent on Paxton, and the highly personal nature of his
truly ridiculous attacks
against Talarico, it seems unlikely that he will have a similar level of allyship with Texas government actors as he did in prior years. Talarico’s main anti-corruption message was seemingly aimed straight at Musk’s attempts to buy elections, after all.
And given his high levels of spending on a party that is outright hostile electric vehicles, it seems clear that his
personal
fortunes are far more important to him than the well-being of his companies.
This is all important to note, because Musk has been working towards a scheme to merge SpaceX and Tesla, a deal which would likely be a detriment to
both companies and all of their shareholders
. Musk wants the deal so he can
exercise more control over, and extract more personal wealth from, the combined entity.
But that scheme could rely on a favorable legal environment in Texas courts, an environment that just got less favorable.
And, given Musk’s penchant for childish lashings-out anytime he deems people insufficiently obsequious to his imagined greatness, could we see another situation where Musk encounters the tiniest amount of pushback from state government and then picks up his toys and leaves, as he already did in both California and Delaware? Time will have to tell. Keep your popcorn buckets primed and ready.

title: Shoals and Array announce merger plan in bid to create ‘one-stop shop’ - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Merger between electronic balance of system (EBOS) and tracker company brings a raft of products for solar and battery storage installations into a single business. Shoals shareholders are expected to own roughly 65% of the merged company.
Matthew Lynas
04 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
Shoals Technologies Group and Array Technologies have proposed a merger that would combine two US Nasdaq listed solar companies into a single entity, with a product range covering electronic balance of system (EBOS) and tracker products.
Subject to shareholder approval, the stock-for-stock merger would see Shoals shareholders own around 65% of the combined company, with Array shareholders owning the remaining 35%. Investor documents for the merger forecast combined revenue of $2.2 billion to $2.4 billion in 2027.
Under the proposed deal structure, Array would continue as the legal successor company, which avoids the need to refinance Array’s existing debt, and all Shoals shares will be exchanged for Array common shares. A new corporate name and ticker symbol for the NASDAQ listed company will be announced at a later date.
Shoals CEO Brandon Moss would take charge of the newly combined entity, while Array CEO Kevin Hostetler will serve as a special advisor.
The deal is being pitched by Shoals and Array as a way to drive incremental revenue growth from the two companies’ existing customer base, while also offering potential to develop new products and expand internationally.
In a call to investors on Nov. 4, Moss noted that only 20% of the two company’s combined project volume used products from both companies in 2025-26, which the CEO identified as a significant cross-selling opportunity, with $2.5 billion of incremental sales potential if each company sold its full product suite into every project served by the other.
“The power of this combination is not simply that we will have a broader product set,” said Moss, who argued that the merger represents a combination of companies with leading products in some categories as well as products with technical points of difference.
Moss also suggested the merger could support new product development by allowing the business to integrate components at an earlier stage, citing integrated wire management and tracker designs, pre-engineered EBOS and SBOS kits, and digital design tools that coordinate mechanical and electrical layouts.
The idea of merging Shoals and Array is not new. Shoals CEO Moss noted that it had been floated since before he was appointed in 2023. The two companies also already share a chairman of the board – Brad Forth.
When asked why the right time was to merge, Moss highlighted current business performance, noting “unbelievably strong order books” and recent new product development from both Shoals and Array.  “Theres is a tremendous amount of synergies between the two companies,” Moss said.
The merged company also plans to buy back $317.5 million of a special class of Array investor shares that currently entitles their holders to priority payments. Buying back the “Preferred Stock” is expected to cut future payouts and leave more cash available for the business. The combined company also expects to benefit from Shoals’ approximately $1.6 billion of tax amortization and $237 million of Net Operating Losses, which are expected to reduce taxable income and limit cash tax obligations for several years.
Shoals and Array expect the proposed merger to complete in early 2027. If approved, Shoals shareholders will receive 1.6931 Array shares for each Shoals share.

content:
Markets & Policy
Energinet has submitted two proposals for consultation that could see electricity producers, such as solar power plants, offered quicker grid connections in exchange for accepting restrictions on production.
Patrick Jowett
04 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
Denmark’s national transmission system operator (TSO) Energinet is proposing two new products offering permanent limited grid access to electricity producers.
The products are designed to limit production in order to accommodate transmission grid capacity, the TSO explains, with one intended for transmission grid producers and the other for distribution grid producers.
Energinet says the basic principle of the two products is that a producer would accept that their feed-in to the grid may be limited when there is insufficient capacity in the grid. In return, a producer is exempt from the connection fee that is normally payable when connecting to full grid access.
“By entering into an agreement on limited grid access, flexible systems can also demonstrate their grid friendliness,” the TSO’s explanation continues. “In this way, they achieve higher priority in the pooled case processing and thus also the opportunity to potentially be connected to the electricity grid more quickly.”
Energinet says the solutions may be relevant for different types of production plants that can act flexibly in their feed-in to the electricity grid, such as solar and wind power plants, as well as battery systems in the feed-in direction.
A consultation on the two products is open until November 13, with Energinet inviting relevant actors and other stakeholders to provide input. The TSO says responses will support further work on the methods. A webinar will take place on November 6 as part of the consultation, giving stakeholders the chance to ask questions on the solutions.
“The two products for producers that we are now sending out for consultation are important pieces in the overall puzzle that should give all players equal opportunities to demonstrate their grid friendliness and thus move forward in the queue to get on the electricity grid,” commented Kia Marie Jerichau, Energinet’s VP of Business and Markets.
Energinet’s latest update adds the two products are part of a broader effort to develop flexible solutions, with work on an additional three products offering limited grid access also underway.
“The ambition is to have a broad range of options for grid access, where different needs and degrees of flexibility can play a greater role in the way the capacity in the electricity grid is utilised,” the TSO said.
Last month, the Danish government
adopted an emergency plan for grid connections
, replacing its previous first-come, first-served principle with a new model that gives grid companies opportunity to prioritise who gets access.

title: Malaysia’s data center industry gets 500 MW solar, 1 GWh battery storage boost - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
A 500 MW solar project paired with a 1 GWh battery storage system is planned in Malaysia to supply renewable electricity to DayOne’s data centers. The project, backed by IOI Corporation and Tenaga Nasional Berhad, will operate under the country’s Corporate Renewable Energy Supply Scheme.
Emiliano Bellini
04 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Asia-Pacific
Batteries
Energy Storage
Highlights
Utility-scale
A 11 MW solar farm in Malaysia
A 500 MWac solar photovoltaic project coupled with a 250 MW/1,000 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) is set to be developed on approximately 1,300 acres of land in Bahau, Negeri Sembilan, Malaysia.
The massive solar-plus-storage project will be developed by IOI Corporation Berhad (IOI), one of Malaysia’s leading integrated palm oil producers, in partnership with
Tenaga Nasional Berhad
(TNB), the country’s largest electricity utility, and a consortium of unspecified small and medium-sized enterprises.
“The project will be supported by TNB’s long-term renewable energy offtake agreement with DayOne Data Centres Limited, a leading global digital infrastructure platform headquartered in Singapore,” IOI said in a statement. “Under the agreement, DayOne is expected to procure up to 500MWac of renewable energy over a 21-year period to support its data centre operations in Malaysia, as announced by the parties on 11 June 2025.”
The project marks IOI’s first large-scale renewable energy investment under Malaysia’s
Corporate Renewable Energy Supply Scheme
(CRESS), which allows corporate electricity consumers to procure renewable power directly from independent developers through the national grid. The scheme aims to encourage private investment in renewable energy infrastructure while supporting the decarbonization of energy-intensive industries.
Malaysia is expanding its utility-scale solar and energy storage capacity to meet rising electricity demand from data centers. In August 2025, clean energy company Gentari and engineering group Gamuda
unveiled plans to jointly develop 1.5 GW of solar capacity
, alongside battery storage, to supply hyperscale data centers under CRESS.
The rapid growth of Malaysia’s data center industry has also raised concerns about electricity supply, grid capacity and water availability. A
March 2026 analysis
highlighted the challenges of meeting rising electricity demand while maintaining grid stability and ensuring sufficient dispatchable generation. Uncertainty over grid access charges has also been identified as a key factor affecting the commercial viability of corporate renewable energy projects.
In September 2026, Malaysia
revised the CRESS framework
to improve project bankability and stimulate investment. The changes introduced a fixed system access charge of MYR 0.14 ($0.03)/kWh for qualifying firm renewable electricity supply projects and a minimum 10-year contract term between developers and corporate consumers. Projects must begin commercial operations by the end of 2028 to qualify for the reduced charge. At the time, 11 renewable energy developers and eight corporate consumers had registered projects totaling approximately 3.15 GW under the scheme.

title: Dutch grid operator reports ongoing connection bottlenecks - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Insufficient capacity on the high-voltage grid within parts of eastern Netherlands means some customers will be placed on a waiting list during the first six months of next year.
Patrick Jowett
04 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
Netherlands
Utility-scale
Customers in some eastern municipalities in the Netherlands are to be placed on a waiting list for connections to the high-voltage grid due to insufficient capacity, Dutch grid manager Liander has confirmed.
Liander operates across the provinces of Gelderland and North Holland, as well as large parts of the provinces of Flevoland, Friesland and South Holland, which are spread across the western, northern and eastern regions of the Netherlands.
An update published at the end of October on grid capacity for customers with large-scale consumption connections, of more than 3 x 80 amperes, listed 14 new bottlenecks on Liander’s network where maximum connection has been reached.
Of this total, 11 of the bottlenecks relate exclusively to the consumption, or purchase, of electricity, two of the bottlenecks concern the feed-in of electricity and one concerns both. The most impacted region is Friesland, with five bottlenecks. Liander identified four each in Gelderland and North Holland and one Flevoland.
In an additional update published on Monday (November 2), Liander said there is currently insufficient capacity on the high-voltage grid to connect new customers on the waiting list beginning Jan. 1, 2027, without putting too much pressure on the reliability of the grid.
The announcement impacts sixteen municipalities all located within the eastern province of Gelderland, bordering Germany.
In these areas, customers with a new application for a grid connection will be placed on a waiting list until at least Jul. 1, 2027. The only exception is any housing projects registered before Jul. 1, 2026, which Liander says can be connected provided there is sufficient capacity on the local electricity grid.
Liander says it will work with transmission system operator TenneT during springtime to assess how much grid capacity will be available from July 2027 onwards. It adds that the precise consequences for individual customers and regions will be “further elaborated in the coming period.”
The operator’s latest update says there is sufficient capacity on TenneT’s high-voltage grid to connect at least a portion of the customers on the waiting list in other areas of Gelderland, and Flevopolder, beginning Jan. 1, 2027. In these areas, capacity will be allocated according to the national prioritisation framework.
The Netherlands began following new rules for the allocation of scarce grid capacity in July, with capacity first directed towards measures necessary for a safe electricity grid and parties that help reduce congestion. Public infrastructure such as hospitals, police and fire stations, housing, drinking water and sewage facilities are prioritised next, followed by any customers without societal priority.
“We have been able to realise a lot of flexible capacity, but unfortunately not yet enough. We realise what this means for customers and developments in this region,” commented Liander CTO Joris de Groot. “Together with TenneT, government authorities, and customers, we will therefore continue to do everything in our power to find extra capacity and accelerate the necessary expansion of the grid.”
Liander’s update concludes that grid operators and government authorities are working to accelerate grid expansions, while also making smarter use of the existing grid, deploying more flexible capacity and investigating how much capacity can be made available within responsible limits.
“These efforts have not yielded sufficient capacity everywhere to connect new customers from the waiting list for the coming period,” the grid operator said. “Consequently, the urgency to find flexible capacity and accelerate grid expansions remains undiminished. In this way, we can keep the grid safe in the future and continue connecting customers.”

content:
Applications & Installations
Vietnam’s Dak Lak province has approved a $355 million floating solar project on the Ea Sup Thuong reservoir. The facility is expected to be completed by late 2028.
Emiliano Bellini
04 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Asia-Pacific
Highlights
Utility-scale
A floating PV plant operated by Vietnamese utility EVN at the Da Mi reservoir
Authorities in Vietnam’s Dak Lak province have approved a $355 million floating solar project with a planned capacity of 452 MW on the Ea Sup Thuong reservoir.
The Dak Lak Provincial People’s Committee approved the investment under Decision No. 3526/QĐ-UBND, issued on Oct. 31. The project is scheduled for completion by the end of 2028 and would rank among the world’s larger inland floating PV installations.
The facility will feature a floating 35 kV electrical collection network and a 35/220 kV substation equipped with two 250 MVA transformers. A 6 km, double-circuit 220 kV transmission line will connect the plant to the Krong Buk substation, where two additional 220 kV connection bays will be installed.
The project will also include a battery energy storage system, although its capacity has not been disclosed. The developers will contribute 20% of the total investment through equity, with the remaining 80% to be raised from other sources.
A consortium comprising IPC Engineering and Construction, Tay Nguyen Infrastructure Construction and Development, SD Vietnam Construction Investment, and Ea Sup Investment will develop the project, according to local media outlet Tuoi Tre News. It will occupy approximately 527 hectares, including 524 hectares of reservoir surface.
Vietnam commissioned its first large-scale floating solar project in May 2019, when Da Nhim–Ham Thuan–Da Mi Hydropower Joint Stock Company (DHD), a subsidiary of state-owned utility Electricity of Vietnam (EVN), connected a 47.5 MW installation to the grid at the Da Mi hydropower reservoir in Binh Thuan province. The VND 1.5 trillion ($64 million) project covers approximately 50 hectares.
In late 2020,
two 35 MW floating solar plants
were connected to the grid at the Gia Hoet 1 and Tam Bo irrigation reservoirs in Chau Duc district. Chinese module manufacturer Longi supplied the panels for both installations.
Vietnam has also introduced differentiated feed-in tariffs for floating solar projects. In April 2025, the Ministry of Industry and Trade
ranging from VND 1,228.2 ($0.047)/kWh to VND 1,685.8/kWh for floating PV without storage, depending on the region.

title: Poweroad FLEX-261 series passes dual-standard large-scale fire testing - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
Testing was conducted in accordance with UL 9540A and CSA C800 and provides technical evidence to support fire safety assessments for multi-cabinet C&I energy storage installations. POWEROAD has received a CSA Group Letter of Attestation for passing the tests.
POWEROAD
04 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
Energy Storage
POWEROAD’s FLEX-261 Series has successfully passed large-scale fire testing conducted in accordance with two key fire safety standards: ANSI/CAN/UL 9540A:2026, Sixth Edition, and CSA/ANSI C800:2025. Following the testing, CSA Group presented POWEROAD with a Letter of Attestation documenting the testing and evaluation.
These evaluations support the technical assessment of energy storage projects in the global markets. Large-scale fire testing (LSFT) data can support fire safety reviews, project permitting, and insurance and financing assessments.
The evaluation covered three POWEROAD models — FLEX 261, FLEX 261 AIO, and FLEX 261 AIO-3S — in multi-cabinet commercial and industrial (C&I) battery energy storage system (BESS) configurations. The results provide technical evidence for system design, fire risk assessment, and compliance planning worldwide.
Strong Results Under Challenging Conditions
Conducted in mid-August 2026, the test evaluated fire containment in a multi-cabinet installation under extreme conditions.
The setup comprised five cabinets: one initiating cabinet and four target cabinets. The initiating cabinet was tested at 100% state of charge (SOC), with fire suppression disabled and the cabinet door and deflagration panel manually opened before testing.
The results showed:
No Fire Propagation:
Fire did not spread to the four adjacent target cabinets.
No Thermal Runaway in Target Cabinets:
No cell venting, thermal runaway, or fire was observed in the four adjacent target cabinets.
Cell Temperatures and Voltages Within Normal Operating Ranges:
Measurements in adjacent target cabinets remained within normal operating ranges.
No Cabinet Collapse:
The cabinets maintained their structural integrity during the test.
These results demonstrate the FLEX-261 Series’ fire containment performance and provide technical evidence for fire safety assessments of multi-cabinet C&I BESS installations.
POWEROAD’s safety approach encompasses fire safety, data security, and asset protection. It has established a Joint Energy Storage Safety R&D Center with a national-level fire safety research institute. Its framework includes data security and management assessments, plus product liability insurance covering systems, cells, and lithium battery packs up to USD 5 million.
With more than 1,000 C&I energy storage projects deployed worldwide, POWEROAD continues to apply its safety-focused engineering approach across diverse applications and markets. The FLEX-261 Series test adds further evidence supporting the technical evaluation of its C&I solutions.

content:
Markets & Policy
Lithuania has approved legislative reforms to accelerate renewable energy development, allowing project extensions of up to 48 months, halving developer guarantees and easing permitting requirements.
The measures also aim to speed up grid connections, strengthen infrastructure resilience and tighten energy cybersecurity regulations.
Emiliano Bellini
04 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Commercial & industrial
Highlights
Utility-scale
Green Genius PV project in Lithuania
The the Lithuanian Parliament (Seimas) has adopted a comprehensive package of legislative amendments prepared by the Ministry of Energy to stimulate renewable energy investment, reduce regulatory barriers and strengthen Lithuania’s energy security.
The amendments to the Law on Energy, the Law on Electricity and the Law on Energy from Renewable Sources respond to changing market conditions and a significant slowdown in new renewable energy projects.
Extended project timeline
The government said the amendments introduce more flexible conditions for ongoing energy projects, enabling developers to adapt their investments to evolving market circumstances. Developers holding valid permits will be able to extend project development timelines by up to 48 months and change the nature of their planned investments, including switching between electricity generation, energy storage and electricity consumption projects.
This flexibility will be available for a limited period, with developers given one year to decide on their projects’ future. Those choosing to postpone or modify projects will be required to provide an additional bank guarantee. To ease financial pressures, the performance guarantee payable to network operators will be halved, from €50 ($56.3)/kW to €25/kW. Additional administrative simplifications will further reduce barriers to project implementation.
Energy communities
The reforms also remove permitting requirements for renewable energy communities and citizen energy communities developing installations of up to 100 kW under the so-called prosumer park model. From 1 November 2026, these communities will no longer need permits to develop generation capacity or produce electricity.
The legislation also revises the distribution of renewable energy generation levy payments to residents near power plants. Allocations will be based on each eligible individual’s declared place of residence rather than on a household basis.
The revised mechanism will apply to funds collected for 2026, funds returned in 2027 and unused balances from previous periods. The levy is financed by renewable electricity producers according to their electricity output.
Faster grid connection
Furthermore, the Lithuanian government has allowed large-scale investors to access equipment reserves maintained by electricity network operators, helping facilitate faster grid connections.
The amendments also require electricity and gas transmission and distribution operators to maintain reserves of critical equipment and materials needed to restore supply following accidents, technical failures or deliberate physical interference.
Both measures took effect on Nov. 1.
In addition, improvements to the regulatory framework for direct electricity lines will provide greater flexibility for large electricity consumers and producers, supporting new industrial and energy investments.
Cybersecurity
The legislative package also strengthens Lithuania’s implementation of EU energy legislation by introducing penalties for violations of methane emission reduction requirements and restrictions on Russian gas imports.
It also clarifies institutional responsibilities for implementing EU cybersecurity requirements concerning cross-border electricity flows.
The National Energy Regulatory Council, the Lithuanian Energy Agency and the National Cyber Security Centre will have clearly defined roles, strengthening coordination, regulatory oversight and the protection of critical energy infrastructure.
Lithuania first announced plans to tighten its cybersecurity laws in
November 2024
