title: US nuclear reactors get boost as Urenco ships first advanced fuel
content: A single cylinder of enriched uranium has marked a major turning point for the Western power grid.Urenco USA has successfully produced its first commercial cylinder of Low-Enriched Uranium Plus (LEU+) at its New Mexico facility. Russia has mostly dominated the global market for enriched uranium. It is a major first for the Western world and opens up powerful new options for both aging power plants and next-generation reactor designs. Next-generation Small Modular Reactors, such as high-temperature gas-cooled and sodium-cooled fast designs, feature smaller physical footprints than traditional power plants. Advanced compact cores depend on elevated U-235 concentrations to achieve maximum operational efficiency. Enrichment levels up to 10%Natural uranium consists of over 99% U-238 and under 1% fissionable U-235. For a long time, commercial reactors have operated on standard low-enriched uranium containing a 3% to 5% U-235. The newly introduced LEU+ expands these limits, raising enrichment levels up to 10%. The extra nudge in concentration is important.For existing light water reactors, LEU+ means plants can run much longer between refueling shutdowns, cutting maintenance costs and keeping reliable zero-carbon electricity flowing to the grid with fewer interruptions. For advanced reactor developers, it provides a stable, commercial-scale U.S. fuel source built right here at home.Also, LEU+ acts as a critical stepping stone. It serves as an optimal feedstock for producing High-Assay Low-Enriched Uranium (HALEU) — enriched between 10 percent and 20 percent. It will boost production efficiency for high-tech reactor concepts currently on the drawing board.“A tremendous amount of work has gone into preparing our plant and our staff to reach this achievement,” said Jody Blackshear, Managing Director of Urenco USA. “Through the coordinated efforts of teams from across our site and company, we can now supply an innovative fuel option for our customers and support the next generation of nuclear fuel technologies.” Further, adopting LEU+ could help power plants extend operations by stretching 18-to-24-month refueling schedules out to 24 to 30+ months. Plants gain higher overall capacity factors and spend far less time offline for routine maintenance. Facility to boost domestic supplyCongressional passage of the Prohibiting Russian Uranium Imports Act established a vital strategic context for Urenco’s milestone. Federal restrictions on Russian low-enriched uranium create an urgent demand for domestic alternatives to secure the American power grid. Hence, producing LEU+ in New Mexico strengthens Western energy independence and reinforces domestic supply chains for both current and next-generation nuclear reactors. The development comes on the heels of a key regulatory hurdle cleared in September 2025, when the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission authorized Urenco USA to enrich up to 10% U-235 across all of its gas centrifuge cascades.Now, the company is preparing for a massive scale-up.To meet growing demand, Urenco USA is investing to expand its New Mexico footprint and reach a capacity of over 7 million Separative Work Units (SWU) within the decade. Construction on a new dedicated enrichment plant will kick off in 2029, with the first new cascades going live in 2032 and additional capacity rolling out through 2036.

title: Nuclear fusion reactor gets 13-ton beam box to achieve 108 million °F
content: Engineers in Oxfordshire have lowered a 12-tonne (13-ton) steel structure into position for the UK’s flagship fusion experiment. The move marks a key engineering milestone on the path to limitless clean energy.The component, known as a double beam box, was hoisted into place at the Culham Campus of the UK Atomic Energy Authority (UKAEA). It forms the backbone of a major upgrade to the MAST Upgrade facility, a compact, spherical fusion device designed to test reactor physics.The new box will house two neutral beam injectors. These systems fire high-energy neutral atoms straight into superheated gas, or plasma. The bombardment heats the fuel toward the extreme temperatures required for commercial fusion.Once completed, the double-decker system will double the machine’s neutral beam heating power from 4.4 megawatts to 8.8 megawatts. In turn, core plasma temperatures are expected to soar from 30 million degrees Celsius to roughly 60 million degrees.Requiring specialized metallurgyReaching such heat is vital for the UK’s long-term fusion ambitions. The extreme environment will give researchers an ideal test bed for STEP, or Spherical Tokamak for Energy Production, the prototype commercial plant Britain plans to build in Nottinghamshire.Andrew Thornton, who leads MAST Upgrade operations, called the successful lift a huge step forward for the facility. He noted that doubling the heating power allows the team to explore extreme conditions that were previously out of reach. The experiments will test whether the reactor’s exhaust system can endure the punishment of such high-performance plasma without degrading.Building the hardware requires specialized metallurgy. The vessel is crafted from 316L stainless steel, an alloy trusted in medical implants and offshore platforms for its strength and resistance to corrosion. Because fusion reactors must replicate the empty void of space, the steel also maintains an ultra-high vacuum with minimal outgassing and leakage.When fully assembled with its lid, the chamber will weigh approximately 15 tonnes (16.5 tons) and enclose 20 cubic meters of space.Maintaining high vacuum inside beam boxThe crane lift represents one piece of an ongoing overhaul across the Culham site. Technicians are currently fitting an electron Bernstein wave microwave system to inject extra heat into the plasma core.Nearby, teams are repurposing surplus electrical power gear from the retired Joint European Torus (JET) reactor, which closed in 2023. Further work includes building positive ion injectors and installing an internal cryopump to maintain high vacuum inside the beam box.The engineering work follows scientific success earlier this year. In August, MAST Upgrade operators completed the facility’s fifth experimental campaign, running over 1,100 plasma pulses and achieving record plasma pressure without losing control of the gas. Preventing unstable plasma from tearing apart is one of fusion’s hardest riddles.Engineers expect to fit all remaining interior equipment by late autumn 2027. Once the vessel is sealed and vacuum-tested, the next phase of scientific experiments will begin in 2028.

title: US military backs General Atomics for long-range hypersonic weapons
content: Leidos, an American defense technology company, has selected General Atomics Electromagnetic Systems (GA-EMS) to manufacture components for the U.S. Army and Navy’s shared hypersonic weapons program, extending its role from prototype development to production. Under a multiyear subcontract, the company will supply precision-machined metal parts and cable assemblies for the Common Hypersonic Glide Body (CHGB) through 2031.The work supports two long-range strike programs: the Army’s Dark Eagle and the Navy’s Conventional Prompt Strike (CPS). Both use the same glide body, allowing the services to share a major weapon component while adapting the broader missile systems to their respective land- and sea-based launch platforms.The selection follows a $2.7 billion contract the Army awarded to Leidos in May 2026. That agreement brought the CHGB and Thermal Protection System programs together under a single effort intended to move the technology from prototyping toward production and improve the supply of components.One glide body, two hypersonic weaponsThe Common Hypersonic Glide Body is the maneuvering payload section of the Army-Navy hypersonic weapon. It is carried to high speed and altitude by a rocket booster before separating and gliding through the atmosphere toward its target.Hypersonic flight generally refers to speeds above Mach 5, or five times the speed of sound. Unlike a conventional ballistic missile warhead that follows a largely predictable trajectory after its boost phase, a hypersonic glide vehicle is designed to maneuver during flight. This can make its path harder to predict and complicate interception.The Army’s Dark Eagle, formerly known as the Long-Range Hypersonic Weapon, uses a ground-launched system. The Navy’s Conventional Prompt Strike program is developing a sea-based version intended for deployment aboard submarines and surface ships. Both use the shared glide body, while their launch and booster arrangements differ.The common design is intended to reduce duplicated development work and allow the services to benefit from shared testing and production. The Congressional Research Service describes the glide body as a central component of both programs, along with their shared missile-booster architecture.Precision parts, cables for flight controlGA-EMS will manufacture precision-machined metal components, substructures, and cable assemblies for the glide body. The company specifically identifies cable assemblies for the Elevon Control Module, which is associated with the vehicle’s aerodynamic control surfaces.Elevons combine the functions of elevators and ailerons, helping an aircraft-like vehicle control its pitch and roll. Their movement allows the glide body to adjust its orientation and maneuver during atmospheric flight.The electrical connections supporting these controls are just as important as the mechanical components. Cable assemblies carry signals and power between different subsystems, while precision-machined parts provide the physical structures needed to mount and integrate hardware. Both must meet tight manufacturing and inspection requirements in a system expected to operate under demanding flight conditions.The company said it will use specialized machining equipment, experienced manufacturing personnel, and inspection processes to maintain precision and repeatability. The company previously produced prototype glide-body subassemblies and supplied hardware and cables for a successful CHGB flight test in 2020.Boosting hypersonic weapon productionThe new subcontract reflects a broader effort to turn the Army and Navy’s hypersonic research and testing into a repeatable production program. In May 2026, Leidos said its $2.7 billion Army contract combined the glide body and thermal protection work to streamline development and accelerate deliveries.Thermal protection is a particularly important engineering challenge for hypersonic vehicles. Traveling through the atmosphere at several times the speed of sound generates intense aerodynamic heating, placing demanding requirements on the vehicle’s outer materials and protective structures. The separate Thermal Protection System effort addresses this challenge.The Army and Navy have also conducted joint flight testing of the weapon system. In December 2024, the Department of Defense announced a successful end-to-end test of the conventional hypersonic missile, building on earlier tests of the Common Hypersonic Glide Body.GA-EMS has not yet disclosed the value of its subcontract or the quantities of components it will manufacture. Its work through 2031 will nevertheless add another production partner to a program that depends on coordinating specialized mechanical, electrical, and thermal technologies across two military services.

title: Hypersonic impact turns diamond into graphite, could aid next-gen shields
content: The phrase says diamonds are forever. Hypersonic ballistics say otherwise.In a recent experiment, researchers at Texas A&M and Rice University marched an engineered diamond composite directly into a firing line. Then, they blasted it with aluminum projectiles flying at nearly eight times the speed of sound. The target not only withstood the strike but also morphed under fire.Within microseconds of impact, portions of the ultra-rigid diamond composite underwent an instant, atomic-scale metamorphosis, turning into graphite. This sudden phase transition let the target act as an immediate shock absorber, dispersing kinetic energy at the molecular level thanks to graphite’s softer carbon structure.The study was spearheaded by doctoral candidate Aniket Mote and Dr. Thomas Lacy of Texas A&M, using a 45-foot two-stage light gas gun at the university’s Hypervelocity Impact Laboratory (HVIL). “We found that portions of the diamond composite had transformed into graphite,” Lacy said. “It was exciting to observe this phase change in real time.”Understanding how hard materials change their internal structure under intense mechanical stress provides defense and aerospace engineers with a fresh blueprint for advanced design.Testing methodologyExtreme forces driving modern aerospace and defense systems expose structural materials to rapid deformation, crushing pressure, and sudden failure. Studying the diamond-to-graphite transformation gives a clear look at these rapid physical reactions during high-velocity impacts. Experiments replicating hypersonic stress records phase changes in real time. It reveals exactly how super-hard composites transition between atomic states under intense shock.To forge the target in the first place, Rice University scientists bound small diamond grains with cubic boron nitride and cobalt using spark plasma sintering. This was the process designed to stop traditional melting at high heat.During testing, the team fired projectiles at speeds approaching Mach 8.45 (roughly 6,500 miles per hour). High-speed cameras and ultra-fast sensors caught the microstructural shift in real time.“In the first test, we launched a cluster of 1 millimeter aluminum ‘buckshot’ projectiles traveling at nearly Mach 7.5. And in the second test, we fired a single, large 4 millimeter aluminum projectile at speeds approaching Mach 8.45,” Mote said.Practical applicationsWhy does this matter? Hypersonic travel and space exploration depend on materials that refuse to shatter when pushed past normal physical limits. Rather than using static hardness, future shielding could be designed to intentionally alter its state on impact, neutralizing catastrophic blows before they breach a craft’s body.“The diamond-to-graphite transformation could help guide the design of next-generation materials for extreme environments, to serve national and global research interests,” Lacy said.Diamonds might not actually last forever. But by giving up their rigidity when it counts, they might just save the next generation of materials. This research demonstrates how ultra-hard materials respond to severe mechanical shock, providing insights into energy absorption during high-speed impacts. Experts can tap into these findings to develop advanced protective shielding for aerospace systems, military vehicles, and space exploration craft. The resulting materials will better withstand extreme operational environments by dissipating explosive force at the structural level.The study was published in Materials Today.

title: Russia unveils first home-built hydrogen train with 435 miles of range
content: Russia is shifting to cleaner alternatives for its rail system that currently relies on polluting diesel engines.On Wednesday, October 28, Moscow announced that its first home-built hydrogen-powered passenger train, capable of traveling more than 435 miles (700 km) on hydrogen alone and up to 460 miles (740 km) with onboard battery support, was successfully assembled at a factory in Demikhovo.The first set of these trains will operate on Sakhalin, a Russian island in the Pacific Ocean, north of Japan.The assembled trains, designed for non-electrified railway lines, are the first low-floor passenger railcar model built in Russia to run be hydrogen fuel cells.First Russian-made less polluting railcarIn the long run, they are expected to provide a cleaner alternative to diesel-powered locomotives that emit a toxic mix of pollutants during combustion. The hydrogen power system will emit water vapor rather than the exhaust fumes produced by diesel engines.The inter-city hydrogen trains are being designed and built by Transmashholding (TMH), one of Russia’s largest manufacturers of railway rolling stock and urban transit equipment.The company is working alongside Russian Railways, Rosatom and the Sakhalin regional government to develop hydrogen-powered trains under an agreement signed in 2019.Work on Russia’s first hydrogen-powered train “has been underway for several years, and the assembly phase is due to be completed this year. In practice, the train has already been assembled and is moving into the testing phase,” said Valeri Limarenko, Governor of the Sakhalin Region.Testing of the first hydrogen train, built with the new low-floor design, is scheduled to begin in November this year.The governor added that dynamic tests in Moscow and the Moscow region will start in 2027 before the train is transferred to Sakhalin in the middle of the year.According to reports, the first train sets were assembled at TMH’s Demikhovski Machine-Building Plant and Tver Railcar Works, a TMH subsidiary.Two models, four distance rangesThe trains will be produced in two configurations. The two-car passenger units are expected to cover more than 435 miles (700 km) using the hydrogen power module alone, while onboard battery units can extend the range to about 460 miles (740 km).A second configuration with three passenger coaches, powered by the same hydrogen module, is expected to travel nearly 300 miles (480 km). Its onboard energy storage system can provide an additional 50 miles of range.Both configurations will include a separate technical railcar housing the hydrogen power system. The compartment will be equipped with hydrogen concentration and fire detection sensors to improve safety for passengers and railway staff.According to reports, the hydrogen-powered trains are expected to enter commercial service by the end of 2027 following certification trials scheduled for the same year. They will initially operate on Sakhalin Island, where a dedicated hydrogen testing center is also under development.Production of a second hydrogen fuel cell system is already underway as part of Moscow’s broader plan to create a unified platform for the next generation of urban, suburban and inter-regional trains operating on the 1,520 mm gauge railway network.The green fuel train project also builds on a major modernization of Sakhalin’s railway infrastructure. Work to convert the island’s rail network to Russia’s broad-gauge standard began more than two decades ago, and Russian Railways completed it in 2020. The project replaced the 1,067 mm gauge that had been built in the region before World War II during Japanese rule, preparing the network for the introduction of modern rolling stock such as the new hydrogen-powered trains.

title: US allies could get 1,250-mile deep strike capability that can reach Moscow
content: Allies of the United States in Europe are working to get deep strike capability with two new weapons. The UK and Germany’s next high-precision weapons are expected to be capable of reaching Moscow. The two weapons are expected to be delivered within this decade. Projected range of more than 1,250 miles“We noted the significant progress in our landmark project to develop Deep Precision Strike (DPS) capabilities, with ranges over 2,000 km, to be delivered within the decade, supporting jobs across the supply chain for UK and German industry,” said a joint statement by the UK’s Defense Secretary Wes Streeting MP and Germany’s Defence Minister Boris Pistorius MdB.Wes and Pistorius held the second Defense Ministerial Council under the Trinity House Agreement. Two years after signing the Agreement, both countries governments have made significant progress in strengthening defense cooperation between the United Kingdom and Germany.“The security of the United Kingdom and Germany is inseparable from the security of Europe. We share a responsibility to strengthen the European contribution to NATO, reinforce deterrence and ensure Europe is increasingly able to provide the capabilities and forces necessary for our collective defense. The Trinity House Agreement, reinforced by the Kensington Treaty, provides the framework for us to do this together,” added the statement.The armed forces of the two countries are continuing to deepen cooperation. On land, both countries are developing their strategic partnership to strengthen readiness and interoperability and explore cooperation on future capabilities and uncrewed systems. In the maritime domain, the UK and Germany are advancing cooperation on the procurement of Sting Ray with an Implementing Arrangement signed between our National Armaments Directors today. The two countries previously agreed that German P-8A Poseidon aircraft would fly from the UK on an episodic basis. This year, that commitment was realised for the first time, with RAF Lossiemouth supporting German Navy P-8s on Exercise Dynamic Mongoose in May, and more recently on Exercise Strike Warrior, which concluded early last month. “Through these activities we are strengthening our cooperation in the North Atlantic and North Sea. Our Air Forces will continue to develop their cooperation through the bilateral Flight Plan, including on future uncrewed and collaborative combat capabilities,” said the statement.Deep-strike capability to deliver deterrence optionThe proposed deep-strike capability is intended to provide the United Kingdom and Germany with a significantly enhanced conventional deterrence option. With a projected range of more than 1,250 miles (2,000 kilometres) the programme reflects a broader European effort to strengthen its ability to contribute to NATO’s collective defense. Long-range precision-strike capabilities have become an increasingly important element of modern defence planning. The evolving security environment has highlighted the importance of having credible conventional deterrence options and the ability to respond to emerging threats across extended distances.The two countries have highlighted that their national security is closely connected to the wider security of Europe. They have consequently reaffirmed their responsibility to strengthen Europe’s contribution to NATO and ensure that European allies can provide the necessary capabilities and forces for collective defense. The deep precision-strike initiative forms part of the wider defense cooperation established through the Trinity House Agreement.

title: Collision-proof flexible drone flies at 49 mph without losing agility
content: ETH Zurich researchers have developed FlexiQuad, a flexible four-rotor drone designed to withstand collisions while staying airborne.Unlike conventional drones that rely on rigid frames, the new design uses a deformable structure that absorbs impacts by changing shape. Despite its flexible body, FlexiQuad can maintain stable flight, reach high speeds, and perform agile maneuvers.The design could eventually support applications such as infrastructure inspections, rescue operations, and environmental monitoring in confined spaces and challenging environments.Collision-resistant droneFlexiQuad is a flexible four-rotor drone designed to withstand collisions without losing flight capability. Unlike conventional quadcopters with rigid frames and four arms extending from a central body, the new drone features a deformable, ring-shaped structure that absorbs impact forces.The design lets FlexiQuad briefly change shape when it strikes an obstacle, reducing the forces on its frame and onboard components. Despite its flexible structure, the drone can fly at speeds up to 49 mph (80 km/h) and achieve acceleration levels comparable to conventional rigid drones.According to ETH Zurich, the drone’s main innovation lies in how its frame combines flexibility with structural stiffness. Its ring-shaped body has no central fuselage, with the four rotors, batteries, and flight-control module distributed along the frame. This arrangement allows the structure to deform laterally when it encounters an obstacle while remaining stiff in the vertical direction.The researchers drew inspiration from birds and insects, whose wings can bend in certain directions while remaining relatively rigid in others. With this principle, FlexiQuad absorbs collision energy without compromising the force transmission needed to keep its rotors operating effectively.Tackles tight spacesIn collision tests, the researchers flew the drone into obstacles at speeds of up to around 15.5 mph (25 km/h). Its frame temporarily deformed on impact, reducing the forces acting on the structure and allowing it to continue flying. The researchers said the test speed was limited mainly by the available space needed to accelerate the drone before collision.According to Girardi, FlexiQuad can also reach linear and angular acceleration levels comparable to rigid drones. The flexible structure can also be used to grasp and transport objects. During demonstrations, the drone picked up, carried, and set down a soft first-aid kit. It also lifted a payload heavier than its own weight.The design could support operations in confined or cluttered environments, including inspections of ship ballast tanks, search-and-rescue missions inside collapsed buildings, and environmental measurements in dense forests. Its ability to tolerate physical contact could also help it navigate obstacles that might otherwise interrupt a mission.Another proposed application involves fitting a net inside the hollow center of the frame to capture unwanted or rogue drones. The deformable design lets heavy-duty drones squeeze through narrow gaps, carry extra sensors, and extend flight time.FlexiQuad has a modular design intended to simplify transportation and assembly. Its airframe materials cost less than 15 Swiss francs, with potential for further reductions. The frame can also be opened and folded into a compact form that fits inside a medium-sized suitcase. Quick-release fasteners and slide-in batteries could eventually allow operators to assemble the drone rapidly on-site.However, autonomous operation remains a technical challenge. Following a collision, vibrations in the flexible frame can blur camera images and interfere with navigation. Researchers are using reinforcement learning to teach the drone to stabilize itself after impact using onboard motion sensors, then resume autonomous flight. They are also investigating whether measurements of frame deformation and vibration could provide additional information for flight control.

title: Hyundai unveils 5 MW hydrogen production system for 772 tons yearly
content: Hyundai Motor Group is demonstrating a robot that automatically refuels a hydrogen-powered cleaning truck, alongside modular hydrogen production systems and upgraded commercial vehicle fuel cells. The World Hydrogen Expo 2026 opened November 4 at KINTEX in Goyang, South Korea, and runs through November 6.Organized through Hyundai’s HTWO hydrogen brand and business platform, the display shows how production infrastructure, transportation and industrial applications could form connected hydrogen ecosystems tailored to local resources and demand.Robot takes on truck refuelingHyundai is presenting the first demonstration of its Automatic Charging Robot-Hydrogen, or ACR-H, for commercial vehicles. The exhibit features the system automatically refueling a fuel cell electric cleaning truck.The robot is designed to reduce repetitive refueling tasks and make refueling more convenient for commercial vehicle drivers. It forms part of a broader display covering vehicle operation, maintenance, fleet management, and refueling.Also making its debut is an enhanced-durability fuel cell system for commercial vehicles. Hyundai said improved cells and key components strengthen stack durability, supporting reliability during extended operation and long-distance driving.Its Bluelink Uptime Care fleet management system allows operators to track vehicle operation and component conditions. Functions include abnormality diagnostics, preventive maintenance, and real-time alerts.The mobility display also includes the 2027 NEXO SUV, a hydrogen-powered locomotive model and a flat-type fuel cell module illustrating potential applications in high-volume, long-distance transport.Twelve stacks form a production moduleOn the production side, Hyundai is showcasing modular polymer electrolyte membrane electrolysis technology.Twelve stacks can be combined into one 5-megawatt-class electrolyzer system module capable of producing approximately 700 metric tons (772 US tons) of hydrogen annually. According to the group, the modular architecture can scale to hundreds of megawatts.A 1-megawatt-class containerized demonstration facility is operating in Gwangju. Additional demonstration projects are being pursued in Boryeong, Buan and Jeju.Hyundai is also presenting waste-to-hydrogen solutions centered on HTWO Energy Cheongju. The approach converts organic waste into hydrogen as part of a circular economy model.Other projects being pursued include a biogas-based hydrogen production facility in Paju and locally tailored initiatives in Indonesia.Connecting hydrogen supply with demandBeyond individual technologies, Hyundai’s exhibition presents scenarios connecting hydrogen production and consumption across cities, ports, logistics operations and manufacturing sites.The Saemangeum AI Valley concept links solar power and electrolysis with AI data centers, a robotics manufacturing plant and an AI hydrogen city concept. The model illustrates how hydrogen energy, AI and robotics could be integrated across urban infrastructure and services within a self-sustaining circular ecosystem.Visitors can also board a development model of the ELEC CITY Fuel Cell low-floor intercity bus to explore its accessibility features. Ride programs involving an enhanced UNIVERSE Fuel Cell coach and the New XCIENT Fuel Cell tractor are available to designated industry participants and media.WHE 2026 brings together approximately 190 companies and organizations from 12 countries. Alongside the exhibition, conference and partnership programs focus on hydrogen business opportunities, project investment and international collaboration.Hyundai said its exhibition aims to demonstrate practical hydrogen systems adapted to different regional and industrial needs.

title: 8,800-ton warship that packs 100+ missiles and 100 kW laser unveiled
content: French shipbuilder Naval Group has unveiled a warship concept that combines a large missile arsenal with drone operations, an electromagnetic gun and a high-energy laser. The 170-meter SCX 26 concept illustrates how next-generation surface combatants could operate in naval warfare.Presented at the Euronaval 2026 defense exhibition in Paris, the concept displaces approximately 8,818 US tons (8,000 tonnes) and is designed to reach 30 knots, with a range exceeding 8,000 nautical miles. Its proposed weapons fit includes more than 100 vertical launch system (VLS) cells, a rapid-fire electromagnetic gun, and a 100-kilowatt laser.The SCX 26 is a design study and not a ship currently scheduled for construction. Naval Group describes it as an exercise in exploring technologies and architectures that could shape future naval warfare.A warship designed around dronesOne of the concept’s most prominent features is a large mission bay at the stern, designed to support the deployment, recovery, and maintenance of uncrewed systems. Integrated lifting equipment and a large-capacity elevator would allow the ship to handle different types of drones and helicopters.The bay could be reconfigured depending on the mission, accommodating systems for intelligence gathering, surveillance, electronic warfare, anti-submarine warfare, and force protection. This would allow the vessel to operate as more than a conventional missile-armed combatant. It could also coordinate a wider network of crewed ships, aircraft and uncrewed platforms operating across the air, surface and underwater environments.The ship’s architecture is divided into two integrated modules separated by a flexible zone. This arrangement is intended to make it easier to introduce new capabilities as technologies and operational requirements change, rather than requiring major redesigns throughout the vessel’s service life.More than 100 missile cells and a 100 kW laserThe SCX 26’s proposed armament combines weapons intended for different engagement ranges and threats. Its main missile battery comprises more than 100 VLS cells of different classes, distributed between the bow and stern.Vertical launch systems allow missiles to be stored and fired directly from cells built into a ship’s deck. Depending on the launcher and missile combination, they can accommodate weapons for air defense, anti-submarine warfare, and land or surface attack. For closer-range defense, the ship would carry two Rampart modular launching systems and a 100 kW laser. High-energy lasers concentrate electrical energy into a beam that can heat and damage a target. They could provide another option against drones and other relatively inexpensive threats without requiring a conventional missile for every engagement. The effectiveness depends on factors such as weather, atmospheric conditions, range, and the ability to maintain the beam on a target.The electromagnetic gun is another proposed feature. Unlike conventional naval guns that use chemical propellants, electromagnetic guns use electrical energy to accelerate projectiles. The concept specifies a rapid-fire capability but does not provide details about the weapon’s caliber, range, or performance.Sensors and survivability built into the designThe concept also includes a UHF radar intended for ballistic missile defense, a comprehensive sonar suite for detecting underwater threats, and advanced electronic warfare systems. These would give the vessel a broad view of activity around it, from incoming aerial threats to submarines and electronic interference.Naval Group has also emphasized redundancy and segregation in the ship’s design. Its two masts and the distribution of launchers between the bow and stern are intended to reduce dependence on individual systems or locations.The proposed crew consists of 150 sailors, with accommodation for another 100 personnel, including commanders and specialists. Automation and artificial intelligence would help operators assess information and coordinate systems, while humans would remain responsible for operational decisions.

title: Critical nuclear reactor enters 35-year overhaul amid power crunch
content: Unit 5 at the Bruce nuclear generating station has been taken offline to begin a comprehensive core rebuild. Technicians safely disconnected the reactor on 1 November, launching its scheduled Major Component Replacement (MCR) outage. The shutdown marks the official midway point of Bruce Power’s privately financed Life-Extension Program. The multi-billion-dollar project aims to modernize Units 3 through 8 by 2033.The overhaul will add 30 to 35 years to the operational life of the units. Inside the reactor vault, crews face an intensive mechanical undertaking. Workers must strip out and replace 480 calandria tubes alongside an equal number of pressurized fuel channels. Teams will also fit 960 feeder tubes and hoist massive new steam generators into place. Once reassembled, the renewed reactor will provide low-carbon baseload electricity alongside a steady supply of cancer-fighting medical isotopes for the international healthcare sector.To meet rising demand for electricityThe start of work on Unit 5 arrives at a pivotal moment for Canada’s most populous province. Officials project that electricity demand across Ontario will surge by 90 percent by 2050, driven by rapid industrial expansion and widespread electrification.Project teams are entering Unit 5 with strong momentum after the neighboring Unit 4 outage. In October 2026, engineers on Unit 4 completed the installation of all 480 calandria tubes nearly a month ahead of schedule, setting a site record by outpacing the previous refit by 25 days. Technicians have now moved on to installing the fuel channels.That pace reflects lessons gathered from earlier phases of the multi-billion-dollar program. Unit 3 returned to commercial service this past June, finishing more than seven months ahead of schedule after teams successfully deployed specialized robotics on the reactor face for the first time. The early restart provided vital capacity during peak summer demand and delivered roughly $150 million back to Ontario ratepayers through the Independent Electricity System Operator. Unit 6, the first reactor upgraded under the initiative, also wrapped up ahead of schedule and under budget in 2023, returning $52 million to consumers.Long-term outage schedule“Extending the life of this critical asset will deliver reliable, affordable electricity, while strengthening Ontario’s position as a global energy superpower that can refurbish nuclear plants on time and on budget,” said Stephen Lecce, Ontario Minister of Energy and Mines. Lecce highlighted that 95 percent of Bruce Power’s spending stays within Canada.Eric Chassard, Bruce Power’s President and Chief Executive Officer, noted that performance has improved with every successive reactor refit as methods become more refined.To meet long-term supply targets, Bruce Power will run overlapping reactor outages continuously for the next seven years. Unit 7 will shut down for its upgrade in 2028, with Unit 8 following in 2030. Provincial planners are also evaluating a second major overhaul for Units 1 and 2, which originally returned to service in 2012.“This work is securing a reliable supply of clean electricity for decades to come and reinforcing our region’s role as a leader in Ontario’s nuclear success story,” concluded Lisa Thompson, MPP for Huron-Bruce.

title: Scientists spot elusive particle decay in search for 'Zeptoverse'
content: Scientists at the University of Manchester in the UK have found evidence for a rare particle decay that occurs once in 10 billion particles. The decay was spotted after a major upgrade at the LHCb experiment at CERN, and it also opens up avenues for further investigation at the zeptometre scale in the future. The LHCb experiment at CERN is different from the ATLAS and CMS detectors, since it is a forward spectrometer. Instead of looking for evidence of decay in all directions, LHCb focuses on the forward region of the beamline to study the behavior and decay of beauty and charm quarks. Beauty quarks are heavier than up and down quarks and are produced in large numbers in the LHC. However, they last for just one and a half trillionth of a second before decaying. For more than a decade and a half, researchers from the University of Manchester have been involved in the upgrade of the LHCb experiment, which now allows data collection at five times the rate of what was previously possible. Rare decay spottedPrecise measurements of beauty-quark decays allow scientists to detect the influence of new particles that may be too small to be detected by the LHC. If a decay is rare, it can be more sensitive to the influence of new particles. UK’s contribution to the LHCb upgrade was a Vertex Locator, a silicon pixel detector that sits a mere five millimeters from the beams, letting scientists pinpoint where particles are produced and where they decay. The team detected a ‘Bd to mu mu’ decay, where a beauty quark decays into two muons, which are electron-like particles but a bit heavier. Estimates suggest that these decays happen only once in 10 billion beauty particles, so it is not a surprise that it has never been spotted before. “This decay is remarkably unlikely; the chance of it happening is roughly like going on a romantic date and, on your very first try, finding the one perfect match for you among everyone on Earth”, said Chris Parkes, the Head of the Department of Physics and Astronomy at The University of Manchester, who was also involved in the upgrade of the LHCb experiment. Zeptometre-scale researchThe statistical significance for this find is 3.2 sigma, which is still less than the 5 sigma threshold needed to call this a major physics discovery. Nevertheless, it opens up avenues for physicists to explore particles and forces of nature hiding in spaces as small as a billionth of a trillionth of a meter. This distance is called a zeptometre, and the space is called the zeptoverse. The measurements made in this experiment are still in agreement with the Standard Model of Physics. However, further research into the Zeptoverse could help scientists find signs of new physics, which the Standard Model cannot explain. ““The results from this experiment are expanding our understanding of nature at its most fundamental level,” said Conor Fitzpatrick, Deputy Physics Coordinator of the LHCb collaboration in a press release. “We are excited to have finally seen this elusive signal and are looking forward to the future discoveries that will come from our data.”Even as the upgraded experiment will collect data till early 2030s, a further upgrade could increase data collection by another order of magnitude and reveal more about particles and forces in the zeptoverse.

title: Microbial fuel cell removes 99.99% of sewage antibiotics in 48 hours
content: Researchers have built a single, binder-free electrode that turns a Microbial Fuel Cell (MFC) into a multi-tasking system. It uses bacteria in municipal wastewater to generate electricity while simultaneously degrading a stubborn antibiotic and producing a valuable industrial chemical.Hungry bacteria digest organic waste in the wastewater and release electrons into the system. These flowing electrons help degrade 99.99 percent of the antibiotic within two days.Rather than generating plain water at the counter electrode, the process diverts the chemical pathway to synthesize hydrogen peroxide alongside a modest electrical current. Hydrogen peroxide is a oxidizing and disinfecting agent used in healthcare, environmental management, household cleaning, and manufacturing.This multi-tasking approach demonstrates how complex municipal sewage can simultaneously yield cleaner water, industrial chemicals, and renewable power.“The designed MFC was not only for treating the wastewater but also coupled simultaneous antibiotic removal and hydrogen peroxide generation,” the researchers noted in the study paper.Graphical abstract. Credit: Journal of Power SourcesHydrogen peroxide generationSewage is packed with organic matter and resilient pharmaceutical pollutants like chloramphenicol that treatment facilities fail to break down. A team of researchers in India transformed this environmental hazard into a resource by using a novel microbial fuel cell equipped with a custom iron-nickel carbon nanofiber electrode. Through microbial fuel cells, wastewater can be treated to produce bioenergy simultaneously.A microbial fuel cell normally uses bacteria that consume organic waste to generate electrons, which combine with oxygen at a second electrode to produce plain water. Researchers altered this standard pathway using a custom binder-free electrode made of iron and nickel oxide-tipped carbon nanofibers on flexible carbon cloth. This design forces incoming electrons down a shorter, two-electron path that stops the reduction halfway. The cell synthesizes valuable hydrogen peroxide instead of basic water. This process produces an industrial disinfectant and avoids energy-intensive traditional manufacturing methods.Antibiotic removalTesting on raw sewage spiked with 50 milligrams per liter of chloramphenicol showed the prototype’s high efficiency over a few hours. The electrified biological system achieved a triple benefit by removing 99.99 percent of the chloramphenicol and cutting chemical oxygen demand by 94 percent. Bacteria digesting the organic waste drove these high treatment rates, vastly outperforming passive control tests. At the same time, the system produced 0.74 mM hydrogen peroxide and maintained a steady electrical current and an open-circuit potential above 0.6 V.“Following the performance, the unified FeNiO-CNF/ACF electrocatalyst-based MFC emerges as a promising, economically viable, energy-efficient, and sustainable wastewater treatment, recalcitrant pollutant removal, and fuel generation system in a complex environment simultaneously,” the researchers noted in the study paper.Challenges remain. The overall power output is still small, typical of benchtop microbial fuel cells, and the team is currently studying the toxicity of the antibiotic’s breakdown products. Scale is another hurdle; the laboratory cell handled just 250 milliliters per chamber.Long-term durability remains a primary concern when deploying metal-oxide tips in continuous wastewater treatment. Extended exposure to raw sewage exposes the catalyst to corrosive chemical compounds and dense biological accumulation, which can block active sites over time.The findings were published in the Journal of Power Sources.

title: 235 Wh/L battery uses tin and carbon layers to reduce lithium loss
content: A battery measuring just 2.77 micrometers thick could offer a route to powering wearable electronics, tiny sensors, and medical devices. Developed by a team at Dongguk University in South Korea, the thin-film platform uses tin and carbon layers to control lithium deposition and reduce lithium loss during charging and discharging.Led by Professor Hyun-Suk Kim of the Department of Energy and Materials Engineering, the researchers combined the coating with an added lithium reserve to improve battery stability. The university announced the findings on November 3.Tackling uneven lithium depositionAll-solid-state batteries replace liquid electrolytes with solid materials, offering potential safety and energy-density advantages. However, uneven lithium plating and stripping can destabilize their operation.Anode-less designs address part of the manufacturing challenge by allowing lithium from the cathode to deposit onto a current collector during the first charge, forming the anode in place. This architecture can simplify fabrication and increase volumetric energy density, particularly in thin-film batteries.But lithium can become electrically isolated, forming “dead” lithium, or lose contact with the solid electrolyte during stripping. These processes reduce the lithium available for subsequent cycles and compromise capacity.The Dongguk team investigated whether a coating on the current collector could help control that process. “Our interlayer acts as a seed for Li nucleation, promoting uniform Li plating and reducing Li loss and improving the reversibility of repeated charging and discharging,” Kim said.Tin and carbon guide lithium growthThe researchers screened carbon-only, metal-only, and combined metal/carbon coatings. A tin/carbon bilayer on a copper current collector delivered the best overall performance among the configurations tested, showing favorable lithium deposition and interfacial stability.The two layers perform different roles. Tin lowers the energy barrier for lithium nucleation, helping lithium begin forming at the interface. The carbon overlayer regulates subsequent growth, potentially limiting uneven deposition and stabilizing the region where tin and lithium interact.The team also deposited a thin metallic lithium layer onto the coated collector. This prelithiation step created a reserve to compensate for lithium lost during initial cycling.During the first lithium plating, a three-dimensional textured region containing tin and lithium-tin formed within the interlayer. According to the researchers, this structure could accommodate volume and shape changes during later cycles, helping maintain contact and stability.Ultrathin platform shows storage potentialThe completed battery combined a lithium vanadium oxide cathode, a lithium phosphorus oxynitride solid electrolyte, and the coated copper current collector. It achieved a volumetric energy density of 235.13 Wh/L at its 100th cycle, measured at a reported rate of 0.01 C. Its overall thickness was 2.77 micrometers.“Our approach shows how interface engineering and lithium-inventory management can improve anode-less thin-film batteries,” Kim said.“This approach could support the development of ultrathin batteries for wearable electronics, IoT sensors, and medical devices, as well as scalable anode-less ASSBs for industrial-scale power,” he added.The findings identify a way to manage both lithium deposition and the lithium supply within an ultrathin battery architecture.The study was published in the journal Advanced Energy Materials.

title: 600 MW floating nuclear power barge targets US in world-first SMR bid
content: A Danish nuclear developer wants to bring floating atomic power to American shores. Saltfoss has sent a letter of intent to the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC). The firm wants to start early regulatory talks for its offshore power barge and seaMSR-100 reactor.If approved, the project will mark the world’s first licensed maritime advanced small modular reactor (SMR). The timing is interesting. In March 2026, the NRC introduced 10 CFR Part 53. This modern regulatory rulebook has been designed specifically for advanced reactors. Saltfoss aims to become the first developer to secure a license under this new framework.Instead of building a conventional plant inland from the ground up, Saltfoss plans to split production between two allied industrial hubs.Samsung Heavy Industries will build the standardized steel barges in South Korea, using the country’s high-volume shipbuilding yards. Once the hulls are complete, teams in the United States will handle reactor assembly, fuel loading, and final integration.“As part of its US expansion, Saltfoss will significantly increase its activities in the United States, including reactor assembly, fuel loading and final power plant integration at US facilities,” said the company in a press release.International regulatory alignmentThe company is also coordinating reviews across the Pacific. Saltfoss is working with South Korea’s Nuclear Safety and Security Commission under the nation’s SMR Special Act. South Korea is expected to host some of the earliest commercial deployments.Meanwhile, maritime safety evaluations are already under way. The American Bureau of Shipping is qualifying the barge design through its formal new technology review.“We are combining a US reactor design heritage proven at Oak Ridge National Laboratory with the world-class shipbuilding and nuclear supply chain of South Korea,” said Saltfoss Chief Executive Klaus Nyengaard.The underlying technology relies on a loop-type molten salt design refined over six years. Each standardized seaMSR-100 unit yields 100 megawatts of electricity (MWe). Multiple modules can sit aboard a single barge to deliver up to 600 MWe of constant electricity and high-temperature industrial heat. This capacity can power remote coastal industries, municipal grids, or power-hungry hyperscale data centers.Atmospheric-pressure physicsTraditional reactors operate under massive steam pressure. On the contrary, the seaMSR-100 operates near atmospheric pressure at temperatures between 600°C (1,112°F) and 700°C (1,292°F). It is fueled by conventional low-enriched uranium, avoiding rare or specialized fuel grades.Safety relies on plain physics rather than emergency backup generators. If power fails or core temperatures rise, the system shuts down and the liquid fuel salt drains by gravity into passive dump tanks without operator action.“Its fuel salt solidifies below approximately 500°C, trapping radioactive material and rendering a large release physically implausible; the reactor shuts down and drains by gravity alone, without operator action or external power,” concluded Saltfoss.Saltfoss finalized its conceptual design in 2025 alongside the Idaho National Laboratory and Danish researchers. The company plans to submit its formal Regulatory Engagement Plan to Washington in early 2027.

title: Xiaomi's humanoid robots take on eight-hour car parts sorting task
content: Xiaomi has released a video showing two humanoid robots sorting automotive components during an eight-hour task at its car factory. The demonstration focuses on a workstation where the robots handle and sort center-console side covers as part of an automotive production process.According to the company, its full-size humanoids can independently detect and correct anomalies while coordinating with the factory’s production line system. However, Xiaomi has not disclosed key performance figures, including parts-handling throughput, human intervention rates, or how the robots manage battery power during extended operations.Xiaomi tests enduranceThe firm has released a video showing two humanoid robots sorting automotive components during an eight-hour task at its car factory in China.The November 3 demonstration focuses on a center-console side-cover sorting workstation, where the machines repeatedly handle components and move them between containers and storage racks. The company said its full-size humanoid robots can autonomously detect and correct anomalies while coordinating their actions with the factory’s production line system. The test offers another look at Xiaomi’s efforts to develop humanoid robots that can perform repetitive industrial tasks over extended periods.8 hours on the production line. 🤖Xiaomi’s full-size humanoid robot takes on an 8-hour task at the Center Console Side-Cover Sorting Workstation at Xiaomi Auto Factory.Beyond sustained operation, it can autonomously detect and correct anomalies while coordinating with the… pic.twitter.com/brpO3S5bCn— Xiaomi Tech (@XiaomiTech_) November 3, 2026The video posted by Xiaomi Tech shows two humanoid robots working between large containers mounted on mobile platforms and upright racks containing individual storage slots. The machines repeatedly move components from the containers and place them into designated rack positions as part of the sorting process.A cumulative working-time counter tracks the demonstration, while on-screen overlays identify the operation as autonomous. The footage also includes accelerated playback at speeds of up to 100 times, compressing the extended operation into a shorter video.The workstation requires more than simply picking up and placing individual components. The robots must identify and handle the appropriate parts, position themselves around the containers and racks, and coordinate their movements with the surrounding production environment. According to the company, the humanoid can independently identify and correct anomalies while coordinating with the production line system. This suggests that the work extends beyond basic object manipulation to include fault detection and recovery during factory operations.However, Xiaomi has not explained which types of anomalies the robots can recognize or how they correct them. The company has also not released figures for sorting throughput, successful handling rates, human interventions, or the number of components processed during the eight-hour run.Battery management is another unanswered question. The demonstration does not establish whether the robots operated continuously on a single charge, received battery replacements or underwent charging during the task.Robots tackle manufacturingThe latest demonstration follows Xiaomi’s earlier efforts to introduce humanoid robots into automotive manufacturing.In March, the company reported a 90.2 percent success rate during a three-hour autonomous pilot involving simultaneous dual-side self-tapping nut installation at its Beijing electric vehicle factory. The robots completed the task while meeting a 76-second production cycle requirement.That trial focused on precision assembly, while the latest demonstration kvzorvh ur component sorting and material handling. Together, the two tests highlight different manufacturing tasks Xiaomi is exploring for humanoid robots.The company has also presented its CyberOne V2 humanoid at its Investor Day, demonstrating interactions with visitors and the handling of gift bags.Xiaomi’s latest test comes amid growing interest in deploying humanoids for automotive production. Audi, for example, has been testing mobile humanoids developed by Agile Robots for parts sequencing at its Ingolstadt Production Lab. Other automakers, including BMW, have also explored humanoid robots for factory operations.For Xiaomi, demonstrating an eight-hour task marks a step toward evaluating how humanoids perform beyond short, controlled demonstrations. However, working duration alone does not establish production readiness.More detailed figures on component-handling speed, task accuracy, recovery from errors, and human intervention would help establish how effectively the robots can operate alongside existing factory automation systems.

title: Photonic chip splits mixed light into 3 modes for sharper imaging
content: Researchers at Stanford University and collaborating institutions have developed a photonic chip that can separate partially coherent light into distinct, mutually incoherent beams, potentially helping cameras, microscopes and telescopes capture information that conventional imaging can miss.The fingernail-sized device uses a network of light-processing components and an optimisation algorithm to identify and physically separate the underlying coherence modes within a mixed optical field.The advance, published October 30 in Nature Photonics, demonstrates a capability that researchers had proposed theoretically decades ago but had not previously achieved experimentally.Most conventional optical systems are designed around coherent light, such as laser beams, whose waves maintain a stable relationship with one another. Ordinary light sources, by contrast, produce light with varying degrees of coherence. When multiple contributions overlap, their combined intensity can conceal information about the underlying optical field.The new photonic light analyser could help recover some of that information by separating the field into its distinct coherence modes.Chip learns light patternsThe researchers built the device using a silicon photonic circuit containing a network of interferometers. These components guide and manipulate light on a chip, much like electronic circuits process electrical signals.The team fed two independent infrared lasers into the chip, creating a partially coherent mixture. The device used a self-configuring network and an optimisation algorithm to identify the dominant coherence modes in the incoming light.Rather than simply separating the original laser sources, the chip diagonalises the light field’s coherency matrix. This produces orthogonal modes that are mutually incoherent, even when the original beams overlap spatially.The researchers demonstrated the approach using a nine-input device. It separated the two strongest coherence modes with more than 98 percent fidelity against a reference tomography method. They also verified that the system could operate beyond two modes in a separate three-mode experiment.Once configured, the chip physically routes the separated modes to different output channels, where they remain available for further optical processing.“Our chip learns the underlying coherence modes of an unknown light field and physically directs them into separate outputs,” said co-author Shanhui Fan, a professor of electrical engineering at Stanford.Imaging gains hidden informationThe ability to distinguish overlapping optical contributions could improve measurements in situations where conventional cameras record similar-looking intensity patterns.For example, two fluorescent particles positioned close together may appear as a single feature under a microscope. Their light could nevertheless contain different spatial and phase information. Separating the coherence modes could help reveal that distinction.The researchers also demonstrated that the chip could measure information contained in phase relationships that intensity-only measurements would miss.The team is now collaborating with NASA to investigate whether the approach could help analyse light from distant galaxies. A single bright feature in a telescope image, for instance, could contain light from multiple stars or other astronomical sources.Beyond imaging, the researchers said the technology could support optical sensing, communication and computing. The same chip architecture can also operate in reverse to generate partially coherent light with a chosen coherence structure.The work establishes a programmable approach to measuring, separating and controlling partially coherent light. Further development will be needed to scale the system to larger numbers of optical modes and faster control speeds before it can be used in practical imaging systems.The research was published in Nature Photonics.

title: First full-scale X-BAT combat drone prototype packs 2,000-mile range
content: Shield AI has completed the first full-scale prototype of its X-BAT autonomous combat aircraft, bringing its ambitious runway-independent fighter concept closer to flight testing. The aircraft uses a vertical takeoff and landing (VTOL) configuration that could allow U.S. forces to launch combat drones without conventional runways. Its design targets operations from naval vessels, remote islands, and other locations with limited infrastructure.Designated X-BAT 001, the prototype recently emerged from Shield AI’s development facility in Frisco, Texas. The company is now transporting the aircraft to its X-Forge 2 flight test facility in Newton, Kansas. Engineers will begin evaluating its propulsion system and vertical-flight capabilities before attempting untethered flight.Testing the vertical flight systemShield AI plans to follow a carefully staged testing program before X-BAT attempts its first independent flight. Engineers will initially run the engine horizontally while the aircraft rests on its launch and recovery vehicle. Vertical engine tests will follow.The team will then use a crane to support the aircraft during early flight experiments. This arrangement should help prevent a prototype loss if the engine stalls or another technical problem emerges. Successful crane-assisted trials would clear the way for untethered flight demonstrations.X-BAT’s propulsion system centers on GE Aerospace’s F110-GE-129E turbofan. The engine incorporates an Axisymmetric Vectoring Exhaust Nozzle (AVEN), which directs thrust to control the aircraft’s orientation during vertical operations.Shield AI and GE Aerospace completed engine ignition, nozzle movement, and integration tests in July. Those trials took place at GE’s facility in Peebles, Ohio. The work helped validate a critical part of the aircraft’s unusual flight configuration.Fighter without runwaysX-BAT takes a different approach to the U.S. military’s growing interest in Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA). Shield AI envisions a larger uncrewed platform capable of carrying substantial weapons loads. The aircraft reportedly measures roughly twice the size of the Air Force’s first-generation CCA designs.Its internal weapons bays should accommodate munitions weighing up to 2,000 pounds. External weapon stations could provide additional flexibility for different combat missions. Shield AI also identifies air-to-ground strikes, counterair operations, and electronic warfare among its intended roles.The aircraft will use the company’s Hivemind autonomy software to manage flight and mission execution. The system targets operations in environments where GPS signals or communications links become unreliable. This capability could prove particularly valuable during operations across contested regions.Shield AI has advertised a range exceeding 2,000 nautical miles with a full mission payload. Its stated combat radius reaches approximately 1,000 nautical miles. Flight testing must establish whether the aircraft can achieve those performance targets.A changing aircraft designNew footage of X-BAT 001 also reveals several differences from earlier design models, as TWZ noted. Its thrust-vectoring exhaust nozzle now extends noticeably beyond the rear edges of its wings. Previous renderings showed a more recessed arrangement.Two prominent structures also appear on either side of the aircraft’s central dorsal spine. Each features a small forward-facing opening. Two additional circular openings sit atop the spine, with mesh screens covering them. Their purpose remains unclear, although they could relate to the propulsion system.The exhaust nozzle provides pitch and yaw control, while Shield AI previously described using wing-mounted bleed-air thrusters for roll control. The newly visible openings could offer clues about that arrangement, but the company has not explained their function.X-BAT has already undergone substantial design changes since its October 2025 unveiling. A half-scale model displayed at the Navy League’s Sea-Air-Space 2026 exhibition featured a revised arrowhead-shaped wing planform. The full-scale prototype now offers a clearer look at the engineering choices behind the aircraft.

title: Raytheon's optical processor could help US forces spot threats faster
content: Raytheon is developing a new type of processor that could help US military systems recognize incoming threats faster. The technology uses light to handle data processing, potentially removing a major bottleneck in today’s electronic systems.The defense contractor secured a Phase 1 award from the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) for its work. The effort falls under DARPA’s Photonic Integrated Circuit Architectures for Scalable System Objectives (PICASSO) program. Its goal is to advance photonic circuits capable of processing information entirely through optical signals.Processing data with lightMost photonic circuits still rely on conventional electronics for important computing tasks. They first convert incoming optical signals into electrical signals before processing the information. That extra step can introduce delays and add complexity to increasingly sophisticated systems.Raytheon’s proposed architecture aims to eliminate that conversion requirement. It will keep signal processing within the optical domain, using light throughout the operation. This approach could help preserve signal strength and information quality during processing.The distinction matters as military platforms collect increasingly large volumes of sensor data. Radar systems, electronic warfare equipment, and other defense sensors must interpret information quickly. Even small processing delays can affect how operators respond to rapidly developing threats.All-optical processing could eventually help military systems handle those demands with greater speed. It may also support more compact circuit designs as engineers increase processing capabilities. However, Raytheon’s Phase 1 effort will focus on developing and demonstrating the underlying technology.DARPA backs photonic developmentRaytheon’s Advanced Technology division will lead the development work. The team brings experience in photonics manufacturing processes and radio frequency engineering. It also has experience developing technologies for military applications.Commercial engineering software provider Synopsys will support the effort. The company will supply design and simulation tools for developing the photonic architecture. Those tools should help engineers model circuit behavior before moving toward physical demonstrations.DARPA’s PICASSO program targets photonic integrated circuit architectures that can scale across different applications. Integrated photonics uses light to transmit and manipulate information within compact circuits. The technology already supports applications in telecommunications and high-speed data transmission.Military applications introduce additional engineering challenges. Defense systems must operate reliably under demanding conditions. Their processing hardware must also accommodate increasingly complex signals without compromising performance.Faster decisions in contested environmentsThe potential military applications extend beyond simply speeding up individual calculations. Faster optical processing could help sensors deliver useful information to operators sooner. That could improve reaction times during engagements involving multiple incoming threats.Electronic warfare presents another possible application. Military platforms must identify and interpret signals in increasingly crowded electromagnetic environments. Processing information faster could help crews recognize changing threats and adjust their responses.However, the technology remains under development. Raytheon has not disclosed a deployment timeline or specific performance targets for the system. The Phase 1 award represents an early step toward demonstrating its capabilities.If successful, the work could offer defense engineers another way to overcome processing limitations. It could also help future military platforms manage growing sensor workloads without relying entirely on conventional electronic architectures.

title: Anthropic unveils cryptographic tool to verify model outputs
content: Anthropic has unveiled FlashProve, an open-source cryptographic system designed to verify whether an AI model actually generated a response without revealing its proprietary weights. The technology could help users, independent auditors and regulators confirm that providers are running the models they claim to serve.The system uses zero-knowledge cryptography to generate mathematical proofs that a specific model produced given output tokens in response to a particular prompt. This could address a growing trust problem as companies increasingly rely on third-party model providers and routing services to access advanced AI systems.Today, users have no reliable way to establish whether a response came from the model they selected or whether a provider secretly substituted a cheaper alternative. FlashProve aims to provide that assurance without requiring users to access or independently run the model.Cryptographic proofs verify outputsFlashProve uses a cryptographic technique called a zero-knowledge succinct non-interactive argument of knowledge (zkSNARK). It allows a provider to demonstrate that a computation was performed correctly without revealing sensitive information about the underlying model.The system works in two stages. First, the provider publishes a cryptographic commitment to its model weights, effectively creating a fingerprint of the exact model being used while keeping the weights private.When a user submits a request, the provider can subsequently generate a proof that the committed model produced the corresponding output tokens. Anyone with the commitment, prompt and response can verify the proof without accessing the model weights.Anthropic demonstrated the approach using Llama 4 Maverick, a 400-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model. Running on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU, FlashProve generated proofs at approximately 110 tokens per second, with each proof measuring around 19 MB for a 1,024-token request.Verification takes approximately 17 seconds using a 24-core CPU, without requiring a GPU.Security meets practical challengesThe technology could have applications beyond checking whether customers receive the model they selected. Anthropic believes cryptographic inference proofs could help detect tampering with model responses, support independent evaluations and give regulators a way to verify which models providers are serving.For example, a company could require a provider to demonstrate that its cybersecurity software was examined by a particular model rather than a cheaper substitute. Regulators could also use such proofs to check whether providers are serving approved models or meeting certain commitments on AI development.However, FlashProve remains a research prototype rather than a production-ready solution. Generating proofs requires substantially more computing resources than ordinary inference. Anthropic’s measurements show that the process takes approximately 70 to 95 times the GPU time required by vLLM, a widely used open-source inference engine.The current system also supports contexts of up to 1,024 tokens and proves an integer version of the model under greedy decoding. It does not yet cover every floating-point or sampled inference result. Additionally, it hides model weights but not the model’s architecture.Anthropic has released the system’s executable code, technical report, protocol specification and formal verification proofs under the Apache 2.0 licence. The company said the release is intended to encourage other researchers to build on the work and improve the technology.The research represents an early step towards making model identity and response integrity independently verifiable, potentially giving users greater confidence in the systems powering their applications.

title: Radar-equipped 40mm naval gun packs power to counter drone swarms
content: BAE Systems is bringing four configurations of its Bofors 40mm naval gun technology under one product family, giving ship operators different ways to tackle incoming aerial and surface threats. The lineup ranges from a gun with independent electro-optical targeting to a radar-equipped close-in weapon system designed to intercept missiles and drones.Called the Sea Tridon family, the lineup includes Sea Tridon, Sea TridonC, Sea Trinity and the Bofors 40 Mk4 Naval Gun. Each configuration serves a different operational requirement, but all four use the company’s programmable 3P ammunition.The announcement reflects a growing challenge for naval forces. Drones, missiles and other relatively inexpensive weapons are adding new demands to shipboard defenses. BAE Systems is positioning its new family as a way to give operators more choices without introducing entirely separate weapons and support systems.Expanding naval firepowerSea Tridon combines a Bofors 40mm gun with an integrated electro-optical fire-control system. Its independent targeting capability gives operators greater control over engagements and simplifies integration with different vessel designs.Sea TridonC takes that arrangement to sea inside a containerized package. Crews can install it aboard military, government or commercial vessels that need additional protection for particular missions. Its design also makes temporary deployment possible without requiring a permanent weapons installation.Sea Trinity brings radar into the equation. The system combines the Bofors 40mm gun with radar-based fire control and 3P ammunition. BAE Systems describes it as a complete close-in weapon system (CIWS), intended to engage incoming missiles, drones and other high-speed threats.The Bofors 40 Mk4 Naval Gun takes a different approach. Its compact, lightweight design allows integration with a vessel’s existing combat management systems. It can engage both aerial and surface targets without the more extensive configuration offered by Sea Trinity.Lena Gillström, president of BAE Systems Bofors, said the maritime threat environment is changing rapidly. She described the family as a flexible option for navies seeking different levels of defensive capability.Six ways to program a roundThe ammunition deserves attention in its own right. All four configurations use Bofors 3P programmable ammunition, which lets crews select the projectile’s fuze settings immediately before firing.The system offers six programmable fuze modes. These allow the same ammunition family to engage different target types, including aircraft, surface vessels, and threats along shorelines.That versatility changes how operators can approach an engagement. Instead of depending on separate ammunition types for different targets, crews can configure the projectile to suit the situation.The shared ammunition also gives the four configurations a common logistical foundation. BAE Systems says the wider family maintains commonality in training, logistics and support, despite differences in sensor integration and fire-control equipment.Gillström said operators could select the configuration that best matches their operational requirements while retaining access to established technology and programmable ammunition.BAE Systems will showcase Sea Tridon at Euronaval 2026 in Paris. The system will appear at stand E30, alongside the company’s wider naval defense offering.
