title: 33 Out of 34 Lupus Patients Shared an Immune Cell Abnormality
content:
Lupus is a chronic autoimmune disease in which the immune system mistakenly attacks the body’s own healthy tissues, causing inflammation and potentially damaging organs. The most common form, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), can affect the joints, skin, kidneys, heart, and brain. Credit: Shutterstock
New research challenges a longstanding explanation for why the immune system attacks healthy tissues in lupus.
Scientists investigating lupus have discovered that errors in immune cells may cause the body to attack some of its own defenses. In a study of 34 patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), 33 had neutrophils containing widespread abnormalities in RNA processing. These changes were absent from blood samples taken from healthy volunteers.
Neutrophils normally help defend the body against infections, but the altered cells produced unusual molecules that other immune cells appeared to recognize as threats. Researchers at the La Jolla Institute for Immunology (LJI) and the University of Washington (UW) found evidence that both T cells and antibody-producing B cells could participate in this response, potentially contributing to the inflammation and tissue damage associated with lupus.
How RNA Errors May Trigger an Immune Attack
The abnormalities involve RNA “splicing,” a process that allows cells to remove unnecessary sections of genetic instructions before using them to produce proteins. In the lupus patients, errors caused sections of RNA to be joined incorrectly. When cells attempted to “read” these altered instructions, they generated unusual peptides, short chains of amino acids that can be recognized by the immune system.
T cells routinely inspect peptides displayed on cell surfaces to identify infections and other threats. When they encounter unfamiliar or “foreign” peptides, especially in the presence of inflammation, they may respond as though they have detected a pathogen. These molecular targets are known as “antigens.” Peptides produced through abnormal RNA processing can become “neoantigens,” potentially making the body’s own cells targets of an immune response.
“When a cell type whose function is pro-inflammatory, such as neutrophils, also expresses potentially immunogenic mutations, the conditions for immune attack are met: T cells sense a foreign antigen plus inflammation or ‘danger’ signals,” explains LJI Professor Stephen Schoenberger, Ph.D.
Study co-leader LJI Professor Stephen Schoenberger, Ph.D. Credit: La Jolla Institute for Immunology
Researchers Find Widespread Abnormalities in Lupus Patients
The findings, published in
, emerged from a collaboration between Schoenberger and UW School of Medicine Professor Tomas Mustelin, M.D., Ph.D. Mustelin’s laboratory had identified unusually frequent RNA splicing errors in neutrophils from lupus patients. Schoenberger, whose research focuses on immune recognition of mutation-derived antigens, investigated whether those errors could produce molecules capable of provoking an immune response.
Schoenberger has previously studied neoantigens in cancer, where mutations can create abnormal molecules that help immune cells recognize and attack tumors. Applying similar methods to lupus, the researchers found that altered neutrophils expressed numerous neoantigens that could alert the immune system. They also identified evidence that B cells, which produce antibodies, were prepared to respond to the affected cells.
“This may get to the very crux of the disease pathogenesis,” says Schoenberger, referring to the biological processes responsible for lupus.
A Different Explanation for Autoimmune Disease
Lupus is a chronic autoimmune disease in which immune activity can damage joints, skin, kidneys, and other organs. Scientists have long investigated why T cells and B cells begin attacking the body’s own tissues. One explanation involves a breakdown of immune “tolerance,” the mechanisms that normally prevent immune cells from responding to healthy tissues.
The new findings support an alternative possibility known as the “neoantigen hypothesis” of autoimmunity. Rather than mistakenly recognizing normal cellular components as dangerous, immune cells may encounter genuinely unfamiliar molecules generated within the body. Their responses could therefore follow the same biological rules used to recognize foreign threats.
“Rather than a failure of immune tolerance, autoimmunity can be caused by the immune system doing exactly what it’s supposed to do, which is to mount an attack on non-self, on things that are foreign,” says Schoenberger.
Are the Abnormalities a Cause or Consequence of Lupus?
Although the researchers identified a potential mechanism for immune “self-attack,” they have not established whether abnormal RNA splicing helps initiate lupus or develops in response to existing inflammation. Neutrophils are already known to contribute to the complex immune processes that sustain the disease.
“Neutrophils clearly participate in a self-amplifying inflammatory circuit in SLE, involving autoantibodies, immune complexes, nucleic acids, type I interferons, and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs),” says Schoenberger. “So now the big question is whether neoantigens are a cause or consequence of this process? Neutrophils might be responding to inflammation that’s already causing tissue damage.”
Determining when these RNA abnormalities develop, and whether the resulting neoantigens directly drive harmful immune responses, will be necessary to establish their role in lupus. The findings give researchers a specific molecular process to investigate as they work to understand how autoimmune inflammation begins and persists.

Zavala, Vincent Gureghian, Gabriela Cervantes, Sadie J. Van den Bogaerde, Samir Adhikari, Mikhail V. Pogorelyy, Paul G. Thomas, Stephen P. Schoenberger and Tomas Mustelin, 28 October 2026,

title: Common Nutritional Supplement Shows Surprising Promise Against Psoriasis
content:
Psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory disease that causes skin cells to build up rapidly, forming thick, scaly patches that may itch, crack, or become painful. Credit: Shutterstock
A common nutritional supplement has shown unexpected promise in treating psoriasis.
A widely available nutritional supplement may help reduce the immune system activity responsible for psoriasis, according to new research from China. Scientists found that pantethine, a derivative of vitamin B5 commonly used to lower cholesterol, can interfere with metabolic processes that drive inflammation. The findings were supported by experiments in mice and a small clinical trial involving people with psoriasis.
In the 12-week trial, 24 patients received standard treatment with topical calcipotriene/betamethasone ointment. Half also took pantethine tablets. Participants receiving the supplement showed improvements in their symptoms, particularly those who started with elevated blood cholesterol levels. Although encouraging, the results are preliminary and do not establish pantethine as an effective standalone treatment.
How Cholesterol Metabolism Affects Immune Cells
The research focused on dendritic cells, immune cells that help organize the body’s defenses. These cells detect and present foreign substances to specialized T cells and release chemical signals that recruit other immune cells. When dendritic cells become excessively active, they can sustain the inflammation associated with psoriasis and other autoimmune diseases.
The scientists discovered unusually high levels of enzymes called Vanins in dendritic cells from patients with psoriasis and several other autoimmune conditions. Vanins convert pantethine into vitamin B5, an essential nutrient involved in cellular energy production. The researchers found that increased Vanin activity depleted pantethine, promoting cholesterol production within dendritic cells and triggering excessive immune activation.
“Emerging evidence highlights that metabolic pathways and their associated metabolites play vital roles in regulating immune cell function and autoimmune progression,” says Wei-Na Zhang, a researcher at the State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Analysis in Beijing. “But therapeutic strategies targeting metabolism in inflammatory diseases remain underexplored.”
Blocking the Enzymes That Drive Inflammation
To investigate this connection, the researchers reduced Vanin levels in dendritic cells. Without these enzymes, the cells became less active and were less capable of stimulating T cells. A drug that inhibited Vanins also prevented the development of psoriasis in mice.
Further experiments showed that replenishing pantethine reduced cholesterol accumulation inside dendritic cells and suppressed their activation. Pantethine treatment also alleviated psoriasis symptoms in mice, providing additional evidence that the metabolic pathway contributes to inflammatory disease.
Psoriasis patients prescribed pantethine capsules in addition to topical ointments show a marked improvement in symptoms after 3 months of treatment (bottom). Credit: 2026 Cao et al. Originally published in Journal of Experimental Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1084/jem.20252558
“We found that pantethine administration effectively alleviated psoriasis in mice, suggesting that insufficient pantethine levels may be the crucial contributor to hyperactivation of dendritic cells and autoimmune inflammation following the up-regulation of Vanins,” Zhang says.
Early Clinical Results Point to a Potential Treatment
Pantethine has long been available as a nutritional supplement because it can inhibit cholesterol synthesis. The new findings suggest that its effects on cholesterol metabolism may also influence immune responses. However, the small human trial cannot establish whether the improvements resulted from the same cellular mechanism demonstrated in laboratory experiments.
“Our investigator-initiated clinical trial demonstrated encouraging therapeutic efficacy of pantethine as an adjunctive therapy in psoriasis, but these findings should be interpreted as proof-of-concept for clinical feasibility rather than direct mechanistic validation,” Zhang says. “Overall, our study uncovers the Vanin-pantethine-cholestrol axis as a key metabolic pathway governing dendritic cell activation and provides a foundation for therapeutic strategies targeting several dendritic cell–mediated autoimmune diseases.”

title: Trapped in Amber for 99 Million Years, a Lizard’s Tail Reveals an Ancient Survival Secret
content:
A lizard tail trapped in approximately 99-million-year-old amber from northern Myanmar (left), alongside a three-dimensional reconstruction produced using microscopic X-ray imaging (right). The amber piece measures just 18 millimeters across. Credit: Dolev Fabrikant
A clean break in 99-million-year-old amber offers rare direct evidence that ancient lizards shed their tails using a defensive mechanism still common today.
A lizard can escape a predator by leaving its tail behind, sometimes with the detached piece still wriggling as the animal makes its getaway. It’s a remarkable defense, but scientists have struggled to determine how far back it goes. Ancient reptile fossils can show where a tail was capable of breaking, yet that doesn’t necessarily mean the animal could shed it to escape danger.
An unusually revealing clue has now emerged from a tiny piece of amber discovered in northern Myanmar. Measuring just 18 millimeters (about 0.7 inches) long, the amber holds a lizard’s tail that detached approximately 99 million years ago. What makes it so valuable is the remarkably preserved point where the tail separated from the body. Researchers say it provides the best-preserved direct fossil evidence of autotomy, the defensive mechanism that allows lizards to shed their tails.
A lizard tail trapped in approximately 99-million-year-old amber from northern Myanmar (left), alongside a three-dimensional reconstruction produced using microscopic X-ray imaging (right). The amber piece measures just 18 millimeters across. Credit: Dolev Fabrikant
An ancient tail mistaken for a twig
For years, no one recognized what was trapped inside the amber. Dolev Fabrikant, a PhD candidate at Tel Aviv University’s New Environmental School, was examining what appeared to be a tiny twig or fragment of an insect when he noticed something unusual about its surface. “I realized that what seemed to be a twig was covered in tiny scales,” he recalls. “It was a lizard’s tail.”
Fabrikant shared his discovery with his supervisor, Dr. Leonidas-Romanos Davranoglou of Tel Aviv University’s School of Zoology and Steinhardt Museum of Natural History, whose reaction was immediate.
“I nearly jumped out of my chair,” says Dr. Davranoglou. “I instantly realized that this tiny fossil could open an extraordinary window into the past, helping us understand the history of one of the most widespread survival strategies among reptiles. Until now, we could only speculate on whether ancient lizards could shed their tails. We now have direct evidence that one could.”
The fossil’s point of separation, reconstructed using X-ray imaging (left), preserves a flower-like arrangement of muscle resembling that of a self-shed tail from a modern lizard (right). This distinctive structure helped researchers distinguish controlled tail shedding from accidental breakage. Credit: Dolev Fabrikant
Scans reveal a clean, deliberate break
Getting a closer look at the fossil was another challenge. The amber was cloudy, and the structures inside were too small for an ordinary microscope to reveal the details researchers needed. Rather than cutting open the specimen, the team turned to micro-CT scanning at Israel’s Volcani Institute.
“Micro-CT takes X-ray images from many angles and combines them into a three-dimensional reconstruction. It allowed us to examine structures hidden by the amber without needing to cut this one-of-a-kind piece open,” explains Dr. Ahmed Nasser, Head of the institute’s Inter-Institutional Analytical Unit.
Research team (Left to right): Dr. Ahmed Nasser, Dolev Fabrikant & Dr. Leonidas-Romanos Davranoglou. Credit: Tel Aviv University
At the severed end of the tail, the scans revealed a distinctive ring of tissue closely resembling the structure found in tails shed by living lizards. The separation itself was relatively clean and symmetrical, without the damage patterns that would be expected if the tail had broken off in an accident.
That distinction matters because other reptile fossils have offered less conclusive evidence. Some preserve natural fracture planes in the tail vertebrae, while others contain regenerated tails, indicating that the animals had lost part of their tails previously. Although these features suggest that ancient reptiles possessed the ability to shed their tails, the presence of fracture planes alone cannot establish that they actually used this defense. In the Myanmar specimen, the preserved tissue and clean separation provide much stronger evidence that the tail was released through autotomy.
Apostolos Christopoulos. Credit: The National and Kapodistrian University of Athens
The lizard’s identity and fate remain unknown
The researchers still cannot determine exactly what kind of lizard left the tail behind. Without the rest of its skeleton, including the skull, there are too few anatomical clues to identify its closest relatives.
“Although we can securely identify this specimen as a lizard, we lack the skull and other skeletal features that would allow a more secure identification. Possible affinities include the groups containing today’s wall lizards or, alternatively, slow worms and monitor lizards,” says Apostolos Christopoulos, a PhD candidate at the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens.
How the tail ended up in amber is another mystery. The lizard might have become stuck in sticky resin and shed its tail to free itself. It is also possible that a predator attacked the animal, prompting it to release its tail, which later landed in resin.

title: 120 Million Years Ago, Something Extraordinary Was Happening in Earth’s Oceans
content:
Giant marine reptiles like long-necked plesiosaurs and marine crocodile relatives, as well as turtles, sharks, crustaceans and others, formed the Paja Biota, “one of the most ecologically complex marine communities found to date,” says researcher Dirley Cortés. Credit: Juan Giraldo
Colombia’s ancient seas supported an extraordinary diversity of top predators, offering clues to how life may undergo major evolutionary changes without a mass extinction.
Mass extinctions have reshaped life on Earth, but they may not be the only way ecosystems undergo dramatic evolutionary change.
Roughly 120 million years ago, the seas covering what is now central Colombia were home to an extraordinary mix of ancient Jurassic survivors and emerging Cretaceous predators. Fossils from this remarkably complex ecosystem suggest that some of evolution’s biggest turning points may unfold without a catastrophic mass extinction.
The Paja Biota’s predator-rich food web
The evidence comes from the Early Cretaceous Paja Formation near Villa de Leyva, Colombia, where the Centro de Investigaciones Paleontológicas (CIP) houses most of the formation’s fossils. The research at McGill University and CIP was conducted by PhD graduate Dirley Cortés and Professor Hans Larsson of McGill’s Department of Biology.
“This geological formation has produced an exceptionally rich fossil record that includes giant marine reptiles like long-necked plesiosaurs and marine crocodile relatives, as well as turtles, sharks, crustaceans and others,” Cortés explained. “Together, these animals formed the Paja Biota, one of the most ecologically complex marine communities found to date.”
Researcher Dirley Cortés at the CIP. Credit: Center for Paleontological Research
previous study
, the researchers estimated the Paja Biota’s food web, the network of feeding relationships among its animals. They found it was among the most complex ever to have evolved, with a high diversity of apex predators, animals at the top of the food chain.
Ocean conditions may explain rare coexistence
“The Paja Formation records an extraordinary process in the history of life, when a ‘perfect storm’ of environmental factors we know to promote ecological complexity coincided with ancient lineages that were about to disappear. At the same time, new groups were beginning to flourish,” Larsson said.
The researchers suspect that greenhouse temperatures, high sea levels, and nutrient-rich coastal waters helped support this exceptional biodiversity and biological transition. New marine connections between the eastern Pacific and early Atlantic oceans through what is now Colombia were probably also part of that rare convergence. Many of these same factors help drive biodiversity today, they noted.
The team identified the pattern in the Early Cretaceous Paja Formation near Villa de Leyva, Colombia, where the CIP houses most of its fossils. Credit: Center for Paleontological Research
Testing whether Biotic Inflections happened elsewhere
Cortés and Larsson propose calling the pattern a “Biotic Inflection,” a period when many evolutionary lineages nearing extinction coexist with newly emerging groups that later diversify.
“I think we’ve discovered a new model of global biodiversity change. Now we’ll need to see just how widespread this could be in Earth’s history and how we can quantify its impacts,” Larsson said.
Testing the proposal will require additional fossil sampling, more precise dating, and comparisons with deposits elsewhere in the world. Those investigations would help establish how widespread the Biotic Inflection pattern was and when similar events may have occurred in Earth’s history.
Reference: “The Paja Formation of Colombia records uniquely high biodiversity during a biotic inflection in an Early Cretaceous Gondwanan marine ecosystem” by Dirley Cortés and Hans C. E. Larsson, 15 May 2026,
Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution

title: Comets Probably Didn’t Bring Life’s Ingredients to Earth After All, New Study Reveals
content:
Comets have collided with Earth throughout its history, with impacts occurring more frequently during the Solar System’s early development. These icy objects carry organic molecules that may contribute to prebiotic chemistry, although the extreme heat and energy of collisions make it difficult for such compounds to survive. Credit: Shutterstock
New research suggests Mars may have been better suited than Earth to receive life’s chemical ingredients from comets, although the chances remain surprisingly slim.
Comets have long been considered possible sources of the chemical ingredients that helped life emerge on Earth. But new research suggests these icy visitors were extremely unlikely to deliver those molecules in sufficient quantities, challenging a theory that has shaped scientific thinking for nearly a century.
Using advanced computer simulations, researchers led by the
University of Cambridge
found that comet impacts would almost always destroy fragile organic compounds before they could contribute to the chemistry of early life. Even under favorable conditions, successful delivery would have been extraordinarily rare. The findings, published in
Scientific Reports
, also suggest that Mars may have offered slightly better conditions for receiving these molecules.
Why Comets May Have Been Poor Carriers of Life’s Ingredients
Comets contain carbon and nitrogen-bearing compounds, including hydrogen cyanide (HCN), a molecule involved in chemical reactions that can produce some of life’s essential building blocks. Their ability to transport these substances across the Solar System has made them central to theories about how prebiotic chemistry began on Earth.
“Historically, scientists thought that comets were important for the origin of life on Earth, because they carried carbon and nitrogen-bearing molecules, so these giant space snowballs were almost like a ‘get out of jail free card’ that brought all the molecules a planet would need to seed life,” said lead author Dr. Richard Anslow from Cambridge’s Institute of Astronomy. “It’s kind of a romantic idea, but our results suggest it’s highly unlikely.”
Illustration of cometary impact. Credit: Scarlett White
The problem lies in the violence of comet impacts. According to the simulations, comets generally approach Earth at speeds and angles that make the survival of their organic cargo extremely unlikely. Most of these molecules would vaporize during impact rather than reach the surface intact. The researchers reached this conclusion by combining models of comet trajectories, atmospheric interactions, impact physics, and the formation and evolution of comet populations.
Even a Successful Impact Might Not Be Enough
To investigate the likelihood of successful delivery, the team concentrated on HCN, which is regularly detected in Solar System comets. Their calculations showed that impacts capable of preserving the molecule and depositing it at useful concentrations would have been exceptionally uncommon.
The number of comets striking Earth also fell sharply during the planet’s first 500 million years, leaving at most a handful of opportunities for meaningful HCN delivery. Even if some molecules survived, they would likely disperse before the chemical reactions needed for life’s emergence could advance far enough.
“It would really have to be a one-in-a-million occurrence, because not only would you need an impact at just the right speed and just the right angle, you would also need everything to happen after that point, in terms of the concentration and the speed at which the chemical origins of life got going,” said Anslow. “We can’t rule out for certain that it happened that way. But it seems to be a really rare occurrence – at best, a one-off fluke.”
Testing a Theory That Dates Back Nearly a Century
The investigation builds on
earlier research published in 2023
, when Anslow and several colleagues proposed that closely spaced planets could help comets deliver organic molecules. In such systems, gravitational encounters might allow comets to move between planets while gradually slowing down, increasing the chances that their chemical cargo could survive an eventual impact.
The new study examined whether similar conditions could have existed in our Solar System, using recent advances in simulations of comet impacts and planetary dynamics.
“We’re learning more and more all the time about how our Solar System and the Earth formed, and pulling this together with lots of different advances in modeling, which allowed us to investigate this idea that has been around for close to a century,” Anslow said.
If comets were not a major source of Earth’s prebiotic molecules, other explanations remain possible. Asteroids struck the early Earth much more frequently, and their impacts could have triggered chemical reactions that produced organic compounds. Alternatively, the necessary ingredients may have formed through chemical processes occurring on Earth itself, without requiring delivery from space.
Mars May Have Had Better Chances
Although the results cast doubt on cometary delivery to Earth, the researchers identified Mars as a somewhat more favorable destination. Mars is smaller than Earth and currently has a much thinner atmosphere, conditions that could allow more cometary material to reach its surface. This may have increased the chances of organic molecules surviving impacts during the Solar System’s early history, when comet collisions were more common.
However, the simulations do not establish that comets successfully delivered prebiotic molecules to Mars. They indicate only that the process may have been more feasible there than on Earth.
“This is not to say it definitely happened on Mars, of course, but suggests it would be unlikely if it happened on Earth and didn’t happen on Mars,” said Anslow. “Or the other, perhaps more likely, alternative, is that it didn’t happen on either planet.”
Implications for the Search for Life Beyond Earth
The findings could also help astronomers assess the chemical environments of planets orbiting other stars. In planetary systems where several worlds orbit close together, gravitational interactions might slow incoming comets enough to improve the prospects for delivering organic molecules.
Future observatories, including proposed successors to the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), such as the Habitable Worlds Observatory, could help investigate these planetary systems. Identifying environments where “bouncing” comets might survive long enough to deliver their chemical cargo could provide one way to narrow the search for potentially habitable worlds.
Reference: “Cometary impacts an unlikely pathway towards the origins of life on Earth” by Richard J. Anslow, Catriona H. McDonald, Amy Bonsor, Paul B. Rimmer and Auriol S. P. Rae, 28 October 2026,
Scientific Reports
DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-74214-y
The research was supported in part by the Royal Society, the Leverhulme Centre for Life in the Universe, and the Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC), part of UK Research and Innovation (UKRI).

title: The Mystery of Hair Growth Patterns May Finally Have a Simple Explanation
content:
Scientists have uncovered a surprisingly simple mechanism that may explain how hair follicles arrange themselves into distinct patterns across mammalian species. Credit: Shutterstock
A new study reveals how subtle interactions between cells and chemical signals may shape the intricate patterns of mammalian hair.
The precise arrangement of hair follicles across an animal’s skin may arise from a surprisingly simple process. Researchers at the
University of Geneva (UNIGE)
have developed a mathematical model showing how cells responding to chemical signals can generate distinct hair patterns in two mammalian species, without requiring a complex system to determine where each follicle forms.
How Hair Follicles Find Their Positions
Hair follicles begin forming before birth in specialized embryonic structures called placodes. These structures also give rise to feathers and most types of scales. Their arrangement varies between species, but scientists have long debated how developing tissues establish such organized patterns.
For laboratory mice (Mus musculus), the prevailing explanation has been the expansion-induction model. According to this theory, each newly formed placode releases an inhibitory molecule that temporarily prevents others from developing nearby. As the skin expands, new areas move beyond the molecule’s influence, allowing additional placodes to form in the spaces between existing ones.
Although this model can account for the developmental patterns observed in laboratory mice, researchers have not experimentally established that it explains hair follicle organization more broadly across mammals.
Spiny mice (Acomys dimidiatus), a species used to study how hair patterns are organized during embryonic development. Credit: A. Debry & F. Montange
A Simpler Mechanism Driven by Chemical Signals
A research team co-led by Athanasia Tzika, Senior Lecturer, and Michel Milinkovitch, Professor in UNIGE’s Department of Genetics and Evolution, investigated a different mechanism called chemotaxis. This process allows cells to move in response to chemical gradients. It also helps white blood cells navigate toward areas of inflammation.
The researchers created a mathematical model in which mobile cells in the dermis respond to an attractive chemical signal produced by the epidermis, the skin’s outer layer. As the simulated embryonic skin grows, these interactions spontaneously produce placodes in patterns that closely match the developmental sequence observed in laboratory mice.
“Our findings show that the observed patterns do not require a complex system telling each placode where to form,” explain Muhamet Ibrahimi and Ebrahim Jahanbakhsh, researchers in the Department of Genetics and Evolution. “Instead, placodes emerge spontaneously from local interactions between cells and chemical signals.”
Testing the Model in a Different Mammal
The researchers next examined the spiny mouse (Acomys dimidiatus), a rodent whose hair follicles form a highly regular, directionally organized pattern. Unlike the arrangement found in laboratory mice, this distinctive configuration cannot be explained by the traditional expansion-induction model.
Using experimental data obtained through three-dimensional imaging of embryonic skin, the team adapted its mathematical model to reflect the spiny mouse’s particular biochemical characteristics and skin growth patterns. The same chemotactic mechanism successfully reproduced the species’ characteristic follicle arrangement.
These simulations suggest that different mammalian hair patterns could emerge from a shared process governed by cell movement and chemical signaling, with species-specific differences in how those interactions unfold. The results provide a potential alternative to the conventional model, although mathematical agreement with observed patterns does not establish that chemotaxis is the mechanism operating in living skin.
“Our work suggests that simple cellular interactions can generate the remarkable diversity of tissue architectures observed throughout evolution,” concludes Athanasia Tzika. “The differences observed between species therefore result from the same self-organization process, but with variations in the interactions between cells and chemical signals.”
Reference: “Chemotactic self-organization captures the dynamics of mammalian hair follicle patterning” by Muhamet Ibrahimi, Ebrahim Jahanbakhsh, Athanasia C. Tzika and Michel C. Milinkovitch, 2 July 2026,
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2530407123

title: Human-Elephant Conflict Could Explode Across Southern Africa As Scientists Warn of a Growing Crisis
content:
Human-elephant conflict occurs when elephants and people compete for space and resources, particularly in regions where farmland overlaps with elephant habitats. Credit: Shutterstock
Human-elephant conflict could intensify across Southern Africa as expanding farmland and increasingly dry conditions reshape the landscape.
Southern Africa is home to more than 290,000 African savanna elephants (
Loxodonta africana
), representing roughly 70% of the continent’s savanna elephant population. As agricultural communities expand into elephant habitat, crop raids can destroy valuable harvests, threaten household incomes, and undermine local support for wildlife conservation.
Expanding Farmland Is Driving Elephant Conflict
To understand what causes these encounters, Evan Patrick and colleagues analyzed reported elephant crop raids from 2004 to 2020 across 38 communal conservancies in Namibia. They combined statistical methods designed to identify causal relationships with machine learning models that predict where conflicts are most likely to occur. Their analysis extended across a larger landscape encompassing northern Botswana and parts of Angola and Zambia.
“We find that human population growth, cropland expansion, and climate-driven aridity in core elephant-protected areas drive conflict risk,” the authors write.
Population growth was linked to higher crop-raiding rates during both wet and dry seasons, while expanding cropland and developed areas were associated with increased incidents during the wet season. Drier conditions within protected elephant habitats also predicted more wet-season raids in neighboring communities, suggesting that shortages of natural resources may push elephants toward agricultural land.
Where Elephant Crop Raids Are Most Likely
The researchers mapped potential conflict hotspots by examining vegetation cover, proximity to rivers, roads and wildlife fences, population density, and vegetation productivity. Tree cover and vegetation greenness were particularly influential predictors, while roads and fences appeared to shape where elephants encounter human settlements.
High-risk areas included regions north of Namibia’s Etosha National Park, the northeastern Zambezi Region, and parts of northern Botswana surrounding the Okavango Delta and Moremi Wildlife Reserve. Many of these landscapes connect important elephant habitats with areas used for farming.
Crop raids also showed pronounced seasonal differences. Historical records revealed that average incidents per mapped grid cell were more than ten times higher during the wet season than during the dry season, when agricultural activity and vegetation conditions differ.
Conflict Could Increase Under Every Future Scenario
Using projections of climate, population growth, and land use, the team modeled potential changes through 2085. All four scenarios predicted increasing crop-raiding activity and a wider distribution of high-risk areas, although the magnitude depended on future development patterns.
The greatest increases occurred under a scenario involving substantial population growth and land conversion, known as “regional rivalry.” Under this pathway, projected wet-season crop raiding was approximately twice as high as under the more sustainable development scenario. Even the scenario with the most severe climate impacts did not produce the highest conflict levels.
“Aggressive human land-use expansion leads to the most dramatic increases in conflict, with climate impacts playing a significant but smaller role,” the researchers explain.
Reference: “An expanding human footprint drives escalating human–elephant conflict across a transboundary African landscape through 2085” by Evan Patrick, Maxwell Pepperdine, Christy Yu, Sophie Pesek, Olivia Somhegyi, Joana M Krieger, Nickolas McManus, Ezequiel Fabiano, Colgar Sikopo, Patrick R Roehrdanz and Ashley Larsen, 7 July 2026,

title: Mosquitoes Are Picky Eaters – and Scientists Just Figured Out Why They Prefer Certain People
content:
Few things are more annoying than mosquitoes. Their relentless buzzing, itchy bites, and knack for finding exposed skin can ruin an otherwise perfect evening outdoors. Worse still, these tiny pests can carry dangerous diseases, making them far more than just a nuisance. Credit: Shutterstock
Scientists have discovered that different mosquito species are attracted to distinct human scent signatures.
A person who attracts one mosquito species may be far less appealing to another. In a study involving 119 volunteers, researchers at
Florida International University (FIU)
found that three major disease-carrying mosquito species consistently preferred different people. Not a single participant was attractive to all three.
The findings, published in
iScience
, challenge the idea that some people are universally irresistible to mosquitoes. Instead, attraction appears to depend on how individual species detect the chemicals and microorganisms associated with human skin.
Different Mosquito Species Prefer Different Human Scents
The researchers examined three species responsible for spreading diseases such as dengue, Zika, yellow fever, and West Nile virus. Each responded to a different combination of biological signals.
Aedes aegypti
, a mosquito that typically bites during the day, preferred people who wore no added fragrance and whose skin lacked certain volatile compounds. It also showed a slight preference for men. Another daytime feeder,
Aedes albopictus
(Asian tiger mosquito), was more attracted to people with elevated levels of ketones and plant-like chemicals naturally released by the skin.
Culex quinquefasciatus
(southern house mosquito), which feeds after dark, responded more strongly to differences in the skin microbiome. This community of bacteria, fungi, and other microorganisms varies from person to person. Certain bacterial families were associated with increased mosquito attraction, while others appeared to discourage feeding.
A mosquito is examined under a microscope in the lab of FIU professor Matthew DeGennaro. Credit: Christopher Necuze/Florida International University
Human Body Chemistry Helps Explain Mosquito Preferences
Human scent contains more than 1,000 volatile organic compounds, many of which remain poorly understood. To investigate which biological characteristics influence mosquito attraction, the scientists collected odor and skin microbiome samples alongside their preference tests.
Led by Ph.D. student Kaylee Marrero, the study was the first to directly compare how multiple mosquito species respond to the same individuals. The researchers had not anticipated such clear differences between species.
“We didn’t expect the species to prefer different people when we started the study,” Marrero said. “Each species having a distinct microbial signature that they use as a cue was so surprising to me.”
The results suggest that mosquitoes have evolved different ways of detecting and interpreting the complex chemical signals produced by human skin.
“This connected so well with the differences in skin bacteria and odors,” said Matthew DeGennaro, a neurogeneticist who leads the research team and directs the Biomolecular Sciences Institute at FIU. “It is clear to me now that our skin microbiomes define our human odor signature. Each species found its own way to decode that signature.”
Toward More Targeted Mosquito Repellents
Understanding which chemicals attract or discourage individual mosquito species could help researchers develop repellents designed to interfere with specific scent signals rather than relying on a universal approach.
“Isolating the components of human odor that attract or repel mosquitoes could lead to novel strategies to combat vector-borne diseases,” DeGennaro said.
Reference: “Individual humans are more attractive to certain mosquito species” by Kaylee M. Marrero, John S. Castillo, Dani Lucas-Barbosa, Anthony J. Bellantuono, Matthew A. Marrero, Dariel Cid, Andre L. Costa-da-Silva, Niels O. Verhulst and Matthew DeGennaro, 31 July 2026,

title: Scientists Discover a Hidden Factor That Could Be Making Deadly Cancers Harder To Treat
content:
A new scientific review challenges conventional approaches to treating aggressive cancers, suggesting that an unexpected biological factor may hold the key to improving treatment outcomes. Credit: Shutterstock
Scientists are exploring a potentially overlooked factor behind some of the most treatment-resistant cancers: bacteria lurking inside tumors.
Some of the most aggressive cancers may have an overlooked source of treatment resistance: bacteria living inside tumors. Researchers suggest that these microbes could interfere with chemotherapy, weaken immune defenses, and alter surrounding tissues. They propose that combining existing antibiotics with cancer drugs might help overcome resistance in certain difficult-to-treat cancers.
In a review published in
Cancer Biology & Medicine
, scientists from Nankai University, the University of Utah, and Tianjin Medical University Cancer Institute & Hospital argue that “all diagnosed PPO-tumors must be considered to be bacteria-infected.” Their proposal focuses on poor prognosis outcome (PPO) tumors, although the assumption that these tumors harbor bacterial infections remains unproven.
How Bacteria Could Help Tumors Resist Treatment
Pancreatic, colorectal, and certain biliary cancers can be especially difficult to treat. Their tumors often suppress immune responses, undergo rapid genetic changes, and develop dense fibrous barriers that restrict drug delivery.
Researchers have detected bacteria within several of these cancers, including
Fusobacterium nucleatum
Escherichia coli
Enterococcus faecalis
Pseudomonas
species. Some microbes may promote inflammation, interfere with immune defenses, or chemically alter chemotherapy drugs, potentially reducing their effectiveness.
However, as the authors caution, “the mere presence of intratumoral bacteria does not always confer causation.” Cancer genetics and other features of the tumor environment can independently drive aggressive growth and treatment resistance.
Why Advanced Cancer Drugs Face Obstacles
Nanomedicine aims to improve chemotherapy by using microscopic carriers to deliver drugs directly into tumors. Although promising in animal studies, these technologies have often produced limited additional benefits in human patients.
One challenge involves the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect, which can help nanoparticles accumulate in tumors through unusually permeable blood vessels. Human tumors are often more fibrous and structurally complex than experimental tumors, making drug penetration less predictable. The authors highlight an “overpromise” in translating results from rodent models into clinical treatments.
They also propose that bacterial infections might increase the permeability of tumor blood vessels, potentially improving drug delivery. However, this possibility has not been conclusively demonstrated in human cancers.
Could Antibiotics Restore Chemotherapy Effectiveness?
Rather than waiting for more advanced nanomedicines, the researchers propose combining conventional antibiotics and chemotherapy drugs without specialized carriers. The authors argue that “all diagnosed PPO-tumors must be treated from the onset with a carrier-free antibiotic/chemotherapeutic drug combination.”
Animal studies provide preliminary support for investigating this approach. In bacteria-infected tumor models, combining the antibiotic ciprofloxacin with the chemotherapy drug gemcitabine has helped restore treatment sensitivity and suppress tumor growth. Whether similar benefits occur in patients remains uncertain.
What Must Happen Before Clinical Use?
A major challenge is the lack of reliable clinical tests for detecting bacterial infections inside living tumors. Treating patients without confirming infection could also disrupt beneficial microbes and contribute to antibiotic resistance.
The researchers recommend examining existing patient records for evidence that antibiotic and chemotherapy combinations improve outcomes. They argue that “retrospective clinical verification can sometimes be the only pathway to clinical progress.”
Such research could help identify patients most likely to benefit, but additional clinical evidence is needed before routinely combining antibiotics with chemotherapy for aggressive cancers.

title: Permanent Daylight Saving Time Could Send Millions of Kids to School in the Dark
content:
Scientists warn that permanent daylight saving time could create 2 billion additional dark school commutes, putting children’s safety and health at risk. Credit: Shutterstock
Permanent daylight saving time could leave some states with roughly ten times as many dark school commutes, sharpening concerns about children’s safety and sleep.
Keeping daylight saving time through the winter would move sunrise an hour later on the clock, leaving children with fixed school schedules to make more trips in the dark. University of Washington researchers estimate that a nationwide shift would add at least 2 billion dark school commutes compared with the current system of switching between daylight saving time and standard time twice a year.
The U.S. House of Representatives passed
this past summer that would make daylight saving time (DST) permanent, ending the fall return to standard time.
Nineteen states, including Washington, have already preapproved the change
, which would take effect in those states if the bill is signed into law. The legislation is stalled in the U.S. Senate, with
school start times
a central issue because mornings would be darker from November through March.
Dark mornings raise safety and sleep concerns
The study, published October 29 in
Current Biology
, examined both school schedules and U.S. traffic collision data. The collision analysis found that a fatal crash involving a school-aged pedestrian was roughly twice as likely to occur during a dark morning as after sunrise.
Morning light also helps set the circadian clock, the body’s internal timing system, which helps regulate mood, sleep, and appetite. Without that light, the body has more difficulty regulating these functions.
“When we send kids to school in the dark, we are depriving them from an opportunity to get that morning daylight,” said lead author Guadalupe Rodríguez Ferrante, a UW postdoctoral scholar in biology. “We were asking what’s the cost for these children. We wanted actual numbers, a real number of kids based on the geographic location of each school.”
Horacio de la Iglesia, UW professor of biology, discusses how permanent Daylight Saving Time will affect commutes for school children. Credit: Sarah McQuate/University of Washington
Early school starts mean more dark commutes
For 14 of the 19 states that had preapproved permanent DST, the researchers combined school start times, enrollment data, and latitude and longitude measurements. They calculated how many days each child would travel to school in the dark, then added those trips together to compare permanent DST with the current system.
All 14 states would see an increase. Washington would have almost 35 million additional dark trips to school, while Georgia would have the largest increase among the states studied, at 71 million.
Communities on the western edge of their time zones, such as Forks, Washington, would be particularly affected, as would those with early school start times. In Mississippi and Alabama, schools start before 8 a.m. on average. Each state would go from about 2 million dark school commutes under the current system to more than 20 million under permanent DST.
“Some districts probably never experience a dark commute under the current system, and, if this passes, suddenly they will wake up to this new reality that their kids are going to school in the dark,” Rodríguez Ferrante said. “Keep in mind that we used the actual start time listed for each school, and a lot of schools offer breakfast or other things before school, so the kids could be getting there even earlier.”
The nationwide estimate came from extrapolating the results from the 14 states to the rest of the country, with an assumption that makes the total likely conservative.
“For the estimation, we assumed students would be leaving home around 8 a.m.,” Rodríguez Ferrante said. “That’s pretty late, so our calculation is likely an underestimation of the real number.”
Delaying school could erase the evening benefit
“It’s called the ‘Sunshine Protection Act’ because you get an extra hour of light at the end of the day. But you will take that hour from the morning. You could call it the Sunshine Destruction Act,” said senior author Horacio de la Iglesia, a UW professor of biology. “These dark mornings will inequitably affect children who have to go to school at a certain time. It’s a very tangible metric that anybody from any state or socioeconomic background can relate to. Nobody wants their kids to go to school in the dark.”
The researchers also argue that permanent DST would undo the benefits of
delayed start times for high school students
. Those later starts are intended to accommodate teenagers’ circadian clocks, which are shifted compared with those of younger children and adults.
“I’ve heard the argument, ‘If we’re in permanent DST, we can just delay the school start time to address these issues,'” de la Iglesia said. “Well, if we do that, you will end up going to work later. And everything is going to get delayed. You will get out of work an hour later, and you will miss the opportunity to enjoy your evening light. And essentially, we’re just going to be realigning everybody to solar time. That, by definition, is Standard Time.”
Reference: “Over a billion more dark-morning school commutes for K–12 children under the Sunshine Protection Act” by Guadalupe Rodríguez Ferrante, Nirekh S. title: A Hidden Weakness in the Brain’s Defenses Could Help Explain Alzheimer’s Disease
content:
Animal experiments reveal how excess fibronectin disrupts communication between brain cells and weakens a protective barrier, suggesting a possible new approach to Alzheimer’s prevention. Credit: Shutterstock
A protein buildup damaged the brain’s protective barrier in animal experiments, pointing to a possible target for Alzheimer’s treatment.
Roughly one in five people carries at least one copy of APOE ε4, the strongest common genetic risk factor for Alzheimer’s disease. Yet many people with the variant remain mentally sharp into their 80s without developing the disease. Understanding what protects some of them could help researchers find ways to protect others.
APOE ε4 carriers accumulate unusually high levels of a protein called fibronectin at the blood-brain barrier, a tightly packed layer of cells around brain blood vessels that helps remove toxic substances. Two years ago, Columbia University researchers
discovered
that a rare mutation in FN1, the gene that encodes fibronectin, limits this buildup and its damage, helping protect some carriers against Alzheimer’s. A drug that mimics that effect might offer similar protection.
The team’s latest study, published in
Nature Aging
, found that excess fibronectin can make the barrier leak in animal experiments and traced the damage to disrupted signals between cells.
“This new study takes us from a genetic clue to a disease mechanism,” says Caghan Kizil, the study’s corresponding author and professor of neurological sciences in the Department of Neurology and the Taub Institute for Research on Alzheimer’s Disease and the Aging Brain at Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons.
“We knew that changes in fibronectin could protect against Alzheimer’s, but we didn’t know why excess fibronectin was harmful in the first place. This study gives us that detailed mechanism—and with it, ideas for how to reproduce that natural protection.”
The magenta color reveals the damaging fibronectin around the brain’s blood vessels in APOE ε4 carriers. Credit: Caghan Kizil / Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons
In human brain tissue and cerebrospinal fluid, the liquid surrounding the brain and spinal cord, high fibronectin levels were associated with inflamed astrocytes. These cells, also called astroglia, help maintain the blood-brain barrier. Genetic and epigenetic analyses, which examined genetic variation and gene regulation, also linked FN1 to vascular disease and changes in VEGFA, a growth factor needed to maintain healthy brain blood vessels.
“The convergence of these independent human datasets strengthens the case that fibronectin is part of the APOE ε4-related vascular disease process,” says Badri Vardarajan, associate professor of neurological science in the Department of Neurology, Gertrude H. Sergievsky Center, and Taub Institute, who collaborated on the discovery of the protective FN1 mutation.
Excess fibronectin causes barrier leaks in animals
To investigate how fibronectin affects the barrier, the researchers also used human stem-cell models, three-dimensional vascular cultures, and experiments in zebrafish and mice. Their methods included single-cell sequencing and spatial imaging. Across the systems they examined, the findings pointed to APOE ε4 increasing fibronectin and promoting its accumulation around brain blood vessels.
In mice carrying human APOE ε4, brain fibronectin levels were nearly twice those in mice carrying the normal human APOE version, APOE ε3. The higher levels coincided with evidence that the blood-brain barrier was leaking. That comparison alone could not establish whether fibronectin caused the damage, so the researchers performed a more targeted test. They increased human fibronectin specifically in astrocytes to determine whether excess protein in those cells was enough, by itself, to compromise the barrier.
“The animal experiments allowed us to move beyond association,” says co-first author Prabesh Bhattarai, an associate research scientist in the Kizil lab. “When we increased fibronectin in astroglia, the barrier became permeable. When we reduced fibronectin, barrier function improved.”
The researchers traced the damage to disrupted communication between cells. Excess fibronectin sends abnormal signals through integrins, proteins that sense a cell’s surroundings, and an enzyme called focal adhesion kinase. This disrupts a chain of growth factors called VEGF, HBEGF, and IGF1. These factors allow astrocytes and blood-vessel cells to communicate and work together to maintain the barrier.
“Single-cell analysis allowed us to examine this pathway in the different cells that maintain the brain’s blood vessels,” says co-first author Elanur Yilmaz, an associate research scientist in the Kizil lab. “We observed the same biological pattern across experimental models and human Alzheimer’s tissue, making the mechanism especially compelling.”
The human findings suggest that the same damaging processes likely occur in Alzheimer’s patients who carry APOE ε4, although the evidence that excess fibronectin itself can cause barrier leakage came from the animal experiments.
Targeting fibronectin without disrupting tissue repair
The findings suggest three possible treatment strategies for people with APOE ε4. Researchers could try to prevent excess fibronectin from accumulating, block the harmful signals it triggers, or restore the growth signals needed to keep the blood-brain barrier healthy. The team is exploring these possibilities in laboratory experiments.
Any future treatment would need to target pathological fibronectin while preserving its normal roles in tissue structure and repair. Understanding the mechanism provides a foundation for developing more selective interventions and determining when they might be most useful.
“By showing how fibronectin contributes to early vascular damage, this study gives us new therapeutic targets and potential ways to measure whether treatments are working,” says Richard Mayeux, chair of the Department of Neurology and a collaborator on the project. “Clinically, it connects a major genetic risk factor for Alzheimer’s to an early disease process that may be possible to modify.”

title: A Rare Radioactive Element Reveals a Hidden Secret About the Heaviest Atoms
content:
Graphical illustration of the nuclear chart and of the RISIKO mass separator used in these studies. Credit: Sebastian Raeder
Using advanced laser spectroscopy on extremely rare radioactive material, researchers have uncovered new insights into the structure of heavy atomic nuclei.
The nucleus of fermium-255 is far from spherical. Scientists have now determined its shape for the first time, finding that it is strongly elongated, much like a rugby ball. The high-precision measurements, published in
Physical Review Letters
, also correct earlier nuclear data and provide new evidence supporting theoretical models of the heaviest elements.
Fermium-255 contains 100 protons and 155 neutrons. In such heavy nuclei, the electrical repulsion between positively charged protons creates conditions that can lead to spontaneous fission, in which a nucleus splits into smaller fragments. Nuclear shape influences this process, making it a critical factor in predicting whether even heavier, potentially longer-lived elements can exist.
How Laser Light Reveals the Shape of a Nucleus
Rather than observing the nucleus directly, researchers studied its interactions with the electrons surrounding it. Electrons close to the nucleus are sensitive to its size, shape, and magnetic properties. These interactions produce extremely small differences in atomic energy levels that can be detected through precise laser measurements.
This phenomenon, known as hyperfine interaction, arises from the electromagnetic properties of the nucleus. A deformed nucleus interacts with the electric field of nearby electrons, while nuclear magnetism produces additional effects. Because fermium-255 has an odd number of neutrons, its nucleus also possesses a magnetic moment that contributes to the splitting of electronic energy levels.
Scientists at
Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (JGU)
first observed atomic energy levels in fermium more than 20 years ago. However, the technology available then could not resolve the fine details needed to determine its nuclear structure accurately. Some of the resulting nuclear data remained incomplete or inconsistent.
Schematic presentation of the projected charge density of the fermium-255 nucleus at the mean field level as calculated by nuclear theory. Sizes are given in femtometers (fm). Credit: Michael Bender
Producing Fermium From an Exceptionally Rare Starting Material
Fermium must be manufactured artificially, and obtaining enough atoms for an experiment requires an unusually complex production process. The researchers began with months of neutron irradiation of transuranium material at the High Flux Isotope Reactor at Oak Ridge National Laboratory (USA), producing einsteinium-254.
After initial experiments in the United States, the material traveled to Mainz (Germany) for processing and then to the Institute Laue-Langevin in France for additional neutron irradiation. This produced einsteinium-255, which decays into fermium-255. The material was subsequently returned to Mainz for spectroscopy experiments.
Einsteinium-255 has a half-life of approximately 40 days, allowing it to supply fermium-255 over several weeks. Through repeated chemical separations, scientists obtained individual samples containing tens of millions to about one billion fermium atoms. At JGU’s RISIKO separator, the samples were heated to approximately 1,000 degrees Celsius (1,832 degrees Fahrenheit) to release atoms for laser analysis. Specialized Ti laser systems excited and ionized the atoms, enabling researchers to resolve the hyperfine structure of two optical transitions despite the extremely small quantities available.
New Measurements Challenge Earlier Nuclear Data
Researchers combined the experimental spectra with advanced atomic calculations performed at Jagiellonian University in Kraków, Poland, and the Helmholtz Institute Mainz (HIM). The analysis confirmed that the fermium-255 nucleus has a strongly prolate shape, meaning it is stretched along one axis. It also produced a magnetic dipole moment that differs from previously tabulated values, correcting earlier results that were inconsistent with physical expectations.
The measurements agree closely with modern nuclear theories developed by research groups in France and Germany. By providing more reliable information about nuclear deformation and magnetism, the findings strengthen models of nuclear fission and could improve predictions of the stability of superheavy elements that have yet to be discovered.

title: Researchers use 2D perovskite films to image long-wave infrared light with a standard camera
content:
Researchers use 2D perovskite films to image long-wave infrared light with a standard camera
Researchers at Yale University, Argonne National Laboratory and Brookhaven National Laboratory have demonstrated pixelated long-wave infrared (LWIR) imaging using a solution-processed two-dimensional perovskite. The approach is all-optical: the infrared signal is read out with a standard silicon CMOS camera, so the imager needs no electrical contacts on each pixel and no readout integrated circuit.
Schematic of all-optical LWIR imaging using a centimeter-sized (PEA)₂PbI₄/SiNₓ membrane. Infrared light passing through a mask heats the membrane, and a green probe beam reflected off the sample is recorded by a CMOS camera. From: Light: Science & Applications (Cropped)
The team used a roughly 1 µm-thick (PEA)₂PbI₄ film spin-coated on a thin silicon nitride membrane. The perovskite itself is transparent to LWIR light, so the membrane serves as the absorber, with its Si-N vibrations giving peak extinction of nearly 60% between 9 and 14 µm. When the membrane warms, the film warms with it. Because of the material’s strong exciton-phonon coupling, its reflectance near the 510 nm exciton resonance changes with temperature, by about 0.2-0.3% per kelvin at room temperature. A green LED probe and a camera record that change, converting the infrared signal into a visible-light image.
In the first demonstration, a centimeter-scale membrane imaged a pattern projected with 9.5 µm laser light over a 5 mm field of view. The imager detected power densities down to about 20 pW/µm², with a linear response up to 5 nW/µm², and it showed negligible signal degradation during more than three days of continuous illumination under ambient conditions. The team says that a laser wavelength closer to the membrane’s absorption peak, at 11-12 µm, should push sensitivity into the single-digit pW/µm² range.
Lateral heat spreading blurred the images. To address this, the researchers first used a structured probe beam, then cut the membrane into an array of thermally isolated discs, each 50 µm wide on a 100 µm pitch, supported by a silicon wafer. The team reports that this design eliminates pixel-to-pixel crosstalk. They add that smaller pixel pitches, below 20 µm, may be possible with an optimized etching process.
The researchers describe the work as a proof of concept. It still relies on a mechanical chopper and bench optics, and standard detector metrics such as noise-equivalent power and specific detectivity are not directly comparable to conventional cameras. At the material level, the team reports a figure of merit about an order of magnitude better than that of vanadium oxide, a common microbolometer material. They suggest that the approach could be extended to the far-infrared and terahertz ranges, and that flexible substrates could be used in place of the silicon nitride.

title: 第二届先进储能技术及应用挑战赛在宁启动， 九大赛道迎“真刀真枪”实测-索比光伏网
content:
11月3 日上午，第二届先进储能技术及应用挑战赛启动仪式在南京国际博览中心举行，九大赛道同步开赛，现场实测与项目评比随即展开。
本届挑战赛由中国电力源网荷储一体化创新平台、《中国能源报》社有限公司、《中国汽车报》社有限公司、《中国城市报》社有限公司共同主办，中国电机工程学会、中电联源网荷储专家工作组、中国汽车新闻工作者协会、国网江苏省电力有限公司支持，创能国际会展服务（江苏）有限公司承办，与 CESC2026 第四届储能大会暨储能及智能电网设备应用展览会同期同址举办。
赛事以“赛检联动、工况实测”为核心机制，设置九大赛道，采用“现场擂台挑战”与“现场评审挑战”双轨赛制，将检测认证环节前置到比赛现场，以可追溯、可复核的实测数据评价参赛项目的技术水平。
启动仪式举行 赛事正式开赛
启动仪式由江苏省储能行业协会执行秘书长朱莎主持。
中国能源汽车传播集团经管会委员韩君善代表主办方发言。他表示，储能装机规模虽已迈上新台阶，但“规模大不等于质量强，装机多不等于技术硬”，行业急需一个能把真技术筛出来、把好方案推出去的机制。
本届挑战赛重点推进三方面工作：一是以真实工况淘汰纸面创新，所有参赛产品均需现场实测，高低温、倍率、安全、循环寿命等数据全程留痕、可追溯，通过核验的项目可获多家国家级检测机构联合认证，并直接用于招投标和合规备案；二是以产业需求牵引技术方向，首创“需求擂台”模式，聚焦低空经济储能、AI算力储能、绿色船舶、电动重卡光储充换等六大前沿场景，由电网集团、能源央企和终端用户出题、企业揭榜应战，实现参赛即对接、获奖即落地；三是以全媒体矩阵放大传播声量，中国能源报、中国汽车报、中国城市报将全程跟踪报道，让经实测检验的技术和方案被行业看见、被用户记住。韩君善表示，主办方将把擂台搭公平、把数据晒透明、把资源接到位，让挑战赛真正成为一条从实验室到电站、从论文到订单的通道。
IEEE PES储能技术委员会(中国)执行主席、国家电网有限公司调度控制中心原副总工程师裴哲义代表评审专家组发言。他表示，当前储能技术加速迭代，更需要用真实场景和实测数据来检验技术方案，而不能停留在参数比拼和实验室层面。本届挑战赛聚焦构网型储能、钠离子电池、长时储能等关键赛道，把真实工况实测环节放在重要位置，正是对行业痛点的务实回应。赛事坚决摒弃“交钱拿奖”模式，坚持只用数据与场景说话，由权威检测机构全程见证，在九大赛道现场真实工况下检验各家企业的硬核技术。期待各参赛团队珍惜同台竞技机会，在实测中显露真实力、暴露真问题，在答辩中讲清真逻辑、拿出真水平，在比拼中共同推动储能技术进步与产业落地。
随后，江苏省政府原副秘书长王志忠，中国能源汽车传播集团韩君善，IEEE PES 储能技术委员会（中国）执行主席、国家电网有限公司调度控制中心原副总工程师裴哲义，中材科技（苏州）有限公司党委副书记、纪委书记朱云青，江苏省储能行业协会会长朱俊鹏，西安汇川技术有限公司台区储能总经理杨冠龙共同启动赛事。
仪式后，到场领导与嘉宾合影留念，并赴实测区参观，了解现场测试的工况设置、数据采集与见证流程，随后巡览同期展览、继续观赛。
九大赛道同步开赛
本届挑战赛设置九大赛道，覆盖储能前沿技术、核心设备、安全管控、系统集成、场景应用与氢储能等重点领域，分别为前沿储能技术、储能核心设备、安全防控与热管理、储能相关配套、储能系统集成、储能电站设计建设与智慧运维、源网荷储与微电网、创新场景应用、氢储能全产业链技术。
其中，源网荷储与微电网赛道涵盖
、毫秒级功率切换与黑启动；创新场景应用赛道面向低空经济、AI 算力、绿色船舶、电动重卡等交叉场景，重点考察技术在真实场景下的适配能力。
双轨赛制：实测项目以数据定名次
赛制按技术形态区分两类。现场擂台挑战由组委会统一设定挑战项目与先进指标，覆盖微电网、台区储能、无人机电源飞行模拟、构网型储能等，要求可实测项目完成现场测试，结果不得低于现行国家标准；暂无国家标准的，由专家组按行业标准制定实测门槛。评审组依据实测结果排定名次、认定领先指标并颁发专家评价证书。现场评审挑战由参赛单位自主申报，提交检测报告、用户报告、专利或项目鉴定等佐证材料，现场通过宣讲、实物展示等形式汇报，评审组从创新性与领先性、成熟度与可行性、市场潜力与经济效益、安全性与可靠性、社会与环境效益五个维度现场评分。
三家权威机构同步实测
与常规技术评审不同的是，本届挑战赛把检测认证环节前置到赛事现场。三家权威评测机构专家同步开展现场实测，全程记录并公示实测数据，联合鉴证数据真实性并共同签发实测证书。参赛项目的性能表现不再取决于单方送样或书面材料，而是在同一工况条件、同一时间窗口内接受多方交叉验证。

title: Deutsche Windtechnik secures Alpha Ventus service contract
content:
Ocean Breeze Energy has awarded Deutsche Windtechnik a service contract
for the Alpha
Ventus wind farm.
The contract marks a milestone for the company, which will support Germany's
first offshore wind farm by providing maintenance and troubleshooting services
for all wind turbines, along with associated technical support.
According to the report, additional services will be added in September
2027, including remote monitoring, Marine Coordination Centre/Offshore
Control Centre (MCC/OCC) operations, grid management and 24/7 alarm handling
for each turbine.
The contract follows a competitive tender process. Ocean Breeze Energy
said Deutsche Windtechnik was selected because of its experience, technical
expertise, and a tailored, cost-optimised proposal.
The announcement follows Ocean Breeze Energy's acquisition of the wind
farm in October. Since then, the company has confirmed it will continue
operating the project, despite previous owners having outlined decommissioning
activities.

title: Aventa expands their offshore wind workforce with OPA acquisition
content:
Aventa has expanded its offshore wind and subsea cable services through
the acquisition of Aberdeen-based offshore personnel provider Offshore
Projects Alliance Ltd (OPA).
The agreement will add OPA’s network of offshore professionals to the
group as demand for experienced cable installation personnel continues
to grow across the offshore wind sector.
Following the acquisition, Aventa will be able to provide complete cable
installation teams covering offshore management, supervision, pull-in operations,
jointing, termination and testing activities.
According to the announcement they will also offer client representatives
to offshore wind developers, transmission system operators, cable manufacturers
and installation contractors.
The acquisition aims to strengthen Aventa’s position in Scotland and the
wider UK market, as the Scottish Government has set a target of up to 40
GW of new offshore wind capacity.

title: Cadeler awards Fugro East Anglia TWO survey contract
content:
East Anglia TWOis the latest of four East Anglia offshore wind projects being developed
to generate enough electricity to power approximately 950,000 UK homes.
Under the agreement, Fugro will support Cadeler's role in bringing the
renewable energy project online by providing specialist survey, positioning,
construction support and remotely operated vehicle (ROV) services.
Fugro's FCV 600 work-class ROV will be deployed from a Cadeler installation
vessel to assess 64 monopile locations.
According to the company, Fugro's services will help ensure installation
quality while reducing project risk and providing the geodata required
to support reliable and efficient offshore construction.
Maxime Duthoit, senior project manager at Cadeler, said: "We are pleased
to continue our collaboration with Fugro, whose track record in the offshore
industry and position as one of the market leaders in ROV and survey services
provide confidence in the quality and reliability of the data required
to support successful project delivery."
In the announcement, Fugro also highlighted its role in the Hornsea
3 offshore wind project.
The company said it will again support Cadeler by deploying specialists
aboard the Wind Ally installation vessel to provide positioning and construction
services for monopile installation activities.

title: Kinewell expands operations after securing £1M investment
content:
Offshore wind optimisation software developer Kinewell has secured a £1

The company develops and commercialises software solutions designed to
support offshore wind project design and optimisation.
According to the announcement they are also looking to diversify their
offerings, exploring how their technology can be used to support other
sectors.

Helix and created five skilled jobs. According to the company, the expansion

at The Catalyst puts us right at the heart of one of the North East's largest
innovation hubs and will be key to enabling us to attract and retain the
best talent as we continue to grow."

title: Cadeler’s Wind Apex awarded installation contract for Dogger Bank C
content:
Cadeler’s Wind Apex awarded installation contract for Dogger Bank C TGS 4C | 4C Offshore News
Cadeler’s Wind Apex awarded installation contract for Dogger Bank C
Cadeler has announced a contract with Dogger
to use its installation vessel, Wind Apex, to support turbine transportation
and installation work for the 1.2 GW offshore wind farm.
The contract marks a milestone for Cadeler, representing the first deployment
of Wind Apex following its delivery from the shipyard. The A-Class vessel
has been specially designed to support foundation and turbine installation,
with high deck-load capacity and a heavy-lift crane.
The vessel will work alongside existing installation ships, providing additional
capacity to support the installation of 87 wind turbines planned for the
site off the north east coast of England.
Mikkel Gleerup, CEO of Cadeler, said: "We value the long-standing
relationships we have built with our customers and see these contracts
as a reflection of the trust they place in Cadeler to execute large-scale
offshore wind projects safely and efficiently."
Alan Borland, turbine director at Dogger Bank Wind Farm, said: "Securing
additional specialist vessel capacity for Dogger Bank C is another important
step in the delivery of this world-leading offshore wind project."
Dogger Bank C is one of three phases of the Dogger Bank Wind Farm, each
with a capacity of 1.2 GW. Together, the three phases will be capable of
powering up to six million UK homes annually, making Dogger Bank one of
the world's largest offshore wind farms currently under construction.

title: The Security Companies Trying to Get AI Agents Under Control
content: Before we get to today’s column, a heads up that new models from OpenAI could come as soon as Friday, according to people with knowledge of the models. Those models could include the next generation of its Astra , Sol and cyber focused models, the people said. (Obviously, including a caveat here that model timelines could change.) Meanwhile, you all know by now that a blue wave swept the polls yesterday. The AI industry, we’re sure, was watching as Texas elected Democrats for governor and the U.S. Senate for the first time in decades, and Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress. That creates potential uncertainty for the state’s booming AI data center sector and its most prominent tech leader, Elon Musk . In other news, open-source software company Canonical patched a flaw today that would have allowed bad people to hijack websites and plant their own code on datacenter servers, according to Charge Robotics chief technology officer Max Justicz , who found the flaw. Onto today’s column … When cybersecurity company Cyera went looking in the internal systems of a large financial company, it found AI agents that had been sitting in the customer’s most sensitive data for more than six months. Nobody had known they were there. “We're talking about thousands of agents sitting in production with a lot of sensitive financial information that can basically do whatever they want, whenever they want,” said Danny Brickman , chief business officer at Cyera. Cyera isn’t the only company that has discovered such instances. Identity security company SailPoint discovered more than 10,000 agents that a Fortune 500 company was unaware of in its system, with 70% of them unconnected to any owner, SailPoint president Matt Mills said. In both of those cases, the agents turned out to be wayward elements of the clients‘ own AI systems. They didn’t cause any harm. But both episodes illustrate an increasingly common and alarming phenomenon where agents are going places or doing things that they're not supposed to, and companies aren’t immediately catching them. That trend is fueling growing business for companies promising to label, track, and control all of the AI agents operating within their customers’ systems. It’s also made companies offering such services attractive acquisition targets. In September, Cyera spent $1 billion to acquire Oasis Security , a four-year-old startup that governs what it calls non-human identities, which includes everything from AI agents to devices. Cyera is now in talks to raise capital in a round that could nearly double its valuation to $20 billion, my colleagues reported exclusively last week. The Oasis acquisition was one in a string of similar deals. Last month, HR and finance company Workday acquired C1.ai to manage AI agent identities alongside human identities. Identity security company Okta acquired Permisio Security in August and rival Sailpoint acquired Entro in June, both due to the targets’ specialization in managing AI agent identities. Palo Alto Networks and Crowdstrike, the two biggest publicly traded cybersecurity companies, have also done recent deals in this area. Agentic identity companies are focused on managing two main challenges from AI: verifying whom, if anyone, an agent is acting on behalf of, and—assuming the person responsible for the agent is legitimate—determining whether the agent is really carrying out that person’s will faithfully. To keep AI agents under control internally, many security companies tie every agent to the identity of the human who authorized it. Another AI layer assesses the task the agent has been given, and assigns it temporary permissions—such as for access to certain files or tools—that are as narrow as possible while still allowing it to achieve the task. The security systems then revoke those permissions once the agent is no longer needed, to prevent it from taking other actions, Brickman said. When these controls work successfully, any agents that misbehave within a company’s systems won’t have the permissions they would need to do large-scale damage—and any that do have access can be immediately cut off once detected. Threats can come not only from AI agents controlled by hackers or other malicious actors, but from malfunctioning agents in the company’s own systems and “shadow” agents—legitimate-but-unauthorized AI that employees use for company work without permission. Addressing the security problems around all of this is essential for companies to start adopting agentic AI more widely, executives say. “They all want to adopt AI, they want to innovate with AI, but security, compliance, governance, trust, safety is becoming very, very critical to them,” said Amit Zavery , president of enterprise software company ServiceNow . Part of the security challenge with AI agents is that they commandeer humans’ credentials to gain unauthorized access. That happened with the hack on model platform Hugging Face in July, in which rogue agents from OpenAI used publicly exposed account credentials to access vulnerabilities. That risk has pushed companies to simultaneously increase security and monitoring around existing credentials for their employees, Mills said. Ultimately, the strategy is one of containing and preventing harmful behavior by keeping meticulous track of what both AI agents and human employees are able to act on digitally, said Toby Smithe , chief technology officer of AI behavior–verification company Kodamai . “What I see happening is [… the] digital economy becomes a bit more biological, where inside at a very low level there‘s a lot of stuff going on that is important in many ways, but it’s kind of contained,” Smithe said. “As a result, you can trust that at the boundary it behaves well.” Here’s what else is going on… Big Number Binance said a software engineer inadvertently downloaded malicious code onto his work computer to complete an assignment for a job interview, part of the several steps since June that eventually allowed attackers to gain access to its system to conduct a $6.3 billion hack. People on the Move Canva said Tuesday that 22% of its staff will need to change roles, relocate, or lose their jobs. The graphic design startup is struggling to grow its revenue amid worries that AI visuals will take over its territory. Policy Watch Proposition 40 , the California ballot initiative that would enact a one-time 5% tax on billion-dollar fortunes to fund healthcare and education in the state, was losing as of Tuesday night. Prominent tech billionaires had opposed the measure. And it said revenue would grow more than 80% next year, or more than twice as fast as the growth it had projected in its financial model a year ago. Shopify reported that gross profit margin from its subscriptions business fell, partly as a result of higher spending on AI, sending Shopify stock tumbling 7.6%. Fal , which runs AI video, image and audio models, raised a $1.3 billion Series F funding round led by Bessemer Venture Partners at a $16 billion valuation. The Information first reported on the round here . Security company CrowdStrike agreed to acquire Fiddler AI , which helps companies monitor what their AI agents do, for a reported $400 million . CrowdStrike also agreed to acquire Dreadnode , which tests AI systems for security weaknesses before they launch, for a reported $95 million .
