title: Apollo Is Vastly Outspending the Neoclouds on AI Chips
content: Last week, SpaceX’s announcement that it would lease $40 billion worth of Nvidia Vera Rubin chips was a further signal of Elon Musk’s grand ambitions in the AI race. The deal also underscores the arrival of a new big player in that competition: Apollo Global Management, a 36-year-old private-equity pioneer turned private-lending giant. In the deal with SpaceX, Apollo will purchase the chips through a subsidiary, then lease them to Musk’s company. The arrangement follows a supersized Apollo deal announced in June, one that also involves Broadcom and Blackstone, another large money management firm: a $35 billion fundraising for Apollo to buy Google’s tensor processing units and lease them to Anthropic. Apollo’s deals with SpaceX and Anthropic will upend the AI landscape. Once the deals are complete and Apollo acquires those chips, only the major hyperscalers will own more chips, and Apollo will have a far larger chip stockpile than any of the neoclouds—the startups that have sprung up to meet skyrocketing demand for the cloud computing services AI development requires. Apollo earns fees from putting together the deals and managing funds that finance the chips. As the chart above shows, Apollo plans to put far more money into chip purchases than any neocloud has been able to. To assemble this chart, we compiled all of the more than one hundred deals the neoclouds have done to secure and finance chip purchases since 2023—the year in which CoreWeave, the largest neocloud, kick-started the surge in chip financing deals with Blackstone’s help. To identify all these deals, we relied on earlier research from American Compute, a type of insurance broker for GPU deals. The deals within our estimates were completed using a technique pioneered by CoreWeave and Blackstone. In these deals, a neocloud and their financial partners form a special purpose vehicle that issues debt to buy the chips. (Lease payments from the end users of the chips pay off the debt.) Unlike Apollo, many of the neoclouds have committed additional capital to developing data centers to house the chips. Importantly, the chart doesn’t include the convertible bonds and credit facilities the neoclouds have raised to fund their operations. They may have used that money to buy chips. The hyperscalers, meanwhile, don’t need to use SPVs because they can make chip purchases through free cash, equity issuances or traditional corporate debt. Our estimates do not include another giant transaction announced last week: the $63 billion deal arranged by Citigroup, Bank of America and Blackstone to finance Anthropic’s purchase of Broadcom chips. The companies didn’t disclose who will actually own those chips. Chip financing is a new role for Apollo. Co-founded by billionaire Leon Black, it rose to prominence through leveraged buyouts, including its nearly $30 billion takeover of casino giant Harrah’s Entertainment in 2008. Over the last decade or so, Apollo has amassed more capital from insurance companies, which like the type of higher-yield but still investment-grade debt a lot of the chip financings represent.

title: Salesforce’s M&A Blitz Reflects Broader Deal Rush
content: Anyone with an interest in tech will be glued to the TV or social media tonight, monitoring the midterm elections. As my colleague Shane Burke writes below, more than 20 candidates in state governor races support a moratorium on data center development. There’s also the California billionaire tax, Proposition 40, to track. But for those in tech fretting about the results, remember this: Nothing that happens tonight will change the relaxed antitrust regime we’ve got right now. That’s thanks to the Trump administration, not Congress. And that means companies have got two more years to get deals done before the antitrust climate could change. That's why the tech deal scene lately has resembled that old “ Supermarket Sweep ” TV game show where contestants have a limited amount of time to grab stuff off the shelves in a supermarket. We’ve seen deals such as Marvell and Lumentum on Monday, DoorDash and Instacart last week, Fox and Roku in June and many others. It’s not just tech, either (think Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery). Overall, deals worth $2.6 trillion have been announced so far this year, according to Dealogic, 66% more than at this time last year. One particularly aggressive acquirer has been Salesforce, which has been striking a multibillion-dollar acquisition seemingly every other week lately. On Monday, Salesforce announced its purchase of Cresta, which sells AI-powered contact center automation software, for a price we reported to be $2.7 billion. Also on Monday, Salesforce completed the purchase of Listen Labs, a deal the companies announced in September without disclosing a price. Last month, Salesforce unveiled the purchase of Braze , which helps marketers improve customer engagement, for $5.7 billion. In September, it completed the $3.6 billion purchase of Fin, a customer agent firm. All up in the past 12 months, Salesforce has spent or committed to spend at least $25 billion on eight acquisitions, almost all of which were worth at least a billion dollars. Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff is a deal junkie, of course. In the 2010s, he kept the company growing by making deal after deal of ever-larger size, culminating in the $27.7 billion purchase of Slack in 2021. But those deals depressed Salesforce’s profit margins and free cash flow, hurting its stock and eventually triggering activist investor pressure that led to Benioff pulling back from M&A and focusing on efficiency . That had a big impact: Salesforce’s free cash flow as a percentage of revenue has jumped to 35% in fiscal 2026 from 20% in fiscal 2023. That means the company lately has been throwing off more than $14 billion a year, which has allowed vastly expanded stock buybacks and generated cash for acquisitions. Notably, Salesforce has paid for its recent spate of acquisitions almost entirely with cash, a switch from its reliance on stock in the years before 2020. Benioff appears to have recognized the dilutive impact of doing deals with stock: Earlier this year, he said, “We have a much better understanding of how to do acquisitions that are accretive to the business but not dilutive to investors.” Of course, whether the payment is made in cash or stock, the deals still have to generate a return. On that point, the jury is out. The Key States to Watch for Data Center Developers It’s Election Day, and in more than 20 states, voters are deciding the fate of the data center build-out for their region. For now, governors’ races will shape the issue the most. As we reported Sunday , candidates calling for data center pauses could win in up to 15 states, including Michigan, Ohio, Texas and Oregon. Plenty more candidates have promised other restrictions on the industry, such as protections for household electric bills and the environment. Such restrictions will slow down the dizzying build-out of data centers and make constructing them more expensive, introducing even more uncertainty for investors about the payoff on the large AI investments of big tech firms. One of the most heated races is in Texas, home to some of the largest data center projects in the world. In the governor’s race, Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa says she will enact a stricter moratorium than incumbent Greg Abbott has in place, at least until lawmakers set permanent standards. In Georgia, where the race is neck-and-neck, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms is calling for a pause on construction to evaluate economic and environmental impacts. The Atlanta metro area is now the biggest market for data center construction, according to CBRE, so a statewide pause would hit the industry where it’s growing fastest. In Florida, where political action committees affiliated with Anthropic and OpenAI’s Greg Brockman have spent more than $4 million backing Republican Byron Donalds, it’s also a tight race. Democrat David Jolly is calling for a moratorium. None of these three states has elected a Democrat for governor since the 1990s, so any flip would be historic. The same is true for the Alaska governor’s race, where three Republicans and a Democrat are facing off against each other. Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, who has pitched for a data center pause and a host of AI regulations that would hold companies accountable for harm, seems poised to win. Regardless of what happens, these elections are going to close some doors for the data center industry. We’ll see soon.— Shane Burke In Other News • Advanced Micro Devices reported that revenues from selling chips to data centers nearly doubled in the third quarter, but revenues in its gaming segment fell. Overall, AMD’s revenue rose 45% in the quarter. The company projected a rapid revenue acceleration in the fourth quarter. • Shopify reported that gross profit margin from its subscriptions business fell, partly as a result of higher spending on AI, sending its stock tumbling 7.6%. • Binance said a staff engineer inadvertently downloaded malicious code to his work computer to complete an assignment for a job interview, part of several steps since June that eventually allowed attackers to gain access to Binance’s system and conduct a $6.3 billion hack. The engineer didn’t realize the job interview was for a fictitious company, however. • China’s top economic planner said on Tuesday that the country will closely monitor the impact of AI on employment, as Beijing moves to establish safety standards and ethical guidelines covering “the whole life cycle of AI.” Today on The Information’s TITV Check out today’s episode of TITV in which Akash Pasricha speaks with Leo Schwartz and Shane Burke about how tonight’s election will affect the tech sector. title: Uber’s Jill Hazelbaker to Join OpenAI as Chief Corporate Affairs Officer
content: Uber ’s President Jill Hazelbaker is joining OpenAI as its chief corporate affairs officer, filling a role that has been empty since the start of the year. Hazelbaker, who is also a veteran of Google and Snap, will be responsible for global communications and brand strategy. She will attempt to stabilize a team that has had significant turnover in its senior management in recent years and a time when market jitters ahead of a potential IPO are mounting. Hazelbaker has been in on-again-off-again talks with OpenAI over the past year. It’s unclear what changed. At Uber she has been known as a deft and straight-shooting crisis manager who handled the ouster of founder Travis Kalanick, among other things. She also helped Uber win its fight to have Uber drivers classified as contractors, not employees, in California. Her last day with Uber will be Nov. 30. She joins OpenAI as its challenges are mounting. Anthropic has surged further ahead in revenue and profitability, and OpenAI has made limited headway in efforts to regain ground through discounting . OpenAI also has been hit by a wave of cybersecurity and safety problems in recent months. While Anthropic is preparing to go public imminently, OpenAI has delayed its own IPO to next year, with CEO Sam Altman citing concerns about AI safety. The company is in the process of raising fresh capital but has in the past weeks slashed both its fundraising target and its target valuation . It initially sought to raise $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation. It is now looking to raise $20 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation. Hazelbaker is joining the company after a period of tumult in the senior management. OpenAI’s Chief Communications Officer Hannah Wong left the company in January, and Chris Lehane, the company’s chief global affairs officer, has been serving as interim head of communications. The company also recently hired former Citadel Head of Corporate Affairs Josh King as a VP handling financial communications as the company prepares for a potential IPO. In a 2020 profile of Hazelbaker in The Information , Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said, “There may be execs who take the pulse of the room before speaking up. Jill takes her own pulse and then speaks up,” Khosrowshahi says. “The vast majority of the time she is right.”

title: LinkedIn Swapped Out Some OpenAI Models to Keep Its Server Costs Flat
content: The more people use AI features in apps, the more the companies selling those apps have to spend on servers to run them , potentially squeezing their profit margins. But some firms have found ways to keep costs in check. For instance, Microsoft-owned LinkedIn says it has flattened the cost of running its AI-powered Hiring Assistant, which uses large language models to automate candidate search and outreach for recruiters, even as usage of the tool has steadily increased in the past year. More than 25,000 businesses pay for Hiring Assistant, LinkedIn said late last month, up from 20,000 it disclosed in September. While the number of customers has grown steadily over the past year—each paying several hundred dollars to over $1,000 per user per month —the cost of serving the product has remained roughly flat, LinkedIn executives said in interviews. And LinkedIn doesn’t plan to increase spending on graphics processing units in the fiscal year that ends June 2027, even as it expects an increase in the number of customers using its AI features, according to Chief Technology Officer Erran Berger. “We can build these ever more powerful capable tools while keeping costs manageable,” he said. That kind of cost control is critical to Microsoft, which like other large cloud providers is under pressure to cut expenses as it expands capital expenditures for data centers, denting its free cash flows. To pull off the feat, LinkedIn swapped out general-purpose LLMs from OpenAI for smaller AI models it developed in-house through a process known as distillation, or customizing a small model to mimic the quality of a larger model within a more limited set of tasks. Specifically, LinkedIn used OpenAI’s models to “teach” smaller open source models how to automate such tasks, according to vice president of engineering Prashanthi Padmanabhan. (LinkedIn declined to say which open source models it used.) When LinkedIn launched Hiring Assistant a year ago, it relied primarily on OpenAI models for most of its features. Now the smaller models automate features such as searching for job candidates, ranking them based on recruiters’ criteria, and drafting outreach messages to candidates, Padmanabhan said. The smaller models get similar results to what OpenAI models produce for a saving of up to 67% on what LinkedIn was paying to run the OpenAI models a year ago, she said. (Since then, OpenAI has also dropped prices for most of its models and released new models it says are more efficient; LinkedIn declined to specify whether its own models are more cost-effective than OpenAI’s current offerings.) However, LinkedIn typically uses OpenAI models to power its newest AI features, until it can develop customized models to swap in, she said. That explains why the overall computing cost has remained steady rather than fallen. “We still use frontier model for many of our use cases, but over time we‘ve figured out it’s not the best way to scale,” Padmanabhan said. “We want to make sure we're bringing innovation and engineering efficiency so the end to end cost stays flat even as the product grows.” Other companies may be able to save even more money if they follow LinkedIn’s example. LinkedIn and the rest of Microsoft can use OpenAI models for free, and must only pay the computing cost of running them, thanks to Microsoft’s long-term business arrangement with OpenAI. In other words, LinkedIn’s savings came purely from running smaller, more efficient models. Companies that pay full freight to use OpenAI or Anthropic’s models stand to benefit even more by running smaller models from elsewhere. To be sure, LinkedIn has such an advantage over other AI app developers because its agreement with OpenAI also allows it to distill that company’s models, whereas OpenAI bars other companies from distilling its models to develop competing ones. Still, companies including AT&T, Cursor and others can customize open source models effectively without relying on distillation, we reported previously . title: Should OpenAI Be Afraid of Jensen Huang?
content: News flash: A lot of people in Silicon Valley are afraid of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang . They have understandable reasons to be fearful, as Leo, Phoebe and I detailed in our story this morning. The chipmaker has a lot of money and influence to throw around, since Huang has the ear of several top government officials, including President Trump . More importantly for model developers like OpenAI , Nvidia controls the flow of AI chips they need to develop and run today’s most advanced models. It’s been hard enough for AI developers to get access to those chips, so it makes sense that the companies would want to avoid anything that might upset Huang. This has led to a situation where OpenAI has avoided taking a public stance on the current debate over chip sales to China for fear of alienating Nvidia and Huang, which generates plenty of revenue from Chinese companies and wants access to the Chinese market itself. (Nvidia isn’t allowed to sell its most advanced tech directly to that market, but Chinese firms like ByteDance and DeepSeek still find a way to access the chips outside China’s borders or through smuggled hardware .) But how scared do AI developers actually need to be? After all, OpenAI and Anthropic are among Nvidia’s largest customers (either directly or indirectly) and the chipmaker needs them just as much as they need Nvidia’s hardware. Anthropic has been quite outspoken in its support of stricter restrictions on the sale of Nvidia chips to Chinese firms and that hasn’t seemed to hurt its chances of accessing Nvidia chips. The chipmaker even said late last year that it would invest up to $10 billion in the Claude maker, and more recently discussed being an anchor investor for its initial public offering later this month. While Anthropic has struggled to get access to enough compute, as I discussed on TITV yesterday, that has less to do with its relationship to Nvidia and more with being overly conservative in signing compute deals in the past. Uncertainty around whether it can gain access to enough servers to support its business was one of the biggest risk factors that Anthropic noted in its IPO prospectus! Moreover, if Nvidia were to reduce the amount of chips it allocates to OpenAI, Nvidia might end up suffering. OpenAI has been working to diversify its sources of compute, adding chips from AMD , Google and Cerebras , as well as developing its own Jalapeño chip for inference (which OpenAI designed with Nvidia archrival Broadcom ). Taking away Nvidia chips would only further accelerate that diversification process and speed up OpenAI’s effort to lessen dependence on Nvidia. Nvidia has as much to lose as anyone if OpenAI stumbles: it is guaranteeing the lease on OpenAI’s giant Ohio data center campus, to the tune of more than $100 billion. That gives OpenAI more leverage than its silence suggests. But it also shows why OpenAI stays quiet. Unlike Anthropic, which has been generating more cash than it burns, OpenAI still relies on Nvidia’s balance sheet, not just its chips. Here’s what else is going on… AI Deep Dive: Chains of Thought Are Getting Harder to Read, Says U.K. Government’s Joseph Bloom Chains of thought, the written reasoning steps that AI models use, have become a key means for companies to monitor the decision-making of their AI agents. But as AI models improve, their chains of thought are growing less legible, making agents harder to monitor, said Joseph Bloom , the head of model transparency at the U.K. AI Security Institute on the latest episode of The Information’s AI Deep Dive . Can anything save chains of thought? According to Bloom, cross-company efforts are underway to reach some kind of consensus on preserving the monitorability of chains of thought before they degrade completely. Encouragingly, AI developers have already largely agreed to avoid influencing their models’ chains of thought out of concerns doing so would prompt AI models to hide their true reasoning. (You could imagine an AI developer telling a model to stop thinking “bad thoughts” in their chains of thought and the model deciding instead to just keep its “bad thoughts” to itself.) The AI industry could reach a similar consensus with “loop transformers,” a new technique that OpenAI and others are using that improve model performance but could encourage models to reveal less of their “thinking,” though opponents argue that such a norm could be overly strict, he said. One approach that could help compensate if chains of thought continue to degrade is mechanistic interpretability , which aims to understand the internal workings of AI models, rather than just their outward behavior. Bloom previously researched mechanistic interpretability, but compared to some previous guests on AI Deep Dive, he has tempered his expectations that it will save the day. “I used to be a computational biologist,” he said. In biology, “you can understand often what’s going on with a system at some level of detail, but it’s still always going to be somewhat messy”—a lesson that could apply to AI as well.— Rocket Drew People on the Move Former U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll is joining OpenAI to help expand the use of the AI company’s technology in national defense and other military applications. Driscoll is now a “senior counselor” for the AI giant focused on national security modernization, according to his LinkedIn page. Overheard Nvidia has recently told some cloud computing customers to reduce their exposure to Chinese companies, potentially narrowing a key route for China’s AI developers to access advanced computing power, The Information reported. The guidance is intended in part to encourage cloud providers, including Nvidia-backed neoclouds, to bring in a more diverse mix of customers. China’s top economic planner said on Tuesday that the country will closely monitor the impact of AI on employment, as Beijing moves to establish safety standards and ethical guidelines covering “the whole life cycle of AI.” Wang Ruomeng , a senior official with the National Development and Reform Commission , told reporters at a press conference that the agency will pay close attention to how AI changes the existing employment structure, while simultaneously looking to leverage AI’s potential to create new jobs. Earnings Report Anthropic reported nearly $17 billion in revenue in the third quarter ending September, up 47% from the second quarter, the latest sign that its once red-hot revenue growth rate is slowing ahead of a blockbuster IPO this month. In Apple’s first earnings under new chief executive John Ternus , the company reported sales growth slowed in its fiscal fourth quarter. Total revenue for the September quarter was $114.5 billion, up from 12% from the previous year, its slowest sales growth for the year. The iPhone business remained strong, advancing 17% to $57.6 billion. The iPad and wearables segments declined 10% and 8%, respectively. Big Number Oracle filed to raise $20 billion through fresh debt and equity offerings on Monday, its latest funding move as it spends heavily on AI infrastructure. The cloud and software firm is selling $10 billion worth of investment-grade bonds and $10 billion in common stock. Court Watch The New York Times sued Brave , a company that offers a browser and a search API, on Monday, alleging it scraped the outlet’s copyrighted content and distributed it to customers including Anthropic , Perplexity , Mistral , xAI and Cohere . Deals and Debuts See The Information’s Generative AI Database for an exclusive list of private companies and their investors. Chipmaker Marvell Technologies agreed Monday to buy laser maker Lumentum in an all-stock deal worth around $80 billion, a sign of how the AI investment boom has boosted Lumentum’s value. Salesforce signed a definitive agreement to acquire Cresta , which makes AI voice agents for customer service, for $2.7 billion, The Information reported . Moffett AI , which makes AI inference chips, completed a Series C+ funding round worth nearly RMB 1 billion (about $138 million), with investors including Renai Capital , Haitang Fund , Dongheng Petroleum. RoboScience , which builds AI models for humanoid robots, completed a Series A2 funding round worth several hundred million yuan (precise figure undisclosed), led by Hupo Capital , Hongruida Investment and Shanghai Semiconductor Industry Investment Tutor Intelligence , which builds AI-powered warehouse and logistics robots, raised $75 million in a Series B funding round led by Andreessen Horowitz. 42AI , which built an AI model that predicts human behavior, emerged from stealth with $62.5 million in seed funding from its founders and Infinity Group. Trajectory , which makes AI models learn from feedback, raised $45 million at a $300 million valuation in a Series A funding round led by Sequoia. nPhase , which uses AI to manage clinical trial data, raised $30 million in a Series D funding round led by Viking Global Investors . Larridin , which tracks how companies’ AI spending pays off, raised $30 million in a Series A funding round led by Pelion Ventures. Clark , which builds AI agents that perform company audits, raised $11 million in a seed funding round led by Touring Capital. Shareholders of Churchill Capital Corp XI approved its SPAC merger with Agility Robotics , which builds AI-powered humanoid warehouse robots, clearing the way for Agility to go public on the Nasdaq under the ticker AGLT on November 5. OpenAI has signed deals with Magnite and PubMatic , whose software enables advertisers to place their ads on websites and other digital platforms, to fill unused ad space on ChatGPT , The Information reported Monday. title: How Nvidia Uses Its Soft Power to Influence Customers and Shape Policy
content: Last month, OpenAI Senior Research Scientist Noam Brown posted a link in a company Slack channel to a news story about OpenAI’s changing stance on advanced chip sales to China and asked a blunt question: “What is our policy on chip exports?” OpenAI policy leaders responded on Slack by citing past company posts, such as a safety blueprint on frontier AI published in June, that supported general chip export controls but did not address China specifically. They also directed staffers to speak to members of the global affairs team working on new export control policies, rather than discussing it on Slack. Chip restrictions are a delicate topic at the company. Over the past year, OpenAI has avoided taking a public stance on the issue of chip export controls for China because OpenAI leaders, including CEO Sam Altman, have expressed concern that doing so will alienate chipmaker Nvidia and its CEO, Jensen Huang, according to people with knowledge of the company’s strategy. Last year, as Congress turned its attention to export control legislation, a senior OpenAI policy staffer privately said OpenAI was not as vocal on chip export controls as it had been under the Biden administration because it feared antagonizing Huang and Nvidia, according to a staffer on Capitol Hill. Huang has become the most recognizable face of the AI boom by transforming a small gaming-chip company into the world’s most valuable business, worth nearly $5 trillion. Since the start of the second Trump administration, Huang has had an open line to the president, and they have bonded over a shared belief in the importance of AI to the American economy and global competitiveness. The relationship has bought Huang some policy wins, most notably limited sales of Nvidia’s last-generation chips to China, but far from everything the company wants. Nvidia’s aggressive use of its soft power to protect its business and influence policy has at times surprised people who have interacted with the company. Government officials sometimes have felt bullied in exchanges with Huang. Officials at political think tanks say Nvidia officials have threatened to cut back on their funding for expressing views the company disagrees with. And Nvidia customers say they tiptoe around certain subjects, as OpenAI has, to avoid displeasing the chip giant. For example, two executives at cloud companies said fear of angering Nvidia is always at the back of their minds when making decisions. Another cloud executive at a company that uses AMD graphics processing units in its data centers said some customers don’t want the cloud company to advertise their use of AMD chips to avoid backlash from Nvidia. (The executive declined to share the customers’ names for the same reason.) The chipmaker’s most powerful form of leverage with such customers is how it doles out its GPUs, which are the dominant chips for training and running AI models today. The Information has previously reported that in some instances over the past couple of years, some customers felt that Nvidia prioritized those who bought its full suite of hardware and punished those who did not. In Washington, Nvidia’s most divisive move has been its push to loosen export controls that prevent it from selling its most advanced chips in China. The effort has alienated China hawks in both political parties and eroded trust in Huang, despite his close relationship with Trump. With Congress gearing up for another battle over export control legislation after Tuesday’s midterm elections, Nvidia’s influence on the Hill could wane as its detractors grow in number. It didn’t help Huang’s reputation in Washington when The New York Times reported last week that U.S. spy agencies had concluded Huang had a close association with a Chinese businesswoman, Huang Le, whom they believed was a Chinese intelligence asset. The U.S. agencies briefed Trump on their findings, but the president did not act on the information. Trump himself appeared to back away from his unconditional support for Huang, telling reporters on Saturday that he continues to have confidence in Huang unless “we find out something to the contrary.” Chris McGuire, a senior fellow for China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations, said Nvidia has created mistrust among policymakers by exaggerating the capabilities of China’s homegrown AI chips as it seeks looser export controls. “The fact is, all the data says that China’s AI chips lag far behind Nvidia’s in both quality and quantity—but this is not the story that Nvidia tells,” said McGuire, who was senior adviser on technology to the U.S. Department of State during both the Biden and Trump administrations. “However, as policymakers in the administration and on the Hill have come to realize that Nvidia’s assertions about China’s AI chip capabilities are not fully accurate, it has caused Nvidia to lose credibility in Washington.” Said Chris Lehane, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, in a statement: “As we have made clear, OpenAI continues to support the strengthening of export controls. Strong export controls will both support the build out of AI on democratic rails but also give the US and its allies more time to strengthen the safety standards, oversight and international coordination needed to help make sure people always stay in control of AI.” “America cannot win the AI race unless America’s AI infrastructure wins worldwide,” said John Rizzo, a spokesperson for Nvidia, in a statement. “If the world’s clouds rely on foreign-made chips, the model and application layers will be foreign-built as well.” Biden Problems Huang’s relationship with the last presidential administration couldn’t have been more different from the one he enjoys with the Trump White House. In 2022, Nvidia was caught off guard when the U.S. government banned sales of the most advanced AI chips to China, which then included Nvidia’s H100, according to multiple government officials and industry figures who interacted with Nvidia at the time. At the time, the chipmaker had a bare-bones government affairs operation. Huang personally launched a vigorous campaign to get the administration to reverse the move, calling then–U.S. Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo on multiple occasions to make his case, according to people familiar with the calls. According to one Biden official, Nvidia had not yet refined its talking points and was not able to convince administration policymakers to make significant changes. Within months, Huang had a team reengineer the chips, slowing the rate at which they transferred data to get under the ban’s technical thresholds. It subsequently released them as the H800 and A800. While the new chips weren’t as good as Nvidia’s H100s at communicating with each other, they were still advanced enough to allow Chinese companies to train and run powerful AI systems. That led the Biden administration in October 2023 to announce new restrictions banning sale of the reengineered chips in China, which Nvidia responded to by releasing the even more stripped-down H20, for the Chinese market. One semiconductor industry executive who worked with Nvidia described the company’s effort to tweak its products and sidestep the ban as giving the Biden administration “the finger” and taking the stance that it did not have to negotiate with the government. That often adversarial attitude toward some Biden officials came not only from Huang but also from Nvidia’s general counsel, Tim Teter, according to several people who have interacted with him. Those people recalled Teter using unflattering nicknames for government officials, academics and think tank scholars he did not like. After the initial round of Biden export controls came out, Nvidia began to staff up its team in Washington, hiring former senior Homeland Security official Meg King, senior State Department official Ruth Berry and Semiconductor Industry Association Director Eric Breckenfeld in 2023. Two former Biden officials said Nvidia’s new team didn’t improve relations with the administration—instead, they would not productively engage on technical issues around export controls. Nvidia executives denied the seriousness of issues such as chip smuggling, despite what the government regarded as compelling evidence to the contrary. Near the end of the Biden administration, Huang and his team fought another policy, issued in January 2025 and known as the Framework for Artificial Intelligence Diffusion, that further limited exports of advanced chips. One Biden official said the new rules were particularly strict in part because Nvidia did not come to the table and negotiate. The Nvidia CEO told then–National Security Advisor Jake Sullivan that the moves would embolden China’s chip industry, according to people familiar with the conversations. He also questioned why security professionals were now using technology to provoke a military adversary. Huang argued that the U.S. rules were hurting Nvidia, when the alternative was that China could stay hooked on Nvidia tech forever. He said the company’s chips were just normal technology, and he didn’t understand why the government was treating them as though they were something more dangerous. Still, Biden officials found Huang’s interactions offputting: They described him as “pugilistic.” The tenor of his approach was not common among the CEOs they dealt with, former Biden officials said. Tank Battles Huang quickly found a new ally when Trump reentered the White House in January 2025. While Nvidia didn’t have much of a Washington presence during Trump’s first term, according to one former senior Trump official, Huang became a fixture in the White House during Trump’s second term. Huang influenced policy discussions around export controls, especially ahead of May 2025, when the Trump administration announced it was rescinding the Biden-era chip controls. It also greenlit new AI deals and chip exports to several Gulf countries to which Nvidia chip sales had previously been restricted. As Congress began to debate its own legislation to introduce different forms of chip export controls, Nvidia also ratcheted up its lobbying campaigns across Washington. That included putting pressure on think tank scholars advocating for stricter chip export controls. In March 2025, Sam Hammond, the AI policy director at the right-leaning Foundation for American Innovation, wrote an article for City Journal arguing that U.S. companies like Nvidia were helping China catch up with the U.S. in AI due to leaky export control policies and lax enforcement of chip smuggling. Hammond said within hours of publication, Nvidia’s government affairs team requested a meeting with him, where they denied the existence of chip smuggling. According to Hammond, they even demanded he produce the serial number of a smuggled chip to demonstrate that smuggling was a real phenomenon. Hammond crossed Nvidia again in August 2025 when he posted a message on X in response to an article about the Chinese military seeking Nvidia chips for a variety of AI projects: “Nvidia is arming China’s military.” Soon after, Hammond said Nvidia emailed his boss, saying the Foundation for American Innovation wasn’t living up to its pro-innovation values and offering to have their general counsels meet. It’s not unusual for companies to joust with Washington think tanks that criticize them or advocate for policies contrary to their interests, according to people who work for the organizations. As a bridge between academia and government, think tanks play an important role in shaping policy. While companies often donate to them, many think tanks purport to maintain academic and editorial independence, even if the lines often get blurred. Nvidia especially has a reputation for being outspoken about think tank output it disagrees with. A former researcher at the Center for a New American Security, a think tank focused on national security and defense policy that receives donations from Nvidia, said Nvidia is not the only organization that pushes back on think tank scholarship it disagrees with. But the researcher noted Nvidia’s increasing sway in Washington, with its government affairs staff growing substantially since the Biden years. Nvidia tangled with think tanks before Trump’s return to the White House. In 2023, several people familiar with the discussions said Nvidia had tried to use its influence—including funding—to sideline Greg Allen, then director of the AI policy arm of the Center for Strategic and International Studies, an influential think tank focused on national security and geopolitics. Allen staunchly supports chip export controls. One of those people said Nvidia became a major donor to CSIS and coordinated with the think tank on specific policy reports not labeled as sponsored. CSIS did not ultimately fire Allen; he left the think tank earlier this year. The New York Times earlier reported some details on the incident in 2023. A spokesperson for CSIS said in a statement that Nvidia never asked CSIS to fire Greg Allen, and that the think tank discloses funding that supports specific research reports. Other think tanks say they’ve been on the receiving end of threats from Nvidia during Trump’s second term. One fellow at a prominent conservative think tank that received donations from Nvidia said he faced complaints earlier this year over his outspoken public critiques of Nvidia—including claims that the Chinese military was using Nvidia chips. In an internal email thread shared with The Information, leaders at the think tank said Nvidia policy leadership had expressed concerns to the think tank over the “veracity” of the fellow’s public statements and his unwillingness to engage on the issue. According to the email thread, Nvidia leadership said they were supportive of the work of other scholars there, but renewing Nvidia’s donation to the think tank would be a “tough sell internally.” Ultimately, the fellow pushed back on Nvidia’s allegations internally. At a later meeting, the think tank celebrated the episode as exemplifying the independence of its work, according to someone who was there. ‘Trust Deficit’ On Capitol Hill, Nvidia’s hard-line stances on chip export controls have frayed the company’s relations with many lawmakers and their staff, according to those staffers, lobbyists and other policy experts. One high-profile incident involved Brian Mast, a Republican congressman from Florida. As chair of the influential House Foreign Affairs Committee, Mast supported export controls, drawing the ire of Nvidia. In January, Mast posted a thread on X sharing an article that accused Nvidia of pushing conservative influencers to attack export controls. “Jensen Huang, since you’re not on X, I’ll tag your company Nvidia,” Mast wrote. “You and your paid minions are fighting to sell millions of advanced AI chips to Chinese military companies like Alibaba and Tencent. I’m trying to stop that from happening.” Hill staffers, other government officials and lobbyists said Nvidia has strained relationships with many Congressional offices. According to one Hill staffer, the company has created “a trust deficit” in Washington that would take years to recover from. They pointed to other moderate lawmakers increasingly turning their attention on Nvidia, such as Chris Coons, a centrist Democratic senator from Delaware who has become a vocal critic of Nvidia’s chip exports to China. More recently, some Congressional staffers and lobbyists say they have noticed a softer touch in Nvidia’s interactions on Capitol Hill. As evidence that Nvidia’s government affairs operation is maturing, they pointed to its June hiring of former Intel lobbyist and Obama administration Commerce Department senior official Bruce Andrews as its new chief external affairs officer. Staffers and lobbyists said Nvidia has been less aggressive during this year’s Congressional fight over chip export control bills. Some of them attributed the change partly to the fact that David Sacks, a close Nvidia ally, left the White House as its crypto and AI czar in March. Part of the shift can also be chalked up to the fact that the Trump administration cleared Nvidia to sell limited quantities of workhorse H200 chips to Chinese companies last December, though Nvidia has yet to recognize material revenue from the sales due to restrictions by the Chinese government . Plus, Nvidia’s biggest customers are gaining some leverage—which could also sway the balance of power among AI giants in Washington. While OpenAI may be wary of challenging Nvidia on China export control policy, it has been willing to develop its own competitor chip, Jalapeño, which it claims performs better than Nvidia’s Blackwell GPUs on some benchmarks. Unlike Nvidia, OpenAI has said it will deploy its own chips only in the U.S. and allied countries. An OpenAI spokesperson confirmed that the company will not sell its chip to China. Indeed, Nvidia’s core business is facing more challengers than ever as many of its U.S. customers enter the red-hot market of AI chips. That, according to one semiconductor executive, is the reason it is so insistent on retaining the ability to export its chips overseas. But with Congress expected to renew the legislative debate over export controls after Tuesday’s midterm elections, Nvidia’s standing in Washington will face a significant test. “There are so many ways that policymakers could benefit from Nvidia’s incredible technical expertise and deep market insight to help craft policies that both better protect U.S. national security and help U.S. businesses thrive,” said McGuire of the Council on Foreign Relations. “But that type of partnership requires trust, which has to be earned.”

title: The Download: blended meat, restored sight, and the agentic web
content:
The Download: blended meat, restored sight, and the agentic web
Plus: Democrats have dealt tech billionaires a major midterm setback.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
These startups hope “blended” food will cut our appetite for red meat
In the fall of 2025, Jeff Dodge served hungry students steaming marinara sauce and meatballs. The students loved them: 92% of those who tried them wanted them on the menu. Few could guess that mushrooms had been mixed into the meat.
Dodge was testing a new product called 50/Cut from the company Joyn. The blend of seemingly simple ingredients—available as meatballs, burgers, and ground meat—could help solve one of the biggest challenges of the climate crisis: getting people to eat less meat, particularly beef.
Joyn is among a wave of startups creating “blended meat,” which combines plant proteins with the real deal. The logic: The best meat replacement is … better meat.
Get a taste of the startups betting on greener beef.
—Meghan McCarron
This implant can restore sight for patients with macular degeneration
More than 5 million people have an advanced form of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) called geographic atrophy, in which retinal cells die off. Until now, no treatment could restore their vision. A system called PRIMA changes that.
It combines a retinal implant with camera-equipped eyeglasses to improve sight in patients who develop a blind spot in the middle of their vision. After training sessions, more than 80% of recipients could read, do crosswords, and use their phones.
—Linda Marsa
MIT Technology Review Narrated: The agentic web is here
In 2001, a decade after inventing the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision: an internet navigated by autonomous software agents that address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves.
At the time, the idea seemed far-fetched. But a quarter-century on, AI agents are beginning to make it a reality. They can triage your inbox, do your grocery shopping, and even access your bank accounts.
This new era is being called the agentic web, and it will inevitably transform the internet. Whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess.
This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts. Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 Democrats have dealt tech billionaires a major midterm setback
The results could bring tougher scrutiny of AI and data centres. (CNBC)
+ Musk poured millions into Texas, but both his candidates lost. (Wired $)
+ Several winners promised to restrict data centre construction. (FT $)
+ Stock futures slid as Democrats won big. (NBC News)
+ The tech left said it’s ready to “wipe the floor.”  (Vanity Fair $)
2 Google is shutting off Search for schools that reject AI
The company said AI and Search can no longer be untwined. (CNN)
+ Critics accused Google of pressuring schools to adopt AI. (NBC News)
+ AI is the end of search as we know it. (MIT Technology Review)
3 The Binance hackers used fake job interviews in their record heist
They targeted an engineer through LinkedIn. (NBC News)
+ Researchers had repeatedly warned about the tactics. (TechCrunch)
+ The breach could boost demand for specialist crypto custodians. (CNBC)
4 Materials maker 3M will pay $7.35 billion to settle “forever chemicals” lawsuits
The suits involve PFAS in firefighting foam. (WSJ $)
+ New tech could help rid water of PFAS. (MIT Technology Review)
5 Finland is opening a nuclear waste vault built to last 100,000 years
It will bury spent fuel 400 metres underground. (New Scientist $)
+ It's time to make new plans for nuclear waste. (MIT Technology Review)
6 Russia wants underground data centers after Ukrainian strikes
Drone attacks have disrupted services used by millions. (Ars Technica)
7 Anthropic is working on a system to prove AI models’ identity
FlashProve uses cryptography to verify a model’s outputs. (TechCrunch)
+ “Personhood credentials” could prove you’re human. (MIT Technology Review)
8 Old jet engines are being scavenged to power data centers
But environmentalists warn they will produce more pollution. (NYT $)
9 Dinosaur blood has been found in fossils for the first time
The discovery advances research into ancient biomolecules. (Guardian)
10 Chernobyl’s dogs appear to be evolving
Scientists found differences linked to DNA repair and immunity. (Wired $)
Quote of the day
"Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn't work this time 🤷♂️"
—Elon Musk tries to laugh off a costly loss on X after the Republican candidates he spent record sums supporting got drubbed in the US midterm elections.
One more thing
Want to understand the current state of AI? Check out these charts.
If you’re following AI news, you’re probably getting whiplash. AI is a gold rush. AI is a bubble. AI is taking your job. AI can’t even read a clock. Stanford’s 2026 AI Index—the field's annual report card—cuts through the noise.
The data reveals a technology evolving faster than we can manage. From the China-US rivalry and model breakthroughs to public sentiment and the impact on jobs, here are the index’s key findings on the state of AI today.
—Michelle Kim
We can still have nice things
A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)
+ A 99-year-old woman has become the world's oldest wing walker.
+ Strap in for a rider's-eye view of the fastest urban downhill mountain bike run in history.
+ From a bodybuilding Arnie to a weeping Frenchman, these 39 images changed how we see men (for good and bad).
+ 50 years after the Ramones’ first LP dropped, members of Green Day, blink-182, and Rancid played a concert honoring the legendary band.

title: Securing the agentic enterprise with data lineage
content:
In partnership with
Cyberhaven
A sales representative asks an AI agent for customer pricing, and the agent pulls data from multiple sources: restricted pricing systems, internal communications, and archived quotes. The output looks accurate to the agent, so a second agent uses the data to draft the proposal for the sales rep. No human checks either handoff. When it’s discovered that the proposal includes unapproved, confidential, and sensitive information, no one can trace where the problematic data entered the workflow or how it spread across systems, files, and agents.
DOWNLOAD THE REPORT
This scenario illustrates why AI governance needs to evolve, rapidly and dynamically. As more enterprises begin to use agentic AI in daily workflows, they’re realizing that they must manage more than static files; they must manage moving and fragmented data that is continuously ingested, copied, summarized, transformed, reused, and redistributed in new forms. In short, AI security isn’t a tool problem; it’s a data visibility problem.
Consequently, traditional security approaches built solely around applications, systems, networks, or endpoints are no longer sufficient. Securing agentic AI at scale requires understanding how data moves. Teams, therefore, need to establish data lineage in order to effectively manage
governance, accountability, and trust
across human, agentic, and hybrid workflows.

THWS-Hackathon InclusivAI bringt KI und Inklusion zusammen

Prof. Dr. Ivan Yamshchikov, Leiter des CAIRO (re.), mit teilnehmenden Studierenden am Hackathon „InclusivAI“
| Quelle:
THWS/Franziska Koeniger

Download
Interdisziplinäre Studierenden-Teams arbeiten mit künstlicher Intelligenz für Praxispartner aus der Region Würzburg
Initiative für mehr Teilhabe: Rund 130 Teilnehmende haben beim Hackathon „InclusivAI: Mit KI Vielfalt stärken und Barrieren abbauen“ der Technischen Hochschule Würzburg-Schweinfurt (THWS) mitgearbeitet. Das Event fand am Forschungsinstitut CAIRO (Center für Künstliche Intelligenz) in Kooperation mit der Fakultät Angewandte Sozialwissenschaften der THWS in Würzburg statt. Platin-Partner der Veranstaltung war die Caritas Würzburg.
Einen Tag lang entwickelten interdisziplinäre Teams aus fünf bis zehn Studierenden Prototypen für reale Herausforderungen in den Bereichen Barrierefreiheit, Bildung, Arbeitswelt, Mobilität, Kommunikation und digitaler Teilhabe. Die Aufgaben stammten von Praxispartnern aus der Region: Dem Caritasverband für die Diözese Würzburg e. V., den Mainfränkischen Werkstätten, der Caritas-Don Bosco gGmbH sowie dem THWS-Projekt Fit4Germany, die die Teams mit Fachwissen, Daten und Feedback begleiteten. Der Hackathon selbst fand auf Englisch statt. Parallel dazu bot ein deutschsprachiger Gäste-Track am Nachmittag fünf Keynotes und Startup-Pitches rund um KI und gesellschaftlicher Teilhabe. Am Ende des Events stellten die Studierenden ihre Ergebnisse vor.
„Inklusion ist kein Nischenthema für KI – sie ist der Härtetest dafür, ob KI tatsächlich für Menschen gebaut wird“, betont Prof. Dr. Yvan Yamshchikov, der das CAIRO leitet. „Dass sich 130 Studierende aus den Studiengängen Informatik, Sozialwissenschaften, Gestaltung und Wirtschaft angemeldet haben, zeigt, wie groß das Interesse ist, Technologie und soziale Praxis zusammenzubringen.“
Keynotes: Von Assistenzsystemen bis zum humanoiden Roboter
Den Gäste-Track eröffnete Prof. Dr. Ulrich Gartzke, Professor für Management in sozialen Organisationen, mit Erfahrungen aus dem Forschungsprojekt CAREBELLS. Das Projekt entwickelt KI-gestützte Assistenzsysteme für Menschen mit Unterstützungsbedarf. Im Mittelpunkt stand die Frage, wie KI verständlich, vertrauenswürdig und inklusiv gestaltet werden kann. Fabian Schlausch zeigte, wie sein Start-up KLAO ein eigens trainiertes Sprachmodell mit menschlicher Prüfung durch Expertinnen und Experten für Leichte Sprache kombiniert – ein Thema mit Dringlichkeit, denn seit dem Barrierefreiheitsstärkungsgesetz sind auch private Unternehmen zu barrierefreier Kommunikation verpflichtet. Jedoch würden 88 Prozent der Unternehmen und 93 Prozent der öffentlichen Einrichtungen diese Pflicht nicht erfüllen.
Dr. Tobias Koopmann von vAudience widmete sich der Frage, wie KI Pflegekräfte vom Dokumentierungsaufwand entlasten kann. Prof. Dr. Dr. h. c. Robert Grebner, THWS-Präsident von 2012 bis 2024 und heute Forschungsprofessor am CAIRO, berichtete aus dem Projekt Wübota, in dem der erste personengroße humanoide Roboter Würzburgs für die Unterstützung in Alltag und Arbeit weiterentwickelt wird. Den Abschluss bildete Katharina Mosene vom Leibniz-Institut für Medienforschung am Hans-Bredow-Institut mit einem Impuls dazu, wie Bias (Voreingenommenheit) in KI-Systemen entsteht und welche Kompetenzen und Regeln es braucht, damit KI Ungleichheiten abbaut, anstatt sie zu automatisieren.
In den anschließenden Startup-Pitches stellten LivingLines, eine Tablet-App für individuelles, mehrsprachiges Lernen im Mathematikunterricht, und InkluCard, ein digitaler Inklusions-Steckbrief für Menschen mit besonderen Bedürfnissen, ihre Produkte vor.
Caritas Würzburg als Platin-Partner
Die Caritas Würzburg unterstützte den InclusivAI-Hackathon als Platin-Partner. Mit der Caritas brachte der Hackathon einen der größten Träger sozialer Arbeit in der Region an den Tisch – und damit genau die Praxisperspektive, die KI-Lösungen für Inklusion brauchen, um im Alltag von Menschen anzukommen. Die Caritas-Unterstützung schuf den Rahmen, in dem neue Ideen, Austausch und Zusammenarbeit im Mittelpunkt standen.
Der Hackathon war zugleich ein Beispiel für fakultätsübergreifende Zusammenarbeit an der THWS: Das Institut CAIRO richtete den Hackathon gemeinsam mit der Fakultät Angewandte Sozialwissenschaften (FAS) aus und erhielt dadurch sozialwissenschaftliche und sozialpädagogische Expertise. Prof. Dr. Sven Warnke, Prof. Dr. Ulrich Gartzke und Prof. Dr. Steffen Hillebrecht hatten die Aufgaben gemeinsam mit den Praxispartnern mitentwickelt. „Mit der Caritas Würzburg als Platin-Partner und der FAS als Kooperationspartner haben wir genau die Expertise an Bord, die nötig ist“, so Prof. Dr. Yamshchikov.
Weitere Kooperationspartner waren das TGZ Würzburg, die Caritas Don Bosco, das Social Startup Hub Bayern, CAREBELLS, die Mainfränkischen Werkstätten, GRIBS sowie das Zentrum für Digitale Innovationen Mainfranken (ZDI). Für das ZDI begleitete Netzwerkmanager Dr. Christian Andersen den Hackathon und öffnete den studentischen Teams den Zugang zur Würzburger Gründungsszene.
Über das CAIRO
CAIRO ist das KI-Forschungsinstitut der THWS. Acht Professorinnen und Professoren sowie rund 30 Mitarbeitende forschen dort zu Natural Language Processing, Computer Vision, probabilistischem Deep Learning, Robotik, KI und Recht sowie Fragen der Governance und europäischer KI-Souveränität. Das Institut veranstaltet regelmäßig Hackathons mit regionalen Partnern, die den Studierenden reale Challenges anbieten.
Über die THWS
Die Technische Hochschule Würzburg-Schweinfurt (THWS) zählt zu den größten Hochschulen für angewandte Wissenschaften in Bayern und steht seit ihrer Gründung im Jahr 1971 für hervorragende Lehre und angewandte Forschung. Mit rund 9.200 Studierenden, einem breit gefächerten Angebot von mehr als 60 Studiengängen sowie zwei Promotionszentren deckt die THWS ein weites Spektrum ab, das von Technik über Wirtschafts- und Sozialwissenschaften sowie Sprache bis hin zu Gestaltung reicht. Die THWS ist nicht nur regional in Franken und Bayern verwurzelt, sondern auch stark international ausgerichtet, was sich in zahlreichen Kooperationen und Austauschprogrammen weltweit und nicht zuletzt in einem vielseitigen englischsprachigen Studienangebot widerspiegelt.

Der ATHENE Digital Hub Cybersecurity startet eine kostenfreie Online-Plattform für Startups, Partner, Unternehmen und Investmentfirmen – kostenfreies Vernetzungsangebot für Deutschland, Österreich und die Schweiz
Darmstadt / Berlin, den 04. November 2026 – Was sind die neuesten Cybersecurity-Innovationen und wer entwickelt die Lösungen von morgen? Der ATHENE Startup Finder zeigt innovative Cybersecurity-Startups aus Deutschland, Österreich und der Schweiz. Ziel der neuen Online-Plattform ist es, Angebot und Nachfrage im Bereich Cybersecurity besser zu verbinden und Startups bei der Kunden- und Investorensuche zu unterstützen. Erstmals vorgestellt wurde die Plattform auf dem Side-Event „Innovation gemeinsam skalieren“ des Digital-Gipfels der Bundesregierung in Berlin. Weitere Informationen zum kostenfreien Angebot unter
https://startup-finder.athene-center.de
Eine Plattform für mehr Sichtbarkeit und Vernetzung
Der ATHENE Startup Finder bringt vier Zielgruppen zusammen: Junge Cybersecurity-Startups präsentieren ihre Angebote auf der Plattform, Partner machen ihre Unterstützungsangebote für Gründende dort zugänglich, Unternehmen entdecken innovative Cybersecurity-Lösungen, die zu ihrem Bedarf passen, und Investmentfirmen verschaffen sich einen Überblick über neue, vielversprechende Startups. Alle Nutzerinnen und Nutzer können die Plattform kostenfrei nutzen. Der ATHENE Digital Hub Cybersecurity betreibt die Plattform als neutrale Instanz und ergänzt sie durch einen Event-Kalender sowie einen Newsletter. So erhöht der ATHENE Startup Finder die Sichtbarkeit junger Cybersecurity-Unternehmen und unterstützt sie dabei, potenzielle Kunden, Partner und Investoren zu erreichen.
„Der Startup Finder ist vom Ökosystem für das Ökosystem gedacht. Er lebt davon, dass Startups und Partner ihn gemeinsam gestalten und nutzen. Je mehr sich beteiligen, desto leichter finden die richtigen Akteure zueinander“, sagt Clara Pfeuffer, Leiterin des ATHENE Digital Hub Cybersecurity.
Für Startups: Startups legen ihr Profil selbst an und machen sich so sichtbar. Aufgenommen werden gründergeführte, technologiebasierte Cybersecurity-Startups, die jünger als zehn Jahre sind.
Für Partner: Partner mit Unterstützungsangeboten wie Inkubatoren, Venture Builder oder Acceleratoren haben die Möglichkeit, ihre Angebote auf der Plattform bekannt zu machen und Kontakte auf die Plattform einzuladen.
Für Unternehmen: Unternehmen können die Plattform nutzen, um gezielt nach passenden Cybersecurity-Lösungen zu suchen.
Für Investmentfirmen: Investmentfirmen sind eingeladen, sich auf der Plattform über vielversprechende Cybersecurity-Startups zu informieren und ihre Portfolio-Startups auf das Angebot aufmerksam zu machen.
Das kommt als Nächstes: Erweiterte Zugänge, Matching und Events
Der Startup Finder soll schrittweise weiterentwickelt werden. Der Digital Hub als Plattformbetreiber lädt deshalb alle Zielgruppen ein, die Plattform mitzugestalten, und freut sich über Anregungen und Verbesserungsvorschläge. Geplant sind unter anderem eigene, erweiterte Zugänge für Investmentfirmen mit zusätzlichen Informationen und Funktionen sowie ein Bedarfsmatching, das insbesondere mittelständische Unternehmen dabei unterstützen soll, passende Cybersecurity-Lösungen zu finden. Darüber hinaus sollen systematische Vernetzungsmöglichkeiten und Innovationsformate entstehen, etwa Events und Matching-Formate, die Startups, Forschung, Unternehmen und Investmentfirmen gezielt miteinander in Kontakt bringen.

ATHENE ist Deutschlands nationales Forschungszentrum für angewandte Cybersicherheit. Heute ist ATHENE Europas größtes Forschungszentrum für Cybersicherheit und betreibt missionsorientierte Spitzenforschung mit messbaren Auswirkungen auf Politik, Wirtschaft und Gesellschaft. title: Neuer Masterstudiengang Mechanical Engineering International (M.Sc.) an der Hochschule Bochum akkreditiert
content:
Neuer Masterstudiengang Mechanical Engineering International (M.Sc.) an der Hochschule Bochum akkreditiert
Von Simulation bis Robotik: Der Master verbindet Theorie, Praxis und intelligente Fertigung.
Die Hochschule Bochum erweitert ihr Studienangebot um den neu akkreditierten Masterstudiengang Mechanical Engineering International (M.Sc.). Der dreisemestrige, englischsprachige Studiengang richtet sich an Absolvent*innen ingenieurwissenschaftlicher Bachelorstudiengänge aus Deutschland und dem Ausland. Er verbindet fundierte ingenieurwissenschaftliche Kompetenzen mit anwendungsbezogenen Aufgabenstellungen und fördert den fachlichen Austausch in einem internationalen Lernumfeld.
Technische Systeme analysieren, modellieren und optimieren
Aufbauend auf einem einschlägigen Bachelorstudium vermittelt der Masterstudiengang vertiefte wissenschaftliche Kompetenzen in Maschinenbau und Mechatronik. Die Studierenden lernen, technische Fragestellungen systematisch zu analysieren, geeignete Methoden anzuwenden, Ergebnisse nachvollziehbar zu dokumentieren sowie Projektpläne und Lösungskonzepte für technische Aufgabenstellungen zu entwickeln.
Inhaltliche Schwerpunkte liegen unter anderem in den Bereichen intelligente Fertigungssysteme, Strukturoptimierung, Product Lifecycle Management, Robotik sowie Verfahren zur Überwachung und Bewertung technischer Strukturen. Über Profil- und Wahlpflichtmodule können die Studierenden ihr fachliches Profil individuell weiterentwickeln und zugleich interdisziplinäre Kompetenzen aufbauen.
In der Projektarbeit wenden die Studierenden ingenieurwissenschaftliche Kenntnisse und Methoden auf komplexe praktische Aufgaben an, entwickeln technische Lösungen eigenständig und bearbeiten wissenschaftliche Projekte auch im Team.
Berufliche Perspektiven
Mögliche Tätigkeitsfelder für Absolvent*innen liegen unter anderem in Forschung und Entwicklung, Konstruktion, technischem Vertrieb und Projektmanagement – etwa in international tätigen Unternehmen, kleinen und mittleren Unternehmen sowie öffentlichen Einrichtungen. Der Studienabschluss qualifiziert zudem für eine Promotion sowie für den höheren Dienst.
Der vom Fachbereich Mechatronik und Maschinenbau angebotene Studiengang umfasst 90 ECTS-Punkte und kann in drei Semestern absolviert werden. Ein Studienbeginn ist sowohl zum Sommer- als auch zum Wintersemester möglich. Für die Zulassung sind Englischkenntnisse auf dem Niveau C1 des Gemeinsamen Europäischen Referenzrahmens für Sprachen (GER) erforderlich. Grundkenntnisse der deutschen Sprache auf Niveau A2 sind ebenfalls nachzuweisen.
Internationale Bewerber*innen (Nicht-EU/ EWR) können sich ab sofort bis zum 15. Dezember 2026 für das kommende Sommersemester bewerben. Für deutsche und gleichgestellte Bewerber*innen öffnet die Bewerbungsphase im Dezember und endet am 15. Januar 2027.

Wie Gebirge oder Flussläufe das Entstehen von Arten beeinflussen, untersucht der Evolutionsbiologe und Umweltwissenschaftler Prof. Oskar Hagen anhand von Computermodellen. In der jetzt erschienenen Ausgabe des Magazins „Forschung Frankfurt“ erklärt der Experte, wie seine Modelle das „Nachspielen“ der Evolution von vielen Millionen Jahren ermöglichen und erste Prognosen für die Lebensvielfalt im Klimawandel geben. Weitere Beiträge von Forschung Frankfurt berichten über die Kanaren als Biodiversitätshotspots, nehmen das Aussterben des prähistorischen Hais Megalodon in den Blick oder schildern, wie globale Standards für die Nachhaltigkeitsberichterstattung von Unternehmen entwickelt werden.
FRANKFURT. Oskar Hagen ist Herr über Zeit und Raum – zumindest in seinen Computermodellen. Hier kann er Flussdeltas entstehen und Gebirge zu Ebenen werden lassen, und Millionen von Jahren schrumpfen zu Minuten an Rechenzeit. Warum gibt es – untypischerweise – am Oberlauf des Amazonas so viel mehr Fischarten als im Flussdelta? Warum sind im üppig grünen Kongobecken viel weniger Tier- und Pflanzenarten beheimatet als in den Regenwäldern Südostasiens oder Südamerikas? In der jüngsten Ausgabe von „Forschung Frankfurt“ berichtet der Wissenschaftler, wie er und sein Team Computermodelle entwickeln, um die Mechanismen der Evolution besser zu verstehen – und wie sich damit auch Prognosen zum Beispiel für das Aussterben tropischer Fischarten bei steigenden Meerestemperaturen ableiten lassen. Das Thema Artensterben berührt ihn auch persönlich: „Jede Art wurde über viele Millionen Jahre hinweg durch die Evolution geformt. Das allein sollte uns demütig stimmen.“
Weitere Artikel von „Forschung Frankfurt“ handeln zum Beispiel von den Kanaren, auf denen sich in der Abgeschiedenheit vom Festland viele neue Pflanzenarten entwickelt haben – die besonders anfällig für einschleppte Kaninchen und Ziegen sind. In weiteren Texten erklären Forschende, wie man den Speiseplan des einstigen „Königs der Meere“, des riesigen Hais Megalodon, anhand seiner Zähne rekonstruieren kann und warum er ausgestorben ist. Weitere Forschungsgeschichten handeln davon, wie Finanz- und Biowissenschaftler der Goethe-Universität gemeinsam an der Entwicklung einer Umweltklassifikation etwa von DAX-Konzernen arbeiten und wie sie zur Schaffung globaler Standards für die Nachhaltigkeitsberichterstattung beitragen.

Das Fraunhofer IDMT und die Pan Acoustics GmbH haben erfolgreich eine wartungsarme Sensorik zur lokalen Niederschlagsmessung erprobt. Jetzt sucht das thüringische Forschungsinstitut weitere Praxispartner für Pilotinstallationen.
+++ Fraunhofer IDMT und Pan Acoustics erproben wartungsarme Sensorik im Freifeld +++
Wie stark regnet es an welchem Ort? Diese Information lässt sich künftig aus den Strukturschwingungen z. B. eines Photovoltaikmoduls gewinnen. Treffen Regentropfen auf eine Oberfläche, versetzen sie diese in Schwingung. Das Ilmenauer Fraunhofer-Institut für Digitale Medientechnologie IDMT und der Audio- und Akustikspezialist Pan Acoustics GmbH aus Wolfenbüttel haben daraus eine Methode zur Niederschlagsmessung entwickelt. Die dafür eingesetzten Sensoren sind dank ihres energieeffizienten Betriebs und ihrer Bauweise ohne bewegliche Komponenten besonders langlebig und wartungsarm.
Im kürzlich abgeschlossenen Forschungsprojekt »lokalRAIN« haben die Partner den Ansatz im Labor und unter realen Wetterbedingungen erprobt und zu einem funktionsfähigen Demonstrator weiterentwickelt.
Darauf aufbauend will das Fraunhofer IDMT jetzt weitere Pilotinstallationen auf den Weg bringen. »Hierfür suchen wir Praxispartner, mit denen wir das Messsystem unter unterschiedlichen Einsatzbedingungen erproben und für konkrete Anwendungen weiterentwickeln können«, erläutert Jakob Bergner, wissenschaftlicher Leiter des Forschungsprojekts am Fraunhofer IDMT.
Ziel ist ein dichtes Messnetz, das lokale Unterschiede der Niederschlagsmenge besser erfasst. Gerade bei lokal begrenztem Starkregenereignissen kann die Regenmenge schon auf kurzer Distanz stark variieren.
Messgeräte zur Niederschlagserfassung, etwa an Wetterstationen, stehen aufgrund von Wartungsaufwand und Kosten häufig nur an ausgewählten Standorten zur Verfügung. Zusätzliche, räumlich verteilte und vernetzte Messpunkte können helfen, die lokale Niederschlagsverteilung genauer abzubilden.
+++ Vom Regensimulator ins Freifeld +++
Im Regensimulator des Fraunhofer IDMT untersuchten die Forschenden zunächst unterschiedliche Niederschlagsintensitäten und Tropfengrößen sowie verschiedene Photovoltaikmodule, Sensorarten und -positionen.
Anschließend wurden drei Messsysteme unter realen Wetterbedingungen am Fraunhofer IDMT in Ilmenau, bei Pan Acoustics in Wolfenbüttel und im Wettergarten der TU Ilmenau installiert. Die dort gewonnenen Messdaten haben die Forschenden mit Referenzniederschlagsdaten verknüpft und sie für das Training und den Test der Machine-Learning-Modelle genutzt.
+++ Vor Ort auswerten, per Funk vernetzen +++
Körperschallsensoren erfassen die durch Regentropfen ausgelösten Schwingungen der Photovoltaikmodule. Ein Machine-Learning-Modell bestimmt daraus die Niederschlagsintensität. Die Auswertung erfolgt direkt am Messort auf einem energieeffizienten Mikrocontroller.
Statt umfangreicher Rohdaten müssen so nur kompakte Ergebnisdaten übertragen werden. Für diese Funkübertragung entwickelte Pan Acoustics eine eigene Hard- und Softwarelösung. In Tests wurden Funkreichweiten von rund vier Kilometern im städtischen Umfeld und mehr als 35 Kilometern bei ländlicher Sichtverbindung erreicht.
Die Daten der verschiedenen Messpunkte werden in einer zentralen Dateninfrastruktur des Fraunhofer IDMT zusammengeführt und gemeinsam ausgewertet.
+++ Machbarkeit nachgewiesen +++
Die Ergebnisse aus dem Forschungsprojekt zeigen, dass sich die Niederschlagsintensität anhand der Schwingungen von Photovoltaikmodulen zuverlässig abschätzen lässt. Im Bereich zwischen 2 und 5 Millimetern Niederschlag pro Stunde betrug die mittlere absolute Abweichung vom Referenzwert 1,88 Millimeter pro Stunde. Damit wird im Bereich der niedrigen Niederschlagsintensitäten bereits die Genauigkeitsklasse C der Weltorganisation für Meteorologie (WMO) erreicht. Diese Genauigkeitsklasse lässt eine maximale Abweichung von 2 Millimetern pro Stunde bei der Messung der Niederschlagsintensität zu.
»Die Machbarkeit unseres Ansatzes für Leichtregen haben wir nachgewiesen. Jetzt wollen wir weitere Daten für die seltener vorkommenden Starkregenereignisse sammeln und so das Verfahren für unterschiedliche Einsatzbedingungen optimieren«, sagt Jakob Bergner.
Das vom Fraunhofer IDMT und Pan Acoustics entwickelte Verfahren soll hochpräzise Niederschlagsmessgeräte nicht ersetzen, sondern bestehende Messnetze um zusätzliche, wartungsarme Messpunkte ergänzen.
+++ Lokale Niederschlagsdaten für konkrete Anwendungen +++
Ein wichtiges Anwendungsszenario könnte beispielsweise die Einbindung lokaler Niederschlagsdaten in Urban Digital Twins – digitale Zwillinge von Städten – sein. Dort lassen sich Niederschlagsinformationen räumlich darstellen und mit weiteren Daten verknüpfen.
Kommunale Leitstellen und Infrastrukturbetreiber können die Niederschlagsdaten nutzen, um sehr schnell die Lage von Starkregenereignissen zu bewerten und entsprechende Maßnahmen einleiten zu können. Auf längere Sicht helfen die Informationen zudem, Entwässerungssysteme zu planen oder Überschwemmungsrisiken besser einzuschätzen.
Für Versicherungen bieten die ortsgenauen Niederschlagsdaten eine mögliche Grundlage für Risikoanalysen und Schadensbewertungen.
Für Wetterdienste wäre ein dichteres lokales Messnetz eine zusätzliche Datenquelle für ihre Prognosemodelle erhalten.
In der Landwirtschaft können die lokalen Niederschlagsinformationen für eine bedarfsgerechtere Bewässerung eingesetzt werden. Für diesen Anwendungsfall entwickelt das Fraunhofer IDMT in einem weiteren Forschungsprojekt aktuell einen Lösungsansatz, bei dem Sensorknoten für Tests im Bereich Agri-Photovoltaik aufgebaut und vernetzt werden.
+++ Nächste Ziele: mehr Felddaten, weitere Pilotinstallationen, Serienreife +++
Für höhere Niederschlagsintensitäten stehen bislang weniger Trainings- und Testdaten zur Verfügung. Die Datenerhebung und -auswertung soll deshalb für stärkere Niederschläge vorangetrieben werden.
Gleichzeitig will das Fraunhofer IDMT weitere Pilotinstallationen auf den Weg bringen. »Wir haben bereits Anfragen von kommunalen Infrastrukturbetreibern und Feuerwehren erhalten, die Interesse an einer flächendeckenden Niederschlagsmessung in Echtzeit haben«, erklärt Jakob Bergner. Die neuen Pilotinstallationen sollen zeigen, wie sich das Messsystem unter unterschiedlichen Einsatzbedingungen bewährt und für konkrete Anwendungen weiterentwickeln lässt.
Für den Schritt vom Demonstrator zum serienreifen System sind weitere Entwicklungsarbeiten notwendig. Dazu werden unter anderem Sensorgehäuse und Elektronik weiter optimiert, die Qualitätssicherung ausgebaut und die Voraussetzungen für eine spätere CE-Konformität geschaffen.
+++ Über lokalRAIN +++
Das Forschungsprojekt »lokalRAIN – Lokale Regenmessung mit Akustischer Sensorik in IoT-Netzwerken« lief von Oktober 2024 bis Juni 2026. Projektpartner waren das Fraunhofer-Institut für Digitale Medientechnologie IDMT und die Pan Acoustics GmbH. Das Vorhaben wurde im Rahmen des Zentralen Innovationsprogramms Mittelstand (ZIM) gefördert. Fördergeber war das Bundesministerium für Wirtschaft und Energie (BMWE), Förderkennzeichen: KK5048507RL4.
+++ Über die Pan Acoustics GmbH +++
Die Pan Acoustics GmbH mit Sitz in Wolfenbüttel entwickelt und produziert seit über 20 Jahren hochwertige digtal vernetzte Lautsprechersysteme mit dem Prädikat Made in Germany. Typische Anwendungen indoor/outdoor finden sich in den Bereichen Evakuierung, Konferenztechnik und Medientechnik. Das Unternehmen mit hoher Expertise auch in digitalen Funkübertragungsstrecken legt neben höchster Klangqualität besonderen Wert auf längste Zuverlässigkeit, intelligente Technologie und nachhaltige Produktion. Weltweit setzen Kunden aus den Bereichen Kultur, Bildung, Industrie und öffentliche Einrichtungen auf die Lösungen des Unternehmens.
