Quallen haben keinen Knorpel. Trotzdem könnten sie helfen, kaputten Gelenkknorpel zu regenerieren. An der CAU entwickeln Forschende mit Quallenkollagen und Zinkoxid gleich zwei Materialien, die Knorpelzellen beim Aufbau neuen Gewebes unterstützen sollen. Für die beiden neuen Forschungsprojekte erhält die CAU vom BMFTR insgesamt rund 1,5 Millionen Euro.
Wenn wir gehen, laufen oder springen, muss Knorpel in unseren Gelenken großen Belastungen standhalten. Nach einer Verletzung oder bei Arthrose kann dieser sich jedoch im Erwachsenenalter kaum selbst erneuern. Der Körper bildet stattdessen Faserknorpel – eine Art Notfallpflaster, um den nackten Knochen zu schützen. Dieser kann Druck und Stauchungen an Gelenkflächen schlechter abfangen und gleitet schlechter als echter Knorpel. Sogenannter hyaliner Knorpel kann dagegen enormen Druckbelastungen standhalten und ist der perfekte, reibungsarme Stoßdämpfer für unsere Gelenke. Forschende suchen deshalb nach Materialien, die im Körper die Bildung von neuem hochwertigem Knorpelgewebe unterstützen.
Eine besondere Rolle bei der Regenerationsfähigkeit von Knorpelzellen spielt Kollagen, ein wichtiger Baustoff im Gewebe von Tieren. Auch Quallen haben dieses Strukturprotein – und ausgerechnet ihr Kollagen könnte helfen, neue Materialien für die Knorpelregeneration zu entwickeln. An der Christian-Albrechts-Universität zu Kiel sind dazu nun gleich zwei Forschungsprojekte unter der Leitung von Professor Rainer Adelung gestartet. Das Bundesministerium für Forschung, Technologie und Raumfahrt (BMFTR) fördert „AeroMarK“ und „QPiezoR“; die CAU erhält dafür insgesamt rund 1,5 Millionen Euro.
Damit aus Quallenkollagen ein Material für die Knorpelneubildung wird, kombinieren die Forschenden es mit einem weiteren Werkstoff: tetrapodalem Zinkoxid. Es besteht aus winzigen Kristallen mit vier Armen. Viele Kristalle können sich zu Gerüsten mit vielen kleinen Hohlräumen verbinden. Adelung arbeitet seit über 15 Jahren mit diesem Werkstoff, den er nun für beide Projekte unterschiedlich einsetzen will. „Bei AeroMarK nutzen wir das Zinkoxid, nur um die Struktur des Kollagengerüsts vorzugeben und entfernen es sofort wieder, um ein luftiges Aeromaterial aus Kollagen zu erzeugen“, sagt Adelung. „Bei QPiezoR soll es zusätzlich elektrische Signale erzeugen und möglicherweise so die Knorpelbildung anregen.“
Warum Kollagen aus Quallen?
Quallen sind evolutionär sehr alte Tiere. Wie Säugetiere besitzen auch sie Kollagen, das ihrer gallertartigen Struktur Halt gibt. Bei Säugetieren bildet das Protein ein stabiles Gerüst, in das Knorpelzellen eingebettet sind. Einerseits ähnelt Quallenkollagen dem von höheren Tieren strukturell. Andererseits fehlen ihm jedoch bestimmte Bindungsstellen, an denen Knorpelzellen andocken können.
Was zunächst wie ein Nachteil klingt, ist für die Knorpelregeneration von Vorteil: Denn wenn Knorpelzellen an Säugetierkollagen andocken, nehmen sie eine längliche Form an. „Dabei verlieren sie ihre Spezialisierung und bilden nur noch minderwertigen Faserknorpel“, erklärt Dr. Alexandra Cordeiro Baumgartner, die beide Projekte koordiniert. „Doch um hochwertigen, hyalinen Knorpel zu bilden, sollten Zellen möglichst rund bleiben.“
Dass Knorpelzellen, die in Quallenkollagen kultiviert wurden, ihre runde Form behalten, hat Dr. Judith Sewing bereits in Vorarbeiten gezeigt. Für beide Projekte bringt sie nun ihre Expertise bei AMIPLANT ein. Das Medizintechnikunternehmen ist bei AeroMarK assoziierter Partner und bei QPiezoR Verbundpartner.
AeroMarK: Ein Gerüst, das wieder verschwindet
Im Projekt AeroMarK dienen die Zinkoxid-Kristalle als eine Art Vorlage, die dem Quallenkollagen eine Struktur vorgeben soll. Die Forschenden vermischen gelöstes Quallenkollagen mit den Kristallen – sogenannten Tetrapoden –, gefriertrocknen die Mischung und vernetzen das Kollagen, damit es stabil bleibt. Anschließend lösen sie das Zinkoxid wieder heraus. Zurück bleibt eine dreidimensionale, hochporöse Struktur aus reinem Quallenkollagen.
Dieses Gerüst können Wissenschaftlerinnen und Wissenschaftler gezielt anpassen: Über die Menge an Zinkoxid und Kollagen sowie über die Vernetzung lassen sich die Größe der Hohlräume und die Steifigkeit einstellen. Erste luftige Kollagengerüste hat das Team im Labor bereits hergestellt. Nun wollen die Forschenden verschiedene Varianten dieses Aeromaterials entwickeln und vergleichen, um herauszufinden, welche Eigenschaften des Materials die Knorpelregeneration besonders fördern können. Bis zum Projektende im September 2028 will das Team mehrschichtige Gerüste erzeugen, die den unterschiedlichen Schichten des natürlichen Gelenkknorpels möglichst nahekommen – erste Prototypen, die später in präklinischen Studien untersucht werden sollen.
AeroMarK erhält im Rahmen des Förderprogramms „WIR! – Wandel durch Innovation in der Region“ über das Bündnis BlueHealthTech eine Förderung des Bundesministeriums für Forschung, Technologie und Raumfahrt (BMFTR) in Höhe von ca. 650.000 Euro.
QPiezoR: Ein elektrisch aktives Material für die Knorpelregeneration
Im zweiten Projekt „QPiezoR“ bleiben die Zinkoxid-Kristalle im Kollagenmaterial erhalten und sollen dort zusätzlich als Signalgeber wirken. Zinkoxid ist piezoelektrisch. Es kann also bei mechanischer Belastung elektrische Signale erzeugen, ausgelöst etwa durch Kräfte, die bei jedem Schritt und jeder Bewegung auf die Gelenke einwirken. Ob solche Signale tatsächlich dazu beitragen können, dass Knorpelzellen neues Gewebe bilden, will das Team bis Juni 2029 herausfinden.
Zunächst wollen die Forschenden die Struktur ihres neuartigen Materials gezielt weiterentwickeln: Die Tetrapoden müssen sich so miteinander verbinden, dass sie elektrische Signale durch das Material übertragen können. Zugleich soll das Gerüst die unterschiedlichen Schichten des Gelenkknorpels berücksichtigen und auch den Übergang zum darunter liegenden Knochen einbeziehen. In einem weiteren Schritt testen sie dann, ob und unter welchen Bedingungen das Material Zellkulturen beeinflusst.
Das Verbundprojekt QPiezoR wird im Rahmen der Material-Hub-Initiative „MaterialVital – Materialinnovationen für ein gutes und sicheres Leben“ vom BMFTR gefördert; das Kieler Teilvorhaben erhält rund 900.000 Euro.
Ausblick auf eine Therapie für Knorpelregeneration
Langfristig sollen die Materialien dazu beitragen, geschädigten Gelenkknorpel zu regenerieren. Eine mögliche Anwendung wäre ein Patch, der in einen Knorpeldefekt eingesetzt wird und Knorpelzellen eine geeignete Umgebung bietet, um neues Gewebe zu bilden. Erste Voraussetzungen für eine solche Anwendung sind bereits vorhanden: Das aus Adelungs Arbeitsgruppe heraus gegründete Unternehmen Phi-Stone AG stellt tetrapodales Zinkoxid industriell her. Die spätere Herstellung der Materialien als Medizinprodukt ist bei AMIPLANT vorgesehen. Bis zu einer Anwendung am Menschen ist es allerdings noch ein weiter Weg – wie bei allen regenerativen Therapieansätzen.
Über den Forschungsschwerpunkt KiNSIS
Im Nanokosmos herrschen andere, quantenphysikalische, Gesetze als in der makroskopischen Welt. Strukturen und Prozesse in diesen Dimensionen zu verstehen und die Erkenntnisse anwendungsnah umzusetzen, ist das Ziel des Forschungsschwerpunkts KiNSIS (Kiel Nano, Surface and Interface Science) der Christian-Albrechts-Universität zu Kiel (CAU). Aus der intensiven interdisziplinären Zusammenarbeit zwischen Physik, Chemie, Ingenieur- und Lebenswissenschaften entstehen neue Moleküle und Materialien, Sensoren und Batterien, Quantentechnologien, katalytische Verfahren, medizinische Therapien und vieles mehr. www.kinsis.uni-kiel.de

title: BIM, KI und die Zukunft des Bauens: Neue Vortragsreihe am IU Campus Hannover
content:
BIM, KI und die Zukunft des Bauens: Neue Vortragsreihe am IU Campus Hannover
Wie verändern Digitalisierung und Künstliche Intelligenz das Planen und Bauen? Die kostenfreie Vortragsreihe „BIM / KI / Digitalisierung – BAU“ am IU Campus Hannover geht dieser Frage im Wintersemester 2026/2027 nach. Seit dem Auftakt am 6. Oktober 2026 stellen Gäste aus Planung, Beratung, Forschung und Bauausführung ihre Projekte, Erfahrungen und Technologien vor, jeweils mit Beispielen aus der Praxis.
Bildung für alle, praxisnah
Die Reihe unterstreicht den Anspruch der IU, Bildung für alle zugänglich zu machen und praxisnah zu gestalten. Sie richtet sich nicht nur an Studierende, sondern auch an Unternehmen und Fachpublikum. Wer sich für BIM (Building Information Modeling, auf Deutsch: Bauwerkinformationsmodellierung) und KI im Bauwesen interessiert, kann mitdiskutieren, Fragen stellen und Kontakte knüpfen. Die Gäste bringen aktuelles Praxiswissen direkt in den Hörsaal, wo Studierende und Interessierte es direkt mit ihrem Studium oder Job verbinden können.
Neun Abende, ein roter Faden
Die Reihe umfasst sechs Haupttermine am ersten Dienstag des Monats und drei Zusatztermine am dritten Dienstag von Januar bis März 2027. Sie beginnen jeweils um 17 Uhr. Die Schwerpunkte:
1) BIM-Management bei der Deutschen Bahn und aktueller Stand der BIM-Implementierung in der Verkehrsanlagenplanung
2) BIM und KI im öffentlichen Bau, etwa bei PPP-Projekten und in der öffentlichen Vergabe
3) KI in Bau- und Materialtechnologie, von der Forschung bis zur Anwendung
4) Praxisberichte zu Infrastrukturprojekten und digitalen Zwillingen für Brücken
Vortrag, Diskussion, Austausch
Jeder Abend folgt demselben Ablauf: ein Gastvortrag von etwa 45 Minuten, eine Fragerunde und eine moderierte Panel-Diskussion. Dabei können auch Praxispartner aus dem Publikum mitdiskutieren. Beim anschließenden Get-together kommen Studierende, Unternehmen und Gäste ins Gespräch.
Die Beiträge der Gastredner:innen sollen als Fachbeiträge in einem Sammelband bei Springer erscheinen. Die Veröffentlichung ist für Herbst 2027 geplant.

ÜBER DIE IU INTERNATIONALE HOCHSCHULE
Mit über 120.000 Studierenden ist die IU Internationale Hochschule (IU) Deutschlands größte Hochschule. Die private, staatlich anerkannte Bildungseinrichtung mit Sitz in Erfurt nahm im Jahr 2000 ihren Lehrbetrieb auf und ist heute an 24 Standorten sowie an einem virtuellen Campus vertreten. Die IU steht für maximale Flexibilität im Studium: ob dual, im Fernstudium oder am Campus – Studierende aus über 160 Nationen gestalten ihren Bildungsweg individuell je nach persönlicher Lebenssituation. Mit mehr als 200 Studienprogrammen im Bachelor-, Master- und MBA-Bereich vermittelt die IU praxisnahe Kompetenzen. Innovative Lernkonzepte fördern gezielte Zukunftsfähigkeiten für eine zunehmend KI-geprägte Arbeitswelt. Eine moderne, digital gestützte Lernumgebung sowie der Einsatz von Künstlicher Intelligenz ermöglichen effektives, personalisiertes Lernen. Als Vorreiterin in diesem Bereich hat die IU mit „Syntea“ einen eigenen digitalen Lernbegleiter entwickelt, der seit 2023 im Einsatz ist. Ein Netzwerk von über 15.000 Unternehmen – darunter Motel One, Vodafone, die AWO und die Deutsche Bahn – macht die IU zu einem starken Partner in der Ausbildung von Fachkräften und verbindet akademische Lehre konsequent mit der Praxis. title: Hilti und Universität Liechtenstein verstärken Zusammenarbeit
content:
Hilti und Universität Liechtenstein verstärken Zusammenarbeit
Im Rahmen des neuen «Hilti Innovation Hub» finanziert die Hilti Foundation für vier Jahre drei Professuren an der Universität Liechtenstein in den Bereichen Innovation, Technologie, Digitalisierung und Künstliche Intelligenz. Ein zusätzlich von der Hilti Gruppe finanziertes Kompetenzzentrum für nachhaltigeres Bauen verbessert den Wissenstransfer in die Praxis.
Die langjährige Zusammenarbeit zwischen dem Unternehmen Hilti und der Universität Liechtenstein hat Forschung und Praxis besser vernetzt. Um die akademische Basis an der Universität zu festigen, finanziert die Hilti Foundation über den «Hilti Innovation Hub» drei Professuren zu den Themen «Technologie und Innovation», «Künstliche Intelligenz und Datenwissenschaft» sowie «Informationssysteme und digitale Innovation». Damit sollen bestehende Kooperationsbereiche gesichert, neue aufgebaut und Qualität, Geschwindigkeit und Praxisrelevanz des Wissenstransfers erhöht werden.
«Mit der Weiterentwicklung des Engagements seitens der Hilti Foundation und des Unternehmens wollen wir Forschung und Wissenstransfer in und aus Liechtenstein stärken. Durch eine höhere Kontinuität aufseiten Wissenschaft und Forschung können bessere Ergebnisse erzielt werden, die sich praxisnah nutzen lassen», erklärt Michèle Frey-Hilti, Verwaltungsratsmitglied der Hilti Gruppe.
«Für uns sind Forschung und Lehre zentral. Mit der Unterstützung der Hilti Foundation und der Hilti Gruppe können wir auf beiden Seiten noch mehr bewirken», sagt Christian Frommelt, Rektor der Universität Liechtenstein. «Je stärker die Studierenden in reale Fragestellungen eingebunden sind, desto grösser wird der Beitrag zur Fachkräfteentwicklung und damit zur Innovationsfähigkeit der Region.»
Kompetenzzentrum vereint Forschung und Industrie
Im Rahmen der Kooperation werden von der Hilti Gruppe unter anderem gemeinsame Projekte, Doktorarbeiten und Praktika im Unternehmen gefördert. Von besonderer Bedeutung ist das «Kompetenzzentrum für Nachhaltigkeit und digitale Innovation im Bauwesen», das seit Anfang 2026 besteht und von der Hilti Gruppe während zunächst drei Jahren finanziert wird.
Im Zentrum konzentrieren sich die Aktivitäten auf Nachhaltigkeit und Wirtschaftlichkeit von Bauprojekten über deren gesamten Lebenszyklus. Schwerpunkte sind klimafreundlicheres, effizienteres und digitales Bauen, von der Planung über die Realisierung bis hin zum Betrieb von Gebäuden. Dafür werden die Forschung und das internationale Netzwerk der Universität mit dem Praxiswissen und den Marktkenntnissen von Hilti zusammengebracht.
Um die Ergebnisse möglichst schnell in die Bauindustrie übertragen zu können, ist das Kompetenzzentrum als offene Plattform gestaltet, bei der Studierende, Forschende, Unternehmen und internationale Partner zusammenkommen, ihr Wissen austauschen und voneinander lernen.

Thermische und thermochemische Randschichtbehandlungen sind wichtige Verfahren in der industriellen Fertigung. Sie machen Werkzeuge und Bauteile beispielsweise härter, verschleiß- und ermüdungsfester und können ihre Korrosionsbeständigkeit verbessern, gleichzeitig sind diese Prozesse jedoch sehr energieintensiv. Wie sich der Energieverbrauch bei konstanter Bauteilqualität künftig optimieren lässt, untersucht das neue Verbundprojekt »CyPro – Cyber-physische Produktionssysteme zur Energieeffizienzsteigerung und Quali-tätssicherung von thermischen und thermochemischen Behandlungsprozessen«, das vom Fraunhofer-Institut für Schicht- und Oberflächentechnik IST koordiniert.
Energieverbrauch und Bauteilqualität gemeinsam betrachten
Eine besondere Herausforderung bei thermischen und thermochemischen Behandlungsprozessen besteht darin, dass Prozessparameter, Energieverbrauch und Bauteilqualität eng miteinander verknüpft sind. Eine Reduzierung des Energieeinsatzes darf nicht zu Lasten der geforderten Bauteileigenschaften gehen. Das Projekt »CyPro« setzt genau an dieser Schnittstelle an. Ziel ist die Entwicklung eines cyber-physischen Produktionssystems (CPPS), das Prozess-, Energie-, Sensor- und Produktionsdaten kontinuierlich erfassen und miteinander verknüpfen soll. Ergänzend ist unter anderem der Einsatz der optischen Emissionsspektroskopie vorgesehen, um den Zustand des Plasmas in Echtzeit zu überwachen.
Auf Basis der erhobenen Daten sollen erklärbare KI-Modelle entwickelt werden, die Zusammenhänge zwischen Prozessparametern, Energiebedarf und Qualitätsmerkmalen abbilden. Geplant ist, dabei beispielsweise die Nitrierhärtetiefe, die Ausbildung der Verbindungsschicht oder die Korrosionsbeständigkeit der behandelten Bauteile zu berücksichtigen. Im Unterschied zu reinen datengetriebenen »Black-Box«-Ansätzen soll damit nachvollziehbar werden, wie sich Veränderungen der Prozessführung auf Energieverbrauch und Bauteileigenschaften auswirken.
Darüber hinaus sollen die datenbasierten Modelle durch physikalisch basierte Modellierun-gen wie thermodynamische und CFD-gestützte Simulationen ergänzt werden, um so unter anderem Wärmeflüsse, Phasenübergänge und Abwärmepotenziale in der Anlage und ihrer Peripherie untersuchen zu können. Auf diese Weise sollen sich Energieverluste sowohl da-tenbasiert als auch physikalisch fundiert bewerten lassen. Zudem soll ein Planungswerkzeug auf Basis des bestärkenden Lernens perspektivisch nicht nur einzelne Prozessparameter, sondern auch Auftragsreihenfolgen, Anlagenbelegung, Durchlaufzeiten und Lastspitzen berücksichtigen. Geplant ist es, die gewonnenen Informationen in Echtzeit in einem Dashboard bereitzustellen und prädiktive Handlungsempfehlungen für den Anlagenbetrieb zu ermöglichen.
Plasmanitrieren als industrieller Demonstrator
Die Methoden werden zunächst am Beispiel des Plasmanitrierens entwickelt und erprobt. Als industrieller Demonstrator dient eine Plasmanitrieranlage des Fraunhofer IST, an der zentrale Messkampagnen mit definierten Referenzchargen durchgeführt sowie Prozess-, Energie- und Qualitätsdaten erfasst und ausgewertet werden sollen. Die behandelten Bauteile sollen hinsichtlich relevanter Randschicht- und Gebrauchseigenschaften charakterisiert werden, um auf dieser Basis die Sensorik, Datenmodelle und weiteren Komponenten des geplanten CPPS schrittweise integrieren und unter realitätsnahen Produktionsbedingungen zu validieren zu können.
Rund 24 MWh Einsparpotenzial pro Jahr
Eine erste Potenzialabschätzung für die Plasmanitrieranlage zeigt die mögliche Größenordnung: Rund 24 MWh Energie pro Jahr könnten langfristig deutschlandweit ggf. eingespart werden. Davon entfallen nach der Abschätzung rund 17 MWh auf die Rückgewinnung und Nutzung von Abwärme und weitere 7 MWh auf eine optimierte Prozessführung.
Im Projekt soll nun untersucht werden, wie sich diese Potenziale technisch erschließen und unter realitätsnahen Produktionsbedingungen nutzen lassen. Für Produktionsbetriebe und Lohnbehandler könnten sich daraus geringere Strom- und Betriebskosten, reduzierte Last-spitzen und ein geringerer CO₂-Ausstoß ergeben. Gleichzeitig soll die präzisere Überwa-chung und Steuerung der Prozesse dazu beitragen, das Risiko von Qualitätsabweichungen und kostenintensiver Nacharbeit zu reduzieren.
Im weiteren Projektverlauf ist vorgesehen, die beim Plasmanitrieren gewonnenen Erkenntnisse auf weitere thermische und thermochemische Verfahren, insbesondere PACVD-Beschichtungen und Gasnitrieren, zu übertragen. Darüber hinaus soll geprüft werden, inwieweit sich die entwickelte Methodik auf andere industrielle Ofensysteme übertragen lässt, bei denen hohe Temperaturen, lange Prozesszeiten und relevante Abwärmeströme auftreten. Perspektivisch könnte das CPPS auch eine anlagenübergreifende Produktionsplanung er-möglichen, bei der mehrere Wärmebehandlungsanlagen dann energieoptimiert, lastflexibel und möglichst netzdienlich betrieben werden könnten.
Zum Projekt
»CyPro – Cyber-physische Produktionssysteme zur Energieeffizienzsteigerung und Qualitätssicherung von thermischen und thermochemischen Behandlungsprozessen«

content:

Für das Projekt ORka3D untersucht eine Wissenschaftlerin des Fraunhofer IWM Schweißnahtproben mit zyklischen 4-Punkt-Biegeversuchen bis zur Entstehung von Rissen. Die Rissausgangsorte, Dehnungsfelder und Versagenszyklen werden vermessen und mit scanb

Kai Wudtke
| Copyright:
Fraunhofer IWM
Download
Ob Offshore-Windturm, Drehkran oder Baggerarm – tragende Stahlkonstruktionen werden systematisch überdimensioniert, weil die Qualität ihrer Schweißnähte nicht objektiv erfasst wird. Das vom BMWE geförderte Verbundprojekt ORka3D hat ein Verfahren entwickelt, das per 3D-Scan und künstlicher Intelligenz die reale Geometrie jeder einzelnen Schweißnaht erfasst und individuell bewertet. Mit der präzisen Vorhersage der Ermüdungsfestigkeit können Blechdicken um bis zu 40 Prozent reduziert werden, ohne die Sicherheit zu gefährden. Branchenweit entspricht das Einsparpotenzial mehreren 100.000 Tonnen Stahl und mehreren Millionen Tonnen CO₂.
Jede Schweißnaht ist ein Unikat und besitzt am Übergang zum Grundwerkstoff eine geometrische Kerbe, von der aus die meisten Ermüdungsrisse ausgehen. Weil diese Kerbe je nach Schweißverfahren, Brennerführung und selbst der Tagesform des Schweißers individuell ausfällt, behelfen sich Regelwerke bislang mit einem pauschalen Sicherheitsabschlag: Sie unterstellen grundsätzlich die ungünstigste zulässige Geometrie. Die tatsächliche, oft deutlich bessere Qualität der gefertigten Naht bleibt unberücksichtigt. Die Folge sind eine dauerhafte Überdimensionierung von Bauteilen mit mehr Materialeinsatz als nötig und ein bislang ungenutzter enormer Hebel für Ressourceneinsparungen.
Das vom Bundesministerium für Wirtschaft und Klimaschutz geförderte Verbundprojekt ORka3D »Optimierung des Ressourceneinsatzes bei Schweißkonstruktionen durch die automatisierte in-line Lebensdauerbewertung auf Basis von 3D-Scans« hat genau hier angesetzt. Ein Konsortium unter Federführung des Fraunhofer-Instituts für Werkstoffmechanik IWM hat ein Verfahren entwickelt, das die reale Schweißnahtoberfläche per 3D-Scan erfasst und daraus automatisiert eine bauteilspezifische Lebensdauerprognose ableitet, statt diese wie bisher anhand pauschaler Kerbfallklassen abzuschätzen.
»Die geometrische Kerbe am Nahtübergang ist seit Jahrzehnten als Schwachstelle bekannt, blieb aber bislang ungelöst, weil jede Naht geometrisch einzigartig ist. Mit hochauflösenden 3D-Scans und neuronalen Netzen können wir diese Individualität erstmals objektiv erfassen und bewerten –die Auslegung geschweißter Strukturen könnte damit sehr viel materialsparender werden«, erklärt Projektleiter Dr. Jan Schubnell vom Fraunhofer IWM.
Wie die Methode funktioniert
Ein 3D-Scanner erfasst die Nahtoberfläche mit einem Bildpunktabstand von bis zu 5 Mikrometern. Ein Algorithmus extrahiert daraus automatisiert zentrale Geometrieparameter, insbesondere den bislang normativ vernachlässigten Nahtübergangsradius. Ein künstliches neuronales Netz leitet daraus die individuelle Kerbformzahl und eine bauteilspezifische Lebensdauerprognose ab, statt pauschale Kerbfallklassen (sogenannte FAT-Klassen) anzusetzen. Validiert wurde das Verfahren an rund 400 Prüfkörpern sowie an Realstrukturen wie Rohrknoten und Kranauslegern.
Mit der datenbasierten Bewertung der Ermüdungsfestigkeit könnte die Kerbfallklasse von FAT90 auf bis zu FAT140 angehoben werden, was einer Blechdickenreduktion von bis zu 40 Prozent und eine Halbierung der Schweißzeit entspricht. Und das bei gleichbleibender struktureller Sicherheit, da der Nachweis auf individuellen Messdaten statt auf pauschalen Sicherheitsabschlägen beruht.
Hebelwirkung nicht nur für die Energiewende
Besonders deutlich zeigt sich das Potenzial am Beispiel der Windenergie: Bei einer 10-Megawatt-Offshore-Anlage mit einem Turmgewicht von rund 600 Tonnen lassen sich durch optimierte Nahtbewertung etwa 180 Tonnen Stahl einsparen, ohne Sicherheitseinbußen. Beim geplanten Ausbau der Offshore-Windkapazität auf 30 Gigawatt bis 2030 summiert sich dies auf bis zu 360.000 Tonnen Stahl und eine CO₂-Einsparung in Millionenhöhe.
Die Projektpartner arbeiten daran, die Ergebnisse über die Mitarbeit in Fachgremien in Regelwerke zu bringen, mit dem Ziel, die konservativen FAT-Klassen-Konzepte um eine individuelle, datenbasierte Bewertung zu erweitern.
Die Methodik betrifft auch den Brücken- und Kranbau sowie den Baumaschinensektor, Branchen, in denen in Deutschland jährlich viele Millionen Tonnen Stahl verarbeitet werden.
Förderung
Das Projekt ORka3D »Optimierung des Ressourceneinsatzes bei Schweißkonstruktionen durch die automatisierte in-line Lebensdauerbewertung auf Basis von 3D-Scans« wurde im 7. Energieforschungsprogramm vom Bundesministerium für Wirtschaft und Energie BMWE gefördert.
Am Projekt beteiligt waren neben den Fraunhofer-Instituten IWM und LBF die Industriepartner Liebherr, Volvo Construction Equipment, Salzgitter Mannesmann Forschung sowie die Sensorhersteller GOM, Micro-Epsilon und Quelltech, sowie der Ingenieursdienstleister Jörss – Blunk – Ordemann JBO.

content: A 500 MWac solar photovoltaic project coupled with a 250 MW/1,000 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) is set to be developed on approximately 1,300 acres of land in Bahau, Negeri Sembilan, Malaysia. The massive solar-plus-storage project will be developed by IOI Corporation Berhad (IOI), one of Malaysia’s leading integrated palm oil producers, in partnership with Tenaga Nasional Berhad (TNB), the country’s largest electricity utility, and a consortium of unspecified small and medium-sized enterprises. “The project will be supported by TNB’s long-term renewable energy offtake agreement with DayOne Data Centres Limited, a leading global digital infrastructure platform headquartered in Singapore,” IOI said in a statement. “Under the agreement, DayOne is expected to procure up to 500MWac of renewable energy over a 21-year period to support its data centre operations in Malaysia, as announced by the parties on 11 June 2025.” The project marks IOI’s first large-scale renewable energy investment under Malaysia’s Corporate Renewable Energy Supply Scheme (CRESS), which allows corporate electricity consumers to procure renewable power directly from independent developers through the national grid. The scheme aims to encourage private investment in renewable energy infrastructure while supporting the decarbonization of energy-intensive industries. Malaysia is expanding its utility-scale solar and energy storage capacity to meet rising electricity demand from data centers. In August 2025, clean energy company Gentari and engineering group Gamuda unveiled plans to jointly develop 1.5 GW of solar capacity , alongside battery storage, to supply hyperscale data centers under CRESS. The rapid growth of Malaysia’s data center industry has also raised concerns about electricity supply, grid capacity and water availability. A March 2026 analysis highlighted the challenges of meeting rising electricity demand while maintaining grid stability and ensuring sufficient dispatchable generation. Uncertainty over grid access charges has also been identified as a key factor affecting the commercial viability of corporate renewable energy projects. In September 2026, Malaysia revised the CRESS framework to improve project bankability and stimulate investment. The changes introduced a fixed system access charge of MYR 0.14 ($0.03)/kWh for qualifying firm renewable electricity supply projects and a minimum 10-year contract term between developers and corporate consumers. Projects must begin commercial operations by the end of 2028 to qualify for the reduced charge. At the time, 11 renewable energy developers and eight corporate consumers had registered projects totaling approximately 3.15 GW under the scheme. title: Econergy buys up 106 MW of operational UK battery storage capacity - Energy Storage
content: Independent power producer Econergy has acquired a portfolio of four operational battery energy storage system (BESS) projects in the UK, totaling 106 MW. Under the agreement, disclosed in a filing to the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange (TASE), Econergy said it has acquired 100% of the shares in the holding company that owns the four assets, giving it full ownership and control of the portfolio. The company said the projects are expected to generate around £4.7 million in EBITDA in 2027 before planned augmentation works. The four standalone BESS facilities, located in England, currently have a one-hour duration (106 MWh total), with Econergy evaluating plans to augment the systems to three-hour duration (~318 MWh). Econergy didn’t name the seller, and public registry transfer filings have not been made to Companies House yet. Econergy said the longer duration would allow the assets to capture additional value by storing more energy and dispatching it over a longer period, thus providing greater flexibility to respond to changing market conditions by shifting electricity to times of stronger demand. The acquisition increases Econergy’s operational UK BESS capacity from 90 MW to 196 MW, as the company expands from two to six assets that are connected to the grid. Econergy’s existing UK operational assets include the 50 MW / 100 MWh Swangate BESS in West Melton , Yorkshire, England, which entered operation in 2024, and the 40 MW / 120 MWh Dalmarnock project in Glasgow, Scotland, which connected to the grid in October 2026. “We’re pleased to be purchasing these four projects, which represent a business opportunity with clear upside,” said Eyal Podhorzer, CEO and director of Econergy. “The addition of 106 MW of operational storage capacity and the potential to augment the assets to three-hour duration gives us a pathway to build on the portfolio and develop its longer-term value. Alongside our existing assets, and those in development, these projects strengthen our foothold in the UK and a growing platform for further expansion.” The company said it has a 1.6 GW UK energy storage development pipeline. Across Europe, its BESS portfolio totals 5.9 GW, with 3.3 GW expected to be connected to the grid, under construction or pre-construction by 2028. title: AGL seeks approval for 2 GWh battery in Australia - Energy Storage
content: Energy generating and retailing major AGL Energy is seeking approvals under the Australian federal government’s Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation (EPBC) Act for a 500 MW/2,000 MWh battery to be built in central Queensland. The proposed Mount Britton battery project comprises a standalone battery energy storage system (BESS) with 500 MW of power capacity and four hours of total usable storage. The BESS, planned for a 27-hectare site near the town of Nebo about 75 km southwest of Mackay, would connect to Powerlink’s 275 kV transmission network at the existing Nebo substation. In referral documents, AGL said the project could be delivered in multiple construction phases of up to 250 MW each, or as a single 500 MW phase. The Sydney-based energy utility said it expects the BESS to become a significant addition to central Queensland’s energy infrastructure. “When constructed, the project will provide local electricity network resilience through stabilisation services such as frequency and voltage control, and manage energy peak demand periods as the grid transitions to renewable energy,” it said. The Mount Britton BESS project forms part of AGL’s ongoing transition away from coal-fired power generation to a majority of backed-up renewables. “With the changing nature of electricity demand across Australia, there’s an increasing need for more flexible generation and generation from a diverse range of sources and in a range of locations,” the energy utility said, adding that “battery storage can start at short notice and ramp up and down quickly, making them an excellent complement to higher levels of variable renewable generation such as wind and solar.” AGL has more than 2 GW of renewable projects in its pipeline and said it is on track to meet its ambition to add 12 GW of new renewable and firming capacity by the end of 2035 with more than 1.2 GW of grid-scale batteries in operation or under construction. The energy major already owns and operates the 500 MW/1,000 MWh Liddell and the 50 MW/50 MWh Broken Hill batteries in New South Wales, and the 250 MW/250 MWh Torrens Island BESS in South Australia. It is also constructing the 500 MW/2,000 MWh Tomago battery on the New South Wales Central Coast. Its Queensland battery projects include the 125 MW/500 MWh Abermain BESS in the state’s southeast, the 200 MW Aramara battery project, and the 500 MW/2,000 MWh Tuckeroo BESS in the Western Downs region. Of AGL’s current 23 projects under development, 14 are standalone batteries. AGL closed its Liddell coal power station in NSW in 2023 and is due to close Bayswater nearby at the end of 2033, and Loy Yang A in Victoria in 2035. title: Italy authorizes another 480 MW of battery storage - Energy Storage
content: Italy’s Ministry of Environment and Energy Security (MASE) issued two further single authorizations for battery energy storage system (BESS) projects totaling 480 MW on Nov. 2, following nearly 7 GW of approvals over the previous two months. The projects are a 280 MW facility planned by Miura Storage Srl in Tuscany, in the province of Viterbo, and the 200 MW Bess Castegnero project, developed by BESS Pieve Srl in Castegnero Nanto, in the province of Vicenza. Benny Energia, the Rome-based owner of BESS Pieve, plans to build the 200 MW project with 160 battery containers and 160 power conversion systems. Construction is expected to take around 30 months. The energy storage developer told pv magazine Italia that it has a BESS project pipeline of around 2.3 GW. This includes 1.5 GW of projects preparing for construction and intended to participate in Italy’s capacity market and MACSE storage procurement scheme, around 700 MW awaiting authorization, and a 200 MW project in Udine that has been operating for nearly three years. The other project authorized by MASE is Miura Storage’s 280 MW facility in Tuscania. It will comprise 327 battery containers, with construction expected to take five months. title: Slovak utility tenders battery for largest pumped hydro plant - Energy Storage
content: Slovenské elektrárne has launched a tender to build a battery energy storage system at Čierny Váh, Slovakia’s largest pumped storage hydropower plant. The utility published the tender last week, with bids due by Nov. 27. It covers battery supply, engineering, substation work, construction, testing and training. The Slovak power producer, which is controlled by Czech energy group EPH, has not disclosed a contract value or award criteria. The company’s project page describes a battery of up to 120 MW/480 MWh, but Slovak media reports indicate that the final parameters could still change. That is larger than the up to 80 MW/160 MWh that the company and the European Union have previously described. Slovak daily Denník SME has reported that the batteries will be housed in containers and that the project includes a substation expansion and a new transformer. The battery is part of a wider upgrade of the 735 MW plant. Slovenské elektrárne has signed contracts with Voith Hydro and GE Vernova to convert two of its turbine-generators to variable-speed operation. It has reportedly said that that the investment exceeds €200 million ($223.9 million) and is due for completion in 2031. The company said the upgrade will widen the plant’s balancing range to between -712 MW and +790 MW. It said the hybrid site will be able to provide primary, secondary and tertiary balancing, with combined efficiency of up to 77%. The European Climate, Infrastructure and Environment Executive Agency (CINEA) awarded a €62.63 million grant under the Connecting Europe Facility for the variable-speed works, which began in July. CINEA said the battery is not part of the grant-funded phase, but both are part of the same EU Project of Common Interest. Slovenské elektrárne commissioned a 36 MW/72 MWh battery at the site of its former Nováky coal plant in July, which provides frequency containment reserve. The Bratislava-based company is 66% owned by Slovak Power Holding, a unit of Czech energy group EPH, and 34% by the Slovak state. Other European utilities are also pairing batteries with pumped hydro. Enel, for example, has announced plans to retrofit battery storage at a century-old pumped hydro plant in Italy. Iberdrola, meanwhile, has switched on a pumped hydro-battery project in Spain , and a hybrid pumped hydro-BESS project in Finland has doubled its planned battery capacity. content:
Kazakhstan’s pipeline of large-scale solar projects currently stands at 900 MW, the country’s Minister of Energy Yerlan Akkenzhenov has said.
Speaking at a meeting of the Kurultai Committee on Economic Policy, Industry and Energy, Akkenzhenov said solar remains one of the ministry’s priority areas for development.
Kazakhstan’s solar capacity reached
as of April this year, at which point total renewables capacity stood at over 3.7 GW. Renewables currently account for 8.5% of Kazakhstan’s electricity mix, according to additional government figures.
The Kazakh government has set a target of deploying at least 8.4 GW of new renewables capacity by 2035, including approximately 1.8 GW of solar, Akkenzhenov added.
During the same meeting, Akkenzhenov said Kazakhstan plans to commission 13.3 GW of new generation capacity by the end of 2029 in order to “strengthen energy security and meet the growing needs of the economy.”
Of this total figure, 7.4 GW is expected to come from baseload generation. Recent research on the
potential of hybrid wind, solar and battery plants in Kazakhstan
highlighted coal as the dominant energy source in the country’s electricity mix but explained its coal units are on average over 50 years old, leading to frequent equipment failures.
“The implementation of the planned projects will make it possible to meet the projected electricity demand of the population and economy, supply electricity to artificial intelligence infrastructure and large data centers, and establish a 20% surplus of generation capacity,” Akkenzhenov added.
The ministry’s latest update coincides with plans to develop professional standards in Kazakhstan’s renewable energy sector for the first time.
A meeting of the energy ministry’s Sectoral Council on Professional Qualifications in Renewable Energy discussed five draft standards covering solar, wind and green hydrogen on October 29.
The professional standards are expected to cover qualification requirements for specialists in the design, construction, commissioning, operation and maintenance of solar and wind power plants.
According to an update posted by the Ministry of Energy, the draft standards are expected to be published on the country’s Open Portal of Legal Acts for public discussion in the near future.

title: Surplus PV in UK homes: why the heat pump beats the immersion diverter for hot water - pv magazine Global
content:
The usual answer to surplus rooftop PV in a British home has been an immersion diverter. A current clamp on the meter tails detects export, and the diverter feeds that spare power into the immersion element in the hot water cylinder, varying the power to match whatever is spare. The kit is cheap, it works with almost any cylinder, and it suited homes heated by gas, where the cylinder’s hot water would otherwise have come from the boiler.
Homes in England and Wales are replacing gas boilers with air-to-water heat pumps under the
Boiler Upgrade Scheme
, and some of them already have panels on the roof or add them at the same time. In those homes the diverter’s arithmetic stops working the way it used to.
One kWh, two outcomes
An immersion element is a resistance heater. One kWh of electricity in gives one kWh of heat in the water. A heat pump moves heat from outside air into the water, so the same kWh of electricity delivers several kWh of heat.
The government’s Electrification of Heat demonstration project ran one of the largest UK field trials of heat pump performance. Its
interim analysis by Energy Systems Catapult
measured a median seasonal performance factor of 2.80 across 291 air source heat pumps, using a boundary that counts space heating, hot water, back-up heaters and immersion use together. The report notes that summer hot water runs are less efficient than the annual picture, because the heat pump runs less often and works against a higher target temperature.
The comparison does not need a precise summer figure. A heat pump in hot water mode beats the immersion for every kWh of surplus as long as it delivers more than one kWh of heat per kWh of electricity, and a working air-to-water unit clears that bar by a wide margin.
What the surplus is worth
The value of a kWh of surplus PV depends on what it displaces. Take the
Ofgem price cap
for October to December 2026, 26.32 p per kWh of electricity for a direct debit customer, and the EoH median of 2.80 p.
In a heat pump home, the heat pump would otherwise make the cylinder’s hot water from grid power at about 9.4 p per kWh of heat. A kWh of surplus sent through a diverter into the immersion makes one kWh of heat, so it saves about 9.4 p. If the heat pump itself runs on that same kWh of surplus, the electricity it would have bought from the grid comes off the roof instead, and the saving is the full 26.32 p. On these figures, pointing surplus at the heat pump is worth close to three times as much as pointing it at the immersion.
The same arithmetic changes how the diverter compares with export. Under the
Smart Export Guarantee
, each supplier sets its own export rate, and Ofgem requires only that it stays above zero. In a gas-heated home the diverter competed against the gas price. In a heat pump home it competes against 9.4 p, so a household on an export tariff paying more than that would do better selling the power than heating water with the element.
Time-of-use tariffs move the numbers. A household that heats its cylinder overnight on a cheap rate pays far less than the cap for that heat, which shrinks the value of any daytime surplus spent on hot water. The tariff should be chosen before the controls are set. “Somebody on a cheap overnight rate and a good export rate may be better off exporting at midday and heating water at 2am. Somebody on a flat rate should run the cylinder in the solar window. You cannot set the controls without knowing the tariff,” reads Eco Renewables’ guide to
time-of-use tariffs for heat pump homes
Why diverters are still on the wall
The diverter keeps one practical advantage. It can use any surplus, however small, because it can run the element at any power level. A heat pump compressor has a minimum power draw and works best on longer runs, so it needs a steady surplus through a stretch of the day. A British June afternoon with broken cloud gives a diverter something to use and may give a heat pump controller nothing it can act on.
The cylinder also limits the gain. Lifting 200 litres of water by 10 C stores about 2.3 kWh of heat. A heat pump at an efficiency of 2.8 needs about 0.8 kWh of electricity to do it, where an immersion needs the full 2.3 kWh. The heat pump fills the same tank from a third of the surplus, which leaves the rest of the afternoon’s generation for a battery or for export.
The immersion has a second job in a heat pump home: a periodic pasteurisation cycle.
HSE guidance on legionella
says hot water should be stored at 60 C or above to kill the bacteria, a temperature that costs some heat pumps more electricity to reach than their normal hot water setpoint. Scheduling that cycle in the middle of a sunny day lets the PV pay for it, and it gives the diverter a role in a heat pump home without competing with the compressor.
Wiring the heat pump to the panels
The control link is the harder part. Germany’s heat pump association BWP runs the
SG Ready label
, which defines the operating states a heat pump controller must accept from outside. In state 3 the heat pump runs in boosted mode and raises the setpoint in the buffer or hot water store to soak up surplus electricity. State 4 is a definite start command. An inverter, energy manager or battery system with a free contact can signal the heat pump when export passes a threshold the installer sets.
The decision about priority belongs at the design stage. “We work out which load takes the surplus first: the battery, the cylinder through the heat pump, or the immersion. If the battery fills by lunchtime in summer, the heat pump should get the next kilowatt-hour, and the immersion only the scraps,” reads Eco Renewables’ guide to
running a heat pump alongside rooftop solar
and its explainer on
how a heat pump heats a hot water cylinder
covers cylinder sizing and reheat times.
The seasons limit all of this. The surplus is largest in summer, when the heat pump’s only load is hot water, and smallest in December, when space heating demand peaks and a south-facing array in Berkshire produces a fraction of its June output. Hot water is the one heat load that runs all year, which is why it is the natural first home for spare PV.
Where VAT comes in
Installing heat pumps, solar panels and batteries in homes in Great Britain carries 0% VAT until 31 March 2027 under
HMRC notice 708/6
, rising to 5% from 1 April 2027. The
28 October Budget
confirmed that date and added heat batteries, the phase-change stores sold as compact cylinder replacements, to the energy-saving materials list at 5% from the same day. A heat battery charged by its own electric element sits on the immersion side of the arithmetic above, so a home choosing one over a cylinder gives up the heat pump’s multiplier on that store.
Adam Dare is Managing Director of Eco Renewables, an MCS certified installer of heat pumps, solar panels and home batteries in Binfield, Berkshire. He is Heat Geek trained and verified, with a Gas Safe background.

title: India’s solar module manufacturing capacity could reach 3.48 TW by 2047 - pv magazine Global
content:
India’s solar manufacturing industry could become a fully integrated global powerhouse by 2047, creating 3.23 million direct and indirect jobs, attracting $89 billion in manufacturing investment, and eliminating the country’s solar import bill, according to a report by the Indian Solar Manufacturers Association (ISMA).
The report outlines a roadmap for India to move beyond module assembly and develop domestic manufacturing capabilities across the solar value chain, from polysilicon and ingots to wafers, cells, and modules. The transition could enable India to capture a significantly larger share of the value generated by domestically manufactured solar panels while strengthening its position in global markets.
Under a current-policy scenario, ISMA projects India’s installed solar capacity to reach approximately 278 GW by 2030, approaching the 292 GW target, before rising to around 1,370 GW by 2047. The latter figure is slightly below NITI Aayog’s current-policy projection of 1,430 GW to 1,650 GW by 2050.
The Vision 2047 scenario accounts for additional electricity demand from emerging industries and infrastructure. Assuming full implementation of planned programs, ISMA estimates that India’s installed solar capacity could reach 313 GW by 2030 and approximately 2,275 GW by 2047, enough to meet nearly half of the country’s electricity demand.
To support this expansion, India’s solar PV manufacturing industry would need to achieve cumulative production capacities of approximately 3,484 GW for modules, 3,128 GW for cells, 2,630 GW for ingots and wafers, and 2,200 GW-equivalent for polysilicon by 2047.
Manufacturing capacity across the solar value chain is expected to expand rapidly, supported by government-backed projects that mandate the procurement of domestically manufactured solar products.
The expansion could create substantial employment opportunities, with total manufacturing-related jobs increasing from approximately 410,000 currently to 740,000 by 2030 and 3.23 million by 2047. Direct employment in solar PV manufacturing plants could rise from around 140,000 to 1.11 million by 2047.
The share of direct employment in cell, wafer, and polysilicon manufacturing could increase from around 10% currently to approximately one-third by 2030 and more than half by 2047. These segments would generate skilled jobs for technicians, engineers, and chemists.
The report estimates that approximately $89 billion in new solar PV manufacturing investment could be required by 2047 under the Vision 2047 scenario, equivalent to an average of $4.3 billion annually between 2027 and 2047. Nearly 70% of the investment is expected to go toward polysilicon, wafer, and cell manufacturing. India’s Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme had already attracted approximately $8.4 billion in investment as of June 2026, with every dollar of incentives mobilizing around $4 in private investment.
A more integrated domestic manufacturing ecosystem could also substantially reduce India’s dependence on imported solar components. The report projects that the country’s annual solar import bill could fall from approximately $4.4 billion currently to zero by 2041 under the Vision 2047 scenario. India could also account for 26.5% of global solar module supply by 2047, compared with a projected 5.9% under the current-policy scenario in 2030.
“India’s solar manufacturing sector stands at a pivotal moment, with the Vision 2047 pathway presenting an unprecedented opportunity to build a globally competitive, integrated manufacturing ecosystem,” Amit Manohar, secretary general of ISMA, said. “The potential to attract $89 billion in investments, generate over 32 lakh jobs and significantly reduce import dependence underscores the strategic importance of strengthening domestic manufacturing across the entire solar value chain. Realising this ambition will require sustained policy support, a predictable demand pipeline, investments in upstream manufacturing and continued efforts to strengthen India’s global competitiveness.”
The report identifies policy certainty, sustained domestic demand, and timely implementation of manufacturing programs as critical to achieving these goals. It calls for maintaining firm timelines under the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM), completing PLI-supported projects, expanding rooftop and agricultural solar programs, and accelerating investment in upstream manufacturing. It also highlights the need to develop domestic manufacturing equipment, strengthen technical skills, promote advanced solar cell technologies, establish recycling frameworks, and expand export markets.
The Vision 2047 scenario outlines a phased transition, with cell manufacturing scaling up through 2030, wafer production expanding through 2035, and a fully integrated solar manufacturing value chain emerging thereafter.

title: Nickel powder optimization cuts TOPCon solar cell metallization costs by 6.8% without compromising efficiency - pv magazine Global
content:
A research team at the
University of New South Wales
(UNSW) in Australia has investigated the partial replacement of silver (Ag) with nickel (Ni) powders in TOPCon solar cell rear-side metallization and has found that Ni powder characteristics significantly affect electrical performance, printability and cost savings.
“One of the most important findings is that replacing Ag with Ni is not simply a matter of increasing the Ni content. The characteristics of the Ni powder have a significant impact on both electrical performance and printing behaviour,” corresponding author Ning Song told
pv magazine
“With an appropriate nickel powder, we demonstrated a 6.8% reduction in rear-finger raw-metal costs while maintaining almost the same solar cell efficiency. However, increasing the Ni content further did not necessarily deliver greater savings, because additional paste consumption during printing offset the expected benefits,” she added.
The scientists explained that Ni has emerged as a promising Ag substitute due to its relatively low cost and good electrical conductivity. However, Ni oxidation during firing and variations in powder characteristics can affect electrode performance. They also noted that previous studies have demonstrated the feasibility of Ag-Ni hybrid pastes, although their practical cost benefits remain uncertain.
Against this backdrop, the researchers investigated two commercial Ni powders with particle sizes of approximately 1.5 μm and 3.8 μm, replacing 5% to 15% of the metal powder in industrial TOPCon rear-finger pastes. They examined electrical performance, contact resistance, electrode microstructure and printing behavior, while also assessing paste consumption and finger geometry to determine actual raw-metal cost savings.
The team prepared five rear-side metallization pastes containing 90% metal powder, 2% glass frit and 8% organic vehicle. An Ag-only paste served as the baseline, while the other four formulations contained 5% to 15% Ni in the metal powder fraction, using two commercial powders designated Ni-1500 and Ni-4000. The pastes were screen-printed onto industrial n-type TOPCon solar cells measuring 182 mm × 183.75 mm, followed by drying, co-firing at a peak set temperature of 724 C and laser-enhanced contact optimization (LECO).
The experiments were conducted over two industrial production runs, with at least 12 cells per formulation. The researchers measured solar cell efficiency, series resistance and spatial electrical characteristics using calibrated testing equipment and imaging techniques. They evaluated contact and finger resistivities using the transfer length method and four-point probe measurements, respectively. Scanning electron microscopy, energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy were used to examine electrode microstructure and contact interfaces.
The team also measured finger geometry, paste viscosity and actual paste consumption to assess printing behavior. Ag and Ni consumption per watt was calculated from measured paste deposition and average cell power, while rear-finger raw-metal costs were estimated using representative metal prices to evaluate the economic benefits of Ni substitution.
The analysis showed that Ni powder characteristics significantly affected the electrical performance and printing behavior of the TOPCon cells. The finer Ni-1500 powder had a higher specific surface area and oxygen content than the coarser Ni-4000 powder, and exhibited greater resistive losses at the same Ni loading.
At 5% Ni loading, the Ni-1500 formulation maintained the baseline efficiency of 26.349%. However, increasing the loading to 10% reduced efficiency by 0.225 percentage points, to 26.124%. By contrast, the formulation containing 10% Ni-4000 achieved an efficiency of 26.325%, just 0.024 percentage points below the baseline.
Electrical measurements revealed higher contact and finger resistivities with the 10% Ni-1500 formulation, while microscopy identified more voids and a less continuous Ag network. Surface analysis also indicated differences in oxide-related contact chemistry between the formulations. Ni substitution increased printed finger widths and paste consumption, particularly at higher loadings.
The researchers found that the 10% Ni-4000 formulation offered the most favorable balance between cost and efficiency, reducing rear-finger raw-metal costs by 6.8%, equivalent to $561,500/GW. Increasing the Ni-4000 loading to 15% maintained a similar efficiency of 26.302%, but increased paste consumption by 17% compared with the Ag-only baseline, reducing cost savings to just 0.3%.
“These findings highlight the need to evaluate Ni substitution through the combined effects of powder characteristics, electrode formation and actual paste consumption,” the researchers stated. “Further optimization should consider the interactions among Ni powder properties, glass-frit chemistry and paste rheology, together with long-term metallization reliability.”
The findings are presented in the study “
Powder-dependent electrical and printing constraints on Ag substitution in Ag-Ni pastes for TOPCon rear metallization
,” published in
Solar Energy Materials and Solar Cells
. The research team included scientists from Chinese physical vapor deposition (PVD) materials manufacturer Shenzhen APG and Australia-based
SunDrive
SunDrive has developed a proprietary copper electroplating technology that replaces silver in solar cell metallization, aiming to reduce manufacturing costs and improve efficiency.
As previously
reported by
pv magazine
the Australian company has partnered with China’s Maxwell Technologies and Jiangsu Vistar Equipment Technology to develop and commercialize industrial-scale direct-copper plating equipment for heterojunction (HJT) solar cells. The company previously demonstrated a 26.41%-efficient HJT solar cell using its copper-based metallization process. More recently, it
secured AUD 25.3 million ($16.5 million) in Australian government funding
to support the development of a 300 MW commercial-scale production tool.
UNSW has also developed several approaches to reducing silver consumption in solar cell metallization. As previously
reported by
pv magazine
, its researchers demonstrated a silver-lean screen-printing technique that reduced rear-side silver consumption in TOPCon cells by 85%, using intermittent silver contacts combined with silver-free fingers and busbars. In a separate
study with Trina Solar
, the university developed silver-free back-contact solar cells using screen-printed aluminum contacts. UNSW has also investigated copper-plated contacts for TOPCon and heterojunction solar cells, focusing on metallization reliability, corrosion resistance and mechanical stability.

title: Haitian Water plans $118 million solar silver paste facility in China - pv magazine Global
content:
Chinese environmental services and photovoltaic materials company Haitian Water Group plans to invest CNY 800 million ($118 million) in a solar conductive silver paste research and manufacturing facility in Sichuan province, as it expands its operations following the
acquisition of Heraeus’ photovoltaic paste business
The Shanghai-listed company said on Oct. 30 that it had signed an investment agreement with the administrative committee of Sichuan Tianfu New Area to establish a materials research and development center and manufacturing headquarters.
The project will involve at least CNY 300 million in fixed-asset investment, financed through internal funds and external financing.
Haitian Water’s wholly owned subsidiary, Sichuan Haitian New Materials, will implement the project. The subsidiary has registered capital of CNY 400 million, while its parent company will assume joint liability for obligations under the agreement.
The project will be developed in two phases. In the first phase, Haitian Water plans to lease approximately 8,000 square meters at Fengqigu Industrial Park to establish an R&D center and pilot production lines for photovoltaic conductive silver paste.
The second phase will involve constructing a larger manufacturing facility on approximately 3.1 hectares of industrial land in Yongxing, Tianfu New Area. The site will house commercial production lines, facilities for manufacturing auxiliary paste materials, warehouses, offices, and an R&D and sales center targeting overseas markets.
The company has not disclosed the planned annual production capacity or a commissioning schedule. Acquisition of the industrial land remains subject to a public tender.
Haitian Water, traditionally focused on water supply, wastewater treatment and other environmental services, entered the photovoltaic materials market in 2025 through the acquisition of Heraeus Group’s photovoltaic silver paste business.
The transaction,
completed in April 2025
, included two Shanghai-based companies and Heraeus Photovoltaics Singapore Pte. Ltd. It provided Haitian Water with established conductive paste production and R&D capabilities, as well as an international customer base.
The acquired operations now form the basis of Haitian Photovoltaics, which maintains manufacturing and R&D operations in China and a technical service presence in Singapore.
The diversification has significantly reshaped Haitian Water’s revenue mix. In the first half of 2026, its new energy and advanced materials business generated CNY 2.11 billion in revenue, accounting for 73.17% of total sales.
The expansion comes as solar cell manufacturers adopt new metallization technologies. Tunnel oxide passivated contact (TOPCon) cells continue to rely heavily on high-temperature silver pastes, while heterojunction (HJT) cells require low-temperature formulations. Growing adoption of back-contact (BC) cell architectures is also driving demand for specialized conductive pastes.
Meanwhile, rising silver prices are accelerating efforts to reduce precious metal consumption. Manufacturers are developing finer-line printing techniques, silver-coated copper pastes and alternative copper metallization processes, including electroplating.
These developments are increasing the importance of paste formulation, electrical contact performance and compatibility with different solar cell manufacturing processes.
However, the project comes amid intense competition and persistent cost pressures across China’s photovoltaic supply chain. Haitian Water said land acquisition, financing, construction and production ramp-up remain subject to uncertainty, while fluctuations in silver prices and changes in metallization technologies could affect the project’s profitability.

title: Aermec presents high-temperature water-to-water heat pumps with up to 889 kW heating capacity - pv magazine Global
content:
Italian heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) manufacturer Aermec has launched two ranges of high-temperature water-to-water heat pumps designed for industrial heating, centralized heating systems and building refurbishment projects.
The HWSG_H series offers heating capacities from approximately 145 kW to 450 kW and can produce hot water at temperatures of up to 80 C. The larger WFGN_H series provides heating capacities ranging from approximately 443 kW to 889 kW, with maximum water outlet temperatures of 85 C, according to the manufacturer.
The HWSG_H units are available with one or two refrigerant circuits, depending on the model. They feature inverter-controlled screw compressors, electronic expansion valves and plate heat exchangers on both the source and heating sides. The dual-circuit configuration is designed to improve operational continuity and performance under partial-load conditions.
The WFGN_H range comprises five dual-compressor models equipped with screw compressors and shell-and-tube heat exchangers. Aermec said the configuration enables greater heating capacity, improved redundancy and more flexible load management.
The WFGN_H heat pumps can operate with either R1234ze refrigerant, classified as A2L with a global warming potential (GWP) below 2, or R515B, an A1 refrigerant with a GWP below 300. The manufacturer noted that the R1234ze configuration requires additional safety measures related to refrigerant leak detection and ventilation. Aermec
Both refrigerant configurations are available with electronic expansion valves and in standard or acoustically enclosed low-noise versions. An optional four-pass condenser is also available for applications requiring higher water temperature differences and lower flow rates.
Aermec said the new heat pumps are particularly suited to industrial processes and the replacement of conventional boilers in existing buildings where high-temperature radiators or other heating terminals are retained.
Aermec has not disclosed the coefficient of performance (COP), seasonal coefficient of performance (SCOP), dimensions, weight or sound levels of the new heat pumps.
For comparison, its previous HWSG series achieved COP values ranging from 4.41 to 4.62 at heating water temperatures of 40 C to 45 C and source water temperatures of 10 C to 7 C. The earlier models also offered SCOP values of 4.53 to 4.73 under average climatic conditions for 55 C heating applications.
Depending on the configuration, the units measured between 2,960 mm and 3,360 mm in length, 810 mm in width, and 1,775 mm to 2,120 mm in height. Their empty weight ranged from 1,101 kg to 3,095 kg for standard versions and from 1,229 kg to 3,352 kg for low-noise variants.
Sound power levels ranged from 86 dB(A) to 95 dB(A) for standard units and from 78 dB(A) to 87 dB(A) for low-noise versions. Corresponding sound pressure levels measured at a distance of 10 meters ranged from 54.2 dB(A) to 63.1 dB(A) and from 46.2 dB(A) to 55.1 dB(A), respectively. According to the manufacturer, the acoustic figures refer to cooling operation, with sound power determined in accordance with UNI EN ISO 9614-2.

title: France deploys 4.18 GW of solar in first nine months of 2026 as residential market contracts - pv magazine Global
content:
French distribution system operator Enedis has published data on new solar PV grid connections in its service area for the third quarter of 2026. According to its open data, 1,271 MW of new PV capacity was connected to the grid between July and September, including 103 MW of installations paired with energy storage. The latter figure compares with 134 MW in the same period of 2025.
Combined with the 1,418 MW connected in the first quarter and 1,494 MW in the second quarter, cumulative additions reached 4,185 MW in the first nine months of 2026, down 3.5% from 4,336 MW in the corresponding period of 2025. For comparison, a record 5.77 GW of solar capacity was connected to the Enedis grid in 2024.
The number of new installations fell more sharply, declining from 148,257 in the first nine months of 2025 to 94,790 in the same period of 2026, a drop of 36.1%.
Although the year-on-year difference in newly connected capacity was limited to 151 MW, a closer look at the data reveals significant shifts across market segments, particularly in small-scale solar, amid changes to France’s regulatory framework.
Solar installations below 36 kW decline by 31.7%
The contraction was most pronounced in the residential and small commercial segments. Newly connected capacity from installations below 36 kW fell from 729 MW in the first nine months of 2025 to 498 MW in the corresponding period of 2026, a decline of 31.7%.
The figures reflect a slowdown that solar installers have reported for several months. Following the announcement of a reduced 5.5% value-added tax (VAT) rate and subsequent cuts to feed-in tariffs, some installers reported a 30% to 50% decline in residential sales between March 2025 and March 2026.
Meanwhile, battery storage adoption continued to gain ground in the small-scale segment. The capacity of PV installations below 36 kW paired with storage rose from 33 MW in the first nine months of 2025 to 88 MW in the same period of 2026.
The growth reflects continued investment in solar PV among commercial and public-sector customers seeking to reduce their exposure to electricity price volatility. Regulatory requirements for solar installations on rooftops and parking lots are also supporting demand.
Enedis operates the electricity distribution network across approximately 95% of mainland France, with the remaining 5% served by local distribution companies.

title: Colombia's PV capacity tops 2.59 GW - pv magazine Global
content:
Colombia’s operational solar capacity reached 2,590.26 MW at the end of September 2026, accounting for 11.7% of the net effective capacity of the National Interconnected System (SIN), according to the latest report from Colombian grid operator XM.
A total of 39 solar projects, with a combined capacity of 607.32 MW, began commercial operations in the third quarter of 2026. Solar accounted for 87% of the new generation capacity added between July and September.
The figures mark a significant increase from the end of 2025, when Colombia had 1,594.08 MW of operational solar capacity, representing 7.6% of the country’s total generation capacity.
In the first nine months of 2026, operational solar capacity increased by 996.18 MW, or 62.5%, while solar’s share of total generation capacity rose by 4.1 percentage points.
Colombia added 42 power generation projects with a combined capacity of 698.2 MW in the third quarter. They included 39 solar projects, two thermal power plants totaling 81 MW, and one small hydropower plant with a capacity of 9.9 MW.
XM said the additions included distributed generation facilities, self-consumption systems, and utility-scale power plants. Three of the utility-scale projects are subject to centralized dispatch.
One of the largest additions was the Puerta de Oro solar plant, which began commercial operations in July. Developed by Patria Investments, the project has an installed capacity of 360 MW.
The plant features more than 511,000 solar modules and is expected to generate more than 700 GWh of electricity annually. It accounted for nearly half of the solar capacity added to Colombia’s electricity system in the third quarter.
The SIN’s total net effective capacity reached 22,196.2 MW at the end of September. Hydropower remained the largest generation source, with 13,229.16 MW, followed by thermal power at 6,376.62 MW and solar at 2,590.26 MW.
XM said 128 power generation projects across various technologies began commercial operations between January and September, adding a combined 1,038.85 MW.
The grid operator also identified 140 generation projects undergoing initial testing as of Sept. 30, with a combined capacity of 1,147.97 MW.
Solar accounted for 133 of those projects, totaling 1,083.6 MW, or 94.4% of the capacity undergoing testing. The remaining projects included three wind farms totaling 41 MW, three thermal power plants with a combined capacity of 12.9 MW, and one hydropower plant with a capacity of 10.5 MW.
All projects must complete the required technical and regulatory procedures before entering commercial operation.
At the end of December 2025, 98 solar projects with a combined capacity of 1,365.6 MW were undergoing testing. By September 2026, the number of projects had increased by 35.7%, while their combined capacity had fallen by 20.6%.
The figures point to a shift toward a larger number of smaller solar projects in the testing phase, alongside continued growth in operational capacity. However, XM’s published data do not specify how many individual projects completed testing and entered commercial operation during the nine-month period.

title: Chinese scientists develop self-powered PV-TEG system for hotspot detection, thermal management - pv magazine Global
content:
A research team led by scientists at China’s
Southeast University
has developed a self-powered photovoltaic-thermoelectric generator (PV-TEG) system that integrates hotspot detection, local thermal management, and wireless monitoring into a TEG array.
Thermoelectric generators (TEGs) convert heat into electricity through the Seebeck effect, which occurs when a temperature difference between two dissimilar semiconductors generates a voltage. TEGs are commonly used in industrial applications to recover waste heat and convert it into electricity. However, their high costs and limited efficiency have so far restricted their wider adoption.
In PV-TEG systems, PV panels generate electricity during the day, while TEGs harness temperature differences to produce additional electricity.
“The key innovation of our research is that we go beyond the conventional role of TEGs as waste-heat harvesters,” corresponding author Jingming Cai told
pv magazine
. “We demonstrate that the electrical signals generated by these devices can also reveal where thermal anomalies occur within a PV module.”
Cai said that by integrating four TEGs into a compact array, the researchers developed a system that combines hotspot localization, passive thermal management, energy harvesting, and wireless monitoring. “Essentially, we are turning the waste heat of solar panels into a source of both energy and diagnostic information,” he said.
The researchers first developed a three-dimensional multiphysics model of a 500 mm × 500 mm PV region equipped with four rear-mounted TEGs and an aluminum heat sink. The model coupled heat transfer and thermoelectric conversion under baseline conditions of 1,000 W/m2 irradiance and an ambient temperature of 25 C.
The team placed a 20 mm × 20 mm heat source at nine positions and mapped normalized TEG voltage changes to hotspot coordinates. It then evaluated localization accuracy at three additional positions, compared cooling performance with that of a bare PV module, and assessed sensitivity to environmental conditions and thermal contact resistance.
“Multiphysics simulations clarified the coupling among hotspot position, thermoelectric voltage response, and local cooling,” the researchers said. “Distinct hotspot locations generated differentiated four-channel voltage patterns, enabling quantitative mapping from normalized voltage responses to two-dimensional coordinates. The simulated local temperature reduction ranged from 8.15 K to 12.40 K.”
The researchers then conducted outdoor tests in Taizhou, eastern China, installing the PV-TEG system on a rooftop array at a telecommunications facility. They monitored TEG temperatures, supercapacitor voltage, and wireless transmission events from approximately 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. The monitoring electronics activated when the capacitor voltage reached 4.0 V and switched off at 2.8 V to allow recharging.
The team used infrared imaging to compare local point temperatures and regional average temperatures with those of a reference PV region. To evaluate hotspot localization, the researchers applied black tape at three positions to create controlled thermal disturbances, measured the voltage responses of the four TEGs, and reconstructed the anomaly coordinates. They tested each position three times, using infrared imaging to verify the location and temperature of each anomaly.
“What surprised us most was how accurately a small array of just four thermoelectric generators could identify the location of a thermal anomaly,” Cai said. “In our outdoor experiment, we achieved a localization error of approximately 9.93 mm. Meanwhile, the integrated system reduced the local PV surface temperature by up to 7.7 C at the measured point, with an average reduction of 5.4 C across the monitored region.”
Cai said another encouraging result was that the system could operate without an external power supply for the monitoring electronics, completing approximately 45 wireless transmissions during a 10-hour daytime field test. “These findings suggest that even relatively small amounts of photovoltaic waste heat can be valuable when converted into sensing capabilities rather than simply additional electricity,” he said.
Cai said the team now plans to investigate how the system performs under electrically induced PV hotspots and more complex outdoor operating conditions. “Our long-term vision is to make solar panels capable of monitoring their own thermal health, identifying potential faults at an early stage, and reducing the need for energy-intensive monitoring infrastructure,” he concluded.
The researchers described the system in “
A self-powered PV-TEG system for integrated hotspot monitoring and local thermal management based on thermoelectric voltage response
,” which was recently published in
Applied Thermal Engineering
. Scientists from China’s Southeast University and Australia’s University of Technology Sydney contributed to the study.

title: China’s Mengxi grid tops 20 GW of storage as renewables approach 60% of capacity - pv magazine Global
content:
China’s western Inner Mongolia power grid has surpassed 20 GW of operational new-type energy storage capacity, as rapid growth in wind and solar generation increases the need for flexible electricity resources.
According to data released by Inner Mongolia Power Group on October 28, the grid had 20.23 GW/70.47 GWh of operational storage capacity as of October 27, accounting for 11.5% of its total installed power capacity. The figures imply an average nominal storage duration of approximately 3.5 hours.
New installations reached 6.555 GW during the first ten months of 2026, up 47.9% year on year, supported by the commissioning of several large independent storage projects, including facilities in Wuchuan and Baotou.
The western Inner Mongolia grid, also known as the Mengxi grid, is operated by Inner Mongolia Power Group and serves eight prefecture-level areas in central and western Inner Mongolia. It operates separately from the eastern Inner Mongolia grid, which is managed by State Grid.
Wind and solar power account for nearly 60% of the Mengxi grid’s installed generation capacity, making the region an important test case for operating power systems with high renewable penetration.
On October 22, renewable generation on the grid reached a record 720 GWh, representing 60.2% of total electricity generation that day. Wind power contributed 560 GWh, also setting a daily record.
The increasing role of energy storage is reflected in operational data. According to the grid operator, cumulative charging and discharging volumes reached 15.78 TWh and 14.04 TWh, respectively, by October 27, with both increasing by more than 400% year on year.
Storage has also become an important resource for emergency power supply. During the first ten months, the grid conducted 95 emergency storage dispatch operations. The maximum reported power contribution reached 12.25 GW, equivalent to 33% of the grid’s electricity load at the time.
To coordinate these operations, Inner Mongolia Power Group has connected 126 storage stations to a centralized intelligent monitoring platform, enabling operators to monitor and control facilities across the grid.
The operator said it has adopted a dispatch approach combining market-based optimization with centralized emergency interventions. Under normal conditions, electricity market mechanisms guide charging and discharging decisions, while grid operators can call on storage resources when supply shortages arise.
This approach reflects an obvious shift in China’s storage sector, as independent and market-participating facilities increasingly complement batteries installed alongside individual renewable energy projects.
Inner Mongolia Power Group is planning to advance six self-invested storage projects, including developments at Chunkunshan, Hanhai and Erzihao, while supporting grid connections for nearly 10 GW of new storage capacity during 2026. The rapid expansion highlights the growing importance of large-scale storage in China’s renewable-rich regions.

title: 科学网-卸任辽宁大学党委书记后，潘一山院士加盟东北大学
content:
卸任辽宁大学党委书记后，潘一山院士加盟东北大学
近日，东北大学官网“院士风采”栏目更新信息，中国工程院院士潘一山位列其中。
这也意味着，曾任辽宁大学党委书记的潘一山已赴东北大学任职。
公开资料显示，潘一山，1964年5月生，辽宁东港人，教授，博士生导师，系国家级人才项目领军人才、“新世纪百千万人才工程”国家级人选，于2023年当选中国工程院院士。
潘一山曾任辽宁工程技术大学党委书记，辽宁大学党委副书记、校长等职，于2022年任辽宁大学党委书记。
2026年7月，辽宁大学官网更新后显示，原任辽宁大学党委常委、副校长的仇焕广已接替潘一山担任校党委书记职务。
据东北大学官网介绍，潘一山主要从事岩土灾害力学及露天矿开采等研究工作，在冲击地压发生机理、预测防治技术以及巷道防冲支护等方面做出了突出贡献。他建立了冲击地压扰动响应失稳理论，研发了煤岩微震、电荷监测及吸能支架等预测防治成套技术装备，解决了冲击地压矿井安全开采的重大技术难题。
潘一山主持和完成国家自然科学基金国家重大科研仪器研制项目、国家自然科学基金-辽宁联合基金重点项目等国家级重大、重点项目10余项；以第一或通讯作者发表SCI/EI学术论文110余篇，出版专著3部，获授权中国和美国发明专利60余件，制定并发布6项相关国家技术标准；以第一完成人获国家科技进步二等奖3项、省部级科技进步奖一等奖3项。
他曾获全国优秀科技工作者、第二届全国创新争先奖、第14届光华工程科技奖、第三十一届孙越崎能源大奖等荣誉，第一完成人获国家教学成果二等奖2项。此外，潘一山还担任国家安全生产专家组矿压与顶板组组长、辽宁省科协副主席、国际杂志《Geohazard Mechanics》主编、煤矿冲击地压机理与防控技术国家矿山安全监察局重点实验室主任。
东北大学始建于1923年4月，张学良曾于1928年8月至1937年1月兼任校长。1931年“九·一八”事变后被迫流亡办学，先后辗转于北平、西安、开封、四川三台等地。1949年3月，在东北大学工学院和理学院（部分）的基础上成立沈阳工学院。1950年8月，定名为东北工学院，1993年3月，复名为东北大学。1997年1月，原沈阳黄金学院并入东北大学。1998年9月划转为教育部直属高校，是国家首批“211工程”、“985工程”重点建设高校，2017年入选国家首轮世界一流大学建设高校，2022年入选国家第二轮“双一流”建设高校。

title: 科学网-基金委化学科学部完成2026年度专项项目评审
content:
基金委化学科学部完成2026年度专项项目评审
2026年10月15日，自然科学基金委化学科学部在北京召开“化工视角下的免疫治疗增效过程与机制”与“高性能有机热电材料的分子基础”专项项目评审会议。自然科学基金委副主任吴骊珠出席会议并讲话，化学科学部常务副主任杨俊林主持开幕式。
吴骊珠指出，当前新一轮科技革命和产业变革深入发展，科学研究范式加速变革，学科交叉融合不断深化，基础研究成为决定国家科技竞争力和长远发展能力的关键。专项项目是科学基金资助体系的重要组成部分，在支持基础研究创新发展中发挥着重要作用。化学科学部瞄准国家战略需求，及时发掘创新性强、发展潜力突出的科学前沿方向，立足化学化工学科优势，瞄准生命健康与先进能源材料两大前沿领域，本年度布局“化工视角下的免疫治疗增效过程与机制”和“高性能有机热电材料的分子基础”两项专项项目，旨在创新化学化工方法，破解领域瓶颈，推动学科交叉互融、双向赋能，为实现高水平科技自立自强、加快建设科技强国提供基础研究支撑。希望各位评审专家秉持严谨治学态度，充分发挥学术判断力，遴选出能够集中力量、协同攻关的高水平研究队伍。
杨俊林分别介绍两个专项项目的立项背景、申请概况与资助计划，明确评审工作要求。他提出，评审专家要严格把握项目指南定位，坚守科学性与公正性，择优遴选高质量项目。
专家组认真听取各项目申请人汇报，开展质询与充分讨论，经集体投票，顺利完成本次会议的评审任务。自然科学基金委化学科学部及相关部门工作人员参加会议。
